News.title: Andy Burnham’s vow to deliver ‘hope’ will be utterly meaningless if a lurch to the Left plunges us all into recession
News.content:
PM’s gilt trip

ANDY Burnham’s first proper day as Prime Minister brought less-than-fond memories of Labour U-turns past, a worrying grasp of the present — and a nightmare vision for the future.

Before the new PM even got a chance to address MPs for the first time since seizing power, the victim of his leadership coup had delivered one more signature reverse ferret.



Sir Keir Starmer, who pledged only weeks ago to stay on as an MP, announced he was quitting for good.

His unwelcome parting gift leaves Burnham facing a by-election headache against Zack Polanski’s Greens.



But far worse for voters was the markets’ reaction to Burnham’s economic fantasy of wielding more Socialist state control to bring down the cost of living.

A global debt sell-off had already sparked a frenzy among bond traders.

But spooked by Britain’s unsustainable debt — fuelled by ballooning welfare payments — they delivered a uniquely bad punishment beating to us.

It sent the cost of Government borrowing to 5.89 per cent, the highest since 1998 and way beyond the rates which led Liz Truss to resign after her 2022 mini-Budget shambles.

That blows a hole in Chancellor John Healey’s Budget plans — including urgent demands for more defence cash.

It is madness — as the threat of a debt-fuelled global financial crisis grows by the day — for Burnham’s only answer to be MORE borrowing to fund MORE out-of-control spending.



His words yesterday about delivering “hope” will be rendered utterly meaningless if a lurch to the Left plunges us all into recession.

Chagos chaos

IN a staggering decision slipped out, the Government confirmed the PM plans to resurrect Keir Starmer’s insane plan to give away the Chagos Islands.

Billions will be paid to Mauritius for the privilege of losing a key strategic territory — and all the cash will come from the already hopelessly inadequate defence budget.

Donald Trump’s ire over Starmer’s craven surrender of the islands led to the plans being halted earlier this year.

But it is crazy for Burnham to once again infuriate our US allies and wantonly damage UK security in the process.



Cry Freeview

FREE to air TV is a vital lifeline for the elderly and poorer households who cannot afford costly broadband and subscriptions.

It also remains a key security tool for Government information in the event of a catastrophic internet outage.

That’s why ministers must listen to MPs from all sides demanding a planned switch-off in 2034 is delayed.

News.title: Andy Burnham’s holiday romance is over and he’s already dumping entire ice baths on his promises
News.content:
SO, it seems Britain’s new boyfriend now just wants to be friends.

Suited and booted in a tie so hideous it could only have been a gift, there was a whiff of screeching rubber in the air as Andy Burnham finally made it to the House of Commons.



And what a difference six weeks makes.

Free from the constraints of any proper scrutiny, Burnham’s summer lovin’ tour was all things to all people.



That charming lad with the pretty eyelashes promised us all the world if we just trusted him.

Those baddies Thames Water? They “should be” nationalised.

The evil tax trap that drags millions more into income tax? That should be raised.

Defence spending? Hike it! Social Care: Fix it first! Crippling energy bills? Slash ’em!

We were promised a new era of hope, optimism and, above all, a government that could speak to ordinary people.

Yet suddenly, the fluffy TikToks about crisps, singalongs to The Smiths and all those sweet nothings felt like distant memories.



As autumn approaches, that nice boy Andy, who was so chatty when trying to get into our knickers, now says “it’s complicated”.

He says he was going to “do politics differently”, yet suddenly the new guy sounded a lot like the old guy.

“Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be,” said our newly po-faced PM. “Things are not working as they should.”

Apparently, “life is too expensive and too hard for too many” after Brexit ruined the country, and everything is seemingly, well . . . just a bit too tricky.



Holiday romance Andy said if we let him in, he would slip us “the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years”.

Instead, at Tuesday’s back to school reality check, he wasn’t so much pouring cold water on his promises, but dumping an entire ice bath on them.

Defence hikes? They will have to wait for not just November’s Budget, but the multi-year public spending review next year.

Let’s just hope the Russians aren’t banging on the doors of the Baltics by then.



Thames Water nationalisation? That’s just an option now after a beancounter with a big red pen must have explained the notoriously complex and dangerous idea of taking billions of debt on to the public books to him very slowly.

Flashy promises of electoral reform? Kicked into the next Parliament.

Social care fixed? Well, far from being top of the list, that’s now relegated to something Burnham “won’t leave office” without looking at.

It seems that the revolution will have to wait until stakeholders have been engaged, pens have been pushed and Labour MPs have clucked a little more.

Instead, we were treated to his big new solution to Britain’s woes: “A triple helix approach to economic development”.



So much for the straight-talking, brilliant new communicator.

What is it about this job that means politicians enter the black door of No10 and re-emerge regenerated, Stars In Their Eyes-style, spouting meaningless drivel and incomprehensible buzzwords?

Burnham had the cheek to say his Commons statement yesterday set out a “clear, coherent and credible path to growth”.



I must have blinked and missed that bit of the speech.

Of course, this was always going to be much harder than simply a change of tone and frontman. But frankly, Britain does not have time for Burnham to be learning on the job.

He was in a hurry to seal the deal and get into office, despite having watched what had happened to his predecessor who seized power without a proper plan.

But the summer is over now Prime Minister, and the storm clouds are gathering.

On Burnham’s first proper day in the job, UK borrowing costs saw their biggest one day jump in months, pushing ten-year loans to their highest price since the crash.



Liz Truss got decked when those costs hit 4.5 per cent for a few weeks in 2022.

When Labour came to power they were bumping around four per cent. Yesterday they hit 5.23.

Yes, there is global bond market carnage but once again, Britain is in the worst possible position to weather instability.

Decisions on spending and borrowing are having a direct impact on confidence in our country.

When it comes to 25-year UK government bond rates, they’re at their highest rate in nearly 30 years.



Interest rate hikes can only be a matter of time, and any headroom Burnham may have hoped for in the Budget has evaporated.

It’s hardly surprising that he was looking and sounding downbeat yesterday . . . winter is coming.

Starmer steals the thunder

FOR Sir Keir Starmer, revenge was a dish served GREEN.

Word is the ex-PM did not even bother tipping off No10 he was resigning his seat in the Commons – on the day the man who knifed him had his first big day at the office.



You could see what Burnham’s big electoral strategy was going to be . . .

Bash Brexit, hype up climate change, keep away from Trump and go hard after our ally Israel – all in a desperate bid to unite the Left and lure back some LibDem voters.

Bleeding voters to the Greens, his paint-by-numbers approach to foreign policy, so far, has been far from subtle.

And it was showing signs of life, as Zack Polanski’s party slumped and Burnham got a moderate bounce in the polls.

All while the Right remains hopelessly divided as Reform and the Tories battle for supremacy.



Inevitably, the early election chatter has simply refused to die: Burnham would be mad not take advantage of this electorally lucrative battle ground.

But now Sir Keir has thrown a mega spanner in the works.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Triggering a by-election in his lefty North London seat, dominated by graduates and ethnic minorities, he’s handed Wacko Zacko a major shot at entering Parliament and upending Burnham’s entire strategy with a Green resurgence.

You’d have to have a heart of stone not to laugh . . .

News.title: Sweating PM blames Brexit and Mrs Thatcher for Britain’s woes before failing to rule out even more tax hikes
News.content:
ANDY Burnham yesterday tried to blame Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for Britain’s woes — as he failed to rule out soaking the country with more tax hikes.

The new PM used his first Commons speech in the job to warn that “Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be”.



He singled out “a series of wrong turns in the 1980s” as well as the decision to leave the European Union as the reason for a lack of UK growth — rather than the record taxes Labour has imposed.

Mr Burnham faced MPs for the first time since entering No 10 six weeks ago and embarking on a summer tour announcing relatively small cost-of-living giveaways.



Ahead of his marathon three-hour grilling by MPs yesterday, the Labour leader was seen working up a sweat during his morning run.

The PM will feel the heat even more, as long-term government borrowing costs rose to their highest level since 1998.

At the dispatch box for the first time in 16 years, Mr Burnham said: “Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should. Life is too expensive and too hard for too many.”

The ex-Manchester Mayor said his decade away from Westminster had given him a “clear diagnosis” of the source of the UK’s troubles.

The Prime Minister took aim at the legacy of former PM Mrs Thatcher and her programme of privatisation, as well as pulling out of the EU.

He said: “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.”



He added: “Then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain.

“For 40 years, too many places have been drifting.”

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch attacked Mr Burnham for living in the past when he should be focused on the future.



She hit back: “The year is 2026, yet the Prime Minister said in his statement that everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. I may not look it, but I’m 46 years old. He is talking about a woman who became Prime Minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.

“On this side of the House, we are for the future, not the past. That is the difference between them and us. His ideas are all about more government control, more spending, more tax, more politicians.”

She blamed the £70billion of tax rises under this Labour Government for failing to propel Britain out of the economic doldrums.

Mr Burnham is facing harsh economic realities as PM. Yesterday saw the yield on 30-year gilts — a loan to the Government — rise to 5.89 per cent, the highest since 1998.

And the yield on benchmark ten-year gilts rose to 5.223 per cent — the highest since the 2008 financial crash, eclipsing even Liz Truss’s mini-Budget.



Debt is already on the brink of hitting £3trillion and taxpayers are on the hook for £100billion every year, just to pay off the interest on that pile.

The PM yesterday repeatedly refused to rule out tax rises in the October 28 Budget to pay for increased spending.

Ms Badenoch instead challenged him to cut Britain’s ballooning welfare bill, asking whether he would “stand up to his backbenchers in a way that his predecessor (Sir Keir Starmer) never could”.

Mr Burnham insisted he was committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but said it would not be done through “crude cuts”.



He said the answer was better support, particularly for young people who had been “let down” by the education system.

The Prime Minister was also pressed on defence, after refusing to commit to spending three per cent of GDP on it by 2030.

Mr Burnham said Chancellor John Healey would set out the path at the Spending Review.

He said: “This is a changing and challenging world in which we live.



“But can I say very directly, I appointed this Chancellor precisely because of his commitment to the defence of our realm and the arguments he has made.

“He will set out at the Spending Review the path to honouring our international commitments in full, as I said we would when I was before the steps of Downing Street.”

Mr Burnham put his programme for public control of industries at the heart of his address, taking aim at the water industry specifically as a “leaking monument” to a failed economic approach.

On migration, the PM confirmed he and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood would continue looking at return hubs and insisted that co-operation with France was making “significant progress”.

Mr Burnham is due to welcome French President Emmanuel Macron in Downing Street today, with tackling small boat Channel crossings on the agenda.



He also vowed to bring in new laws over the coming months to overhaul the “unfair” leasehold system, including plans to ban leasehold on most new flats and give homeowners more control over their buildings.

He also opened the door to including a change to a proportional representation voting system in Labour’s next manifesto.

Mr Burnham gathered his Cabinet, including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, for just the second time yesterday as MPs returned from their summer breaks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The PM last night pledged to save Jodrell Bank observatory after a backlash over it being defunded.

He told MPs that there “must be a way to save” the Cheshire site, which includes radio telescopes which helped to track the first moon landing.

News.title: British Airways cabin boss guilty of sexually assaulting sleeping air hostess who called him her ‘work husband’
News.content:
CABIN CREEP British Airways cabin boss guilty of sexually assaulting sleeping air hostess who called him her ‘work husband’

A BRITISH Airways cabin boss has been found guilty of preying on a sleeping air hostess after downing beer and wine at his home.

Amardip “Amo” Dhariwal, 55, assaulted the female colleague after boozing with her over dinner.



The ex-lead flight manager was on trial for a single attack on one woman in 2022 — but a jury also heard from two other stewardesses who alleged he raped them on foreign trips.

Dhariwal earlier denied but was convicted of one count of sexual assault by penetration on Tuesday after a two-week trial.



He could face years in jail according to sentencing guidelines.

One British Airways stewardess told The Sun that “dozens of BA crew have been praying for this outcome”.

“This guy was a brute of a boss. The worst kind of manager bully. A proper old school sex pest. Amo was a disgusting creep,” she said.

Reading Crown Court heard he invited the woman to his then-home in Bracknell, Berkshire, for dinner, where they drank beer and wine.



The woman, then engaged and now married, said she dozed off as they watched a film and woke to find Dhariwal touching her intimately.

Prosecutor James Partridge had told jurors: “They met three months prior to the incident on a flight to Cape Town.

“They got on so well that they met for coffee a few times. She went to his house for taco and movie nights.”

She even referred to Dhariwal as her “work husband”.

Mr Partridge added: “They started watching a film. As they watched it, the victim said she had her legs up.



“She awoke to the defendant touching her.”

He said the woman “felt bewildered” and escaped by finding a key while he was upstairs and called a friend “crying and whispering” on the phone.

Dhariwal, now of Southall, West London, told cops: “Anything that happened was consensual.”

The jury was told Dhariwal allegedly raped a colleague in a Singapore hotel room in 2020.

She woke naked in his bed, confused by how she got there, she said.



Local police investigated but took no further action and would not help British cops, it was said.

The other stewardess claimed she was assaulted while asleep and drunk in a hotel room in Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur in 2018.

Dhariwal denied those allegations.

He was handed conditional bail and will be sentenced at the same court on October 19 this year.

The BA air stewardess added: “The brave BA women who came forward and helped get Amo convicted deserve a medal.



“They have saved many other women from being attacked by this depraved individual.”

She claimed he would “target inexperienced BA woman” younger than his daughter and that he “turned into a predator” after splitting with his wife years earlier.

She said “his disgusting behaviour would start on the plane itself”, adding: “Down-route, his tactic was to ply girls with drinks during wild nights out betwen flights, so he could later try and take them back to his room.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“At the end of the boozy night, he would target individual women and say, ‘I’ve got Baileys in my room, come and have a night-cap with me’. And then inside his room he’d claim everything was consensual.

“He was notorious. He had a reputation and women would warn each other about him. You never wanted to be alone with him, even in a public space.”

News.title: Female British tourist, 34, ‘stabbed to death in hotel corridor’ at Portugal holiday hotspot as man, also 34, arrested
News.content:
HOTEL HORROR Female British tourist, 34, ‘stabbed to death in hotel corridor’ at Portugal holiday hotspot as man, also 34, arrested

A BRITISH woman has been stabbed to death in a luxury Portugese hotel as cops arrest a fellow Brit on suspicion of her murder.

The man allegedly knifed the tourist, 34, multiple times in the coastal city of Albufeira – with one local report saying she was killed in front of her child.



Emergency services raced to the Alfagar Alto Da Colina hotel after the alarm was raised at 6:45pm on Tuesday.

The luxury resort is described online as having “striking sea views” and being “within walking distance to the beach”.



Local reports say the woman had been staying there with her partner and her child.

Paramedics said the woman was already dead when they arrived at the scene.

They said she had “multiple knife wounds” after being attacked in a hotel corrdior, adding that there was nothing they could do to save her.

The suspected killer, 34, has been arrested and is being held in custody, cops confirmed.

Portugal national police force and the seperate Policia Judiciaria have launched a probe into the horror killing.

News.title: Man in his 50s ‘spiked and sexually assaulted by woman in her 30s before she robbed him’ at bus stop
News.content:
'ASSAULT' PROBE Man in his 50s ‘spiked and sexually assaulted by woman in her 30s before she robbed him’ at bus stop

A MAN was allegedly spiked and sexually assaulted by a woman before she robbed him at a bus stop.

Police said the victim, a man in his 50s, was approached by the woman at a bus shelter under Spa Bridge in Scarborough, North Yorkshire, last month.

The woman, believed to be in her 30s, is said to have struck up conversation and offered him a drink which he reluctantly accepted.



But the man then lost consciousness before he was sexually assaulted.



North Yorkshire Police said the victim’s cash and belongings were stolen, including some artwork he was carrying.

The force said that following the incident, it’s believed a member of the public approached the victim at the bus shelter to check on him.

It is not exactly known when the shocking incident took place other than between Monday August 10 and Wednesday August 26.



The suspect is described as a woman in her 30s wearing heavy makeup with red streaks in her hair.

She was wearing a long, black skirt and a black top with white markings on the sleeves.

A spokesperson for the force said: “We are appealing for that person to come forward along with anyone else who may have come to the assistance of a man who may have appeared disorientated.

“We’re also appealing to anyone who may have found a discarded wallet or artwork consisting of black and white pencil-drawn landscape scenes to get in touch.



Anyone with information is urged to come forward to the police.

News.title: Labour’s promise to ‘tread lightly’ on our lives in tatters as they plot ‘mansion’ tax on en-suites or nice views
News.content:
WHEN Labour came to power just over two years ago (it feels like 12 already) Sir Keir Starmer promised to “tread more lightly on your lives”.

Yet now it seems that government-funded “inspectors” will be authorised to enter our homes and have a good snoop around for signs of possible “mansion owner” status.





This includes a nice view, a pool, a double garage, stables etc, as well as more than one bathroom.

And if we tell them to stick their ID badge where the sun don’t shine and get off our front porch, it will be classed as a criminal offence and punishable by a fine of up to £200.

It’s treading lightly Stasi-style.

And if all this sounds like a bad joke, you won’t be laughing when you learn that it’s already laid out in an HMRC tax manual obtained under freedom of information laws.

So if you have a conservatory or, God help you, an en suite so you don’t have to share with the kids, you’re going to have to develop Nicola “what Winnebago” Sturgeon levels of denial to avoid being taxed on the house you bought and renovated with money you’d already paid tax on.

Meanwhile, whatever you do, don’t try to make your neighbourhood look a little nicer or you also might find yourself ­feeling the, ahem, light tread of the state too.

Katharine Hoskyns, 89, placed a row of pretty plant pots and a bench along her outer wall in London’s St John’s Wood over 25 years ago and it became a local oasis for neighbours to admire.

But now Westminster City Council have ordered her to remove them after a “series of complaints from residents” who claim the site is attracting “antisocial behaviour”.





Ms Hoskyns says there’s just one neighbour who doesn’t like it (there’s always one) and has now garnered 190 signatures from locals who would like to keep it.

So watch this space. But meanwhile, the pavements of London and many other cities are littered with discarded e-bike rentals, chewing gum, dog mess, overflowing bins and other unsightly scourges that councils appear to ignore.

And don’t get us started on the traveller sites that always seem to spring up on a bank holiday weekend when councils are having a few days off from their, er, arduous schedule.

Once the tarmac is laid and the caravans are in place, it can take months, sometimes years, for locals to see any action from planners who are quick to harangue the rest of us about, say, a hedge overhanging the pavement.

So a round of applause to the villagers near Sawbridgeworth, Herts who, together with their local council and the police, managed to thwart the first phase of a potential travellers’ site in what’s being described as The Battle of Sheering Mill Lane.

Hoorah! At last, a victory for common sense.

Mind you, the land is a “wetland habitat” so there’s every chance the High Court injunction that temporarily blocked the travellers was served on behalf of an endangered animal rather than the poor human creatures that live nearby.

But still, this is the kind of “treading lightly” we can get behind.



PRISON laundry rooms are to be turned into cells to try to alleviate overcrowding.

Alternatively, why not fit all cells with a washing machine and make doing the laundry part of the occupant’s punishment?

As a policy, it’s no less daft.

Former Cabinet minister Jonathan Aitken, who once did a jail term himself for perjury and now works as a prison chaplain, says part of the problem is the “recall prisoners” who are back behind bars for non-criminal breaches of probation rules.

Astonishingly, in London’s HMP Pentonville where he preaches, there are more probation recalls (for missed appointments, curfew breaches etc) than actual sentenced prisoners. ­Madness.

He suggests that penalties other than re-imprisonment would free up much-needed space for those who really should be behind bars.

Well it sure beats the current policy of releasing violent criminals early.

Trickle back in the flow lane

THE original Days Of Thunder in 1990 was one of those films you went to see with your boyfriend because he liked fast cars.



I remember very little about it – except that then heart-throb Tom Cruise’s character was called Cole Trickle, which struck me as curiously unsexy.

And now DOT2 is in production and Tom/Mr Trickle is in his sixties, it takes on a whole new meaning.

BOYS’ LOSS IS SO SAD

STEPPING out with their dad’s favourite team Manchester United should have been the happiest day of their lives for two young mascots at the weekend.

Except their dad was PC Matthew Blades, 37, killed with his colleague Tom Clough when their police car was hit head-on by five youths driving the wrong way down the A66 in Middlesbrough.

His sons’ names and ages haven’t been released, but the oldest is possibly around seven or eight.

And despite his youth and the general excitement of the occasion, his sad, distracted expression tells you that he already knows his life has been changed for ever by the selfish stupidity of others.

TAX ON SCHOOL SHAME

ENERGY Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has defended the decision to send all three of her children to a private school.



She has also doubled down on her support for Labour’s policy to scrap the VAT exemption on private school fees – a move that has forced several independent schools to close after a drop in pupils.

She says it’s “the right thing for the state to decide that we’re not going to cross-subsidise parents that do make that choice to send their children to independent schools and we’re going to put that money into the state sector where the majority of kids go. That is the right policy”.

But surely, those parents are actually cross-subsidising the Government because they’re paying for state school places via their taxes yet choosing not to use them?

So it’s a shameful tax on education, plain and simple.

TATES’ WORLD A JOKE

AS if their former PA saying they were both “nice” wasn’t bad enough, the Tate brothers have seen a further unravelling of their supposed “tough guy” image.

Fighting extradition to the UK on sex charges, their lawyers have now argued that Andrew and Tristan aren’t as wealthy as everyone seems to think.

Apparently, the $50million superyacht they were reported to have bought with cryptocurrency belonged to someone else and they were merely being paid to advertise it.

Likewise, the flashy cars were all leased, and the multiple passports they flashed online were actually cardboard props.

The lawyers have mitigated that it was all just a marketing ploy to try to sell their online “get rich quick” courses to fans in the “manosphere”.



It seems that the castle these guys claimed to be king of was actually made from sand.

So perhaps it won’t be sex charges that facilitate their long overdue downfall . . . it will simply be ridicule.

VICTIMS want the general data on migrant crime to be made public, but the Government is refusing to do so.

Which perhaps tells you all you need to know.

If it was noticeably low, they’d be singing it from the rooftops of Westminster.

DROP IT HARRY

MEGHAN and Harry are reportedly worried about security on their forthcoming school run in the UK.

They shouldn’t fret.

I was speaking to someone at the weekend whose children attend the same school as Princess Beatrice’s daughter, who is nearly five.

And apparently, the late Queen’s granddaughter drops off and picks up without fear, fuss or favour.

So the late Queen’s grandson, his wife and their five-year-old can low-key do the same.

News.title: Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power.

The prime minister said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised and pointed to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".

He reiterated his belief that political power had been centralised and announced he would be making devolution powers available to more areas in England.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong, his theory of growth is completely wrong, he thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said.

Badenoch also warned the prime minister that his new job would be "very different" to his previous Greater Manchester mayoral role where he "did not have to make difficult trade-offs".

Burnham became prime minister on 20 July shortly after Parliament closed for the summer recess.

Tuesday marked the first day of the new parliamentary session and provided his first opportunity to address MPs and take questions.

He told the House of Commons that "Britain is not where we would wish it to be", but promised to "build a new sense of optimism around the country".

Following his 10 years away from Parliament, Burnham said he was returning with a "clear diagnosis" of what had gone wrong in the country.

"From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns," he said.

"Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.

"And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."

In the months before becoming prime minister, Burnham stopped short of calling for full nationalisation but said he wanted to see greater public control of water and energy.

On Tuesday, he promised that a plan to achieve this would be produced "later in the year".

Pressed on his plans for the water sector by Conservative MP Alison Griffiths, Burnham said it was important to "look at all possible solutions".

"It's a very regrettable situation that the privatisation of water has left us in a position where we're going to find it very difficult to reverse," he added.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt â a loan to the British government â rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, will be "fiscal responsibility".

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor Rachel Reeves that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

Burnham was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

News.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
News.content:
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament.

"He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added.

"His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."

Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

News.title: Baby girl who died at Sheffield house was stabbed, police say
News.content:
A newborn baby girl who was discovered fatally injured at a house in Sheffield died as a result of stab wounds, police have said.

The baby was found at a house on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area on Sunday morning, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.

South Yorkshire Police said despite the best efforts of police and paramedics, the baby died at the scene.

Seven people aged between 15 and 37 were arrested on suspicion of her murder. Two of them, aged 26 and 37, were later bailed, but police confirmed on Tuesday a warrant had been obtained to extend time in custody for the remaining five as inquiries continued.

Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward, leading the investigation, said: "We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident.

"Everyone involved in responding to this tragedy - from the first officers and paramedics on the scene to the detectives now leading the investigation - has felt the profound impact of this investigation."

He added: "Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering. We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.

"We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation."

A South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said officers were continuing their investigations in the Holywell Heights area and asked anyone with information that might be useful to contact them.

News.title: Watch: Norway's new king takes oath as mourners pay respects to his late father
News.content:
Norway's Haakon VIII has sworn an oath before parliament in Oslo in the first major step of his reign as King.

During Tuesday's ceremony, parliament also held a minute's silence for Haakon's father, the late King Harald V, who died on Friday.

Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant.

Following the ceremony, mourners began paying their respects at the late King's coffin, which is lying in state at the Royal Palace until 8 September.

News.title: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
News.content:
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of settlements in the West Bank.

Addressing Parliament for the first time as foreign secretary, Ed Miliband said he would introduce a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel "in the coming weeks".

He said the government would examine how to stop UK companies "financing, constructing or advertising new settlements" in the occupied West Bank.

Responding, Gideon Saar told Hebrew-language news website Ynet: "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain."

"If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake," he said.

Last month, Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Miliband said the plans are "illegal under international law" and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's statement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.

All settlements are illegal under international law and, under global pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in the area.

News.title: Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
News.content:
Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects.

But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not.

He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy.

Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties.

Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there.

News.title: Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
News.content:
If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly?

The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses.

Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.

Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries.

But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.

Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.

So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats.

As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.

News.title: More than 110 rescued a week after Nepal deadly floods, army says
News.content:
One hundred and nineteen people have been rescued using air resources in Nepal following deadly floods, a spokesperson for the country's army said.

It comes nearly a week after the disaster that hit both Nepal and neighbouring Tibet, killing more than 1,000 people, with more than 3,900 still missing.

A Nepali army spokesperson earlier said a British male was among those rescued, along with 118 Nepalese people, of whom 44 were female and 74 male.

Later on Tuesday, the British man, Alastair Chambers, told the Telegraph and PA Media he was not rescued and had travelled to the region to help with aid efforts.

The BBC has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield confirmed 36 British people remain unaccounted for - an increase from the 33 previously reported.

More than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River are among the thousands who are still missing.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

On Tuesday, the Nepalese Tourist Board said it had rescued 330 foreign nationals in total.

Saturday saw a rapid development team from the UK arrive in Nepal to provide support for Britons and their families.

News.title: Family mourn 'deeply loved' girl killed in Middlesbrough fire
News.content:
The family of a seven-year-old girl killed in a house fire said their lives had been changed forever by her "devastating loss".

Valentina Foster died alongside her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, in the blaze at Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August. A man has been charged with their murders.

In a tribute, the youngster's parents said their daughter would "always be in our hearts, and her memory will live with us forever".

"She was deeply loved and will be missed beyond words by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched," they said.

"Our lives have changed forever, and we are struggling to come to terms with this devastating loss."

They added she would be "forever missed" by her brothers and sisters.

News.title: Spaces in male prisons fall to lowest level of year, sources say
News.content:
An investment of Â£110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, the justice secretary told MPs the government's plan to free up capacity in the UK's male prison estate will ensure the justice system "commands the confidence of the British public"

"This is the right thing to do, and I pay tribute to his wife Lissie and mother Debbie (Adlam), who campaigned for this," he said.

"We would like to have gone further, but due to the lack of investment in the previous government's 14 years, we are unable to do so."

He added Labour has been forced to take "tough decisions" because it had inherited a justice system "on the brink of failure".

Norris also told MPs the government plans to "bring forward legislation" to end Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences "once and for all â by the end of this Parliament".

IPPS sentences were used where prisoners were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released if the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy called plans to end IPP sentences a "fag packet policy".

He said: "This is the Government's fifth early release policy in just six weeks since the prime minister took office.

"At every stage, we were told ministers had no choice but to include dangerous criminals, because the alternative would be the collapse of the entire system.

"Now the plan is to stop one group of dangerous criminals leaving prison early by letting a different group of dangerous criminals out instead."

Earlier, Norris told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."

Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.

On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.

In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

News.title: Summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record, Met Office says
News.content:
In a rapid attribution study - which looks at how much of a role climate change plays - the Met Office say the average temperature was made around 130 times more likely due to human-induced climate change.

And step back from this summer and there is clue to our changing climate in the temperature record itself.

In a climate that isn't changing, new records should become progressively rarer, because every time a record falls, it raises the bar for the next one.

Think about the 100m race. Each time someone sets a new record, it becomes harder to beat. And there's another thing. Typically records are only ever broken by a few fractions of a second â often just a millisecond or two.

In June 1991, for example, Leroy Burrell ran 9.90 seconds, beating Carl Lewis's 1988 world record of 9.92 seconds by just two hundredths of a second.

Now look at the UK summer temperature record. Until last year, the four hottest summers on record were separated by just five hundredths of a degree.

Then 2025 beat the previous record by 0.34C. And this summer has beaten that new record by another 0.40C.

So after years when the record moved by tiny fractions, in just two summers the bar has been raised by 0.74C.

Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy said that summer 2026 was "remarkable" and we can expect to see extremes occurring more frequently in the future because of climate change.

So why is this happening so quickly here? The UK sits on the western edge of Europe, the fastest-warming continent on Earth - warming at roughly twice the global rate.

There are a few reasons for that. Land heats up faster than the oceans, parts of Europe stretch into the rapidly warming Arctic, and changes in weather patterns have favoured more frequent and intense summer heatwaves.

Scientists are still working out exactly how much each factor contributes, but the result is clear: the background climate in which British weather happens is getting warmer.

None of this means the UK will break its summer record every year. Weather will always give us cooler summers as well as hotter ones. But the pattern is becoming unmistakable: records that once marked the extreme edge of the UK's climate are being overtaken with remarkable speed.

So the question is not whether the UK will experience summers hotter than this one. It is how often they will come - and how much hotter they might be.

News.title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
News.content:
Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.

The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported, external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

Trump's remarks were labelled "nonsense" by Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, as she asked the UK government to issue an official response in the House of Commons.

Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran replied: "The UK has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

"They are and will always remain a British overseas territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders.

"The UK is steadfast in our support for the islanders' rights of self-determination."

Kumaran said she had seen Trump's comments, adding: "Our position remains unchanged."

News.title: Two-day sea search for missing teen on holiday is called off
News.content:
A major sea search for a missing 15-year-old boy has been called off after two days, the coastguard has said.

At about 15:30 BST on Sunday, HM Coastguard received a report that three people were experiencing difficulty in the water at Marloes Sands beach, Pembrokeshire.

Two managed to get out of the water, but the teenage boy, who was visiting the area on holiday from Yorkshire, was unaccounted for. The search was suspended at 19:30 BST on Monday.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency told the BBC that there were currently no plans to resume the search.

Pembrokeshire councillor Claire George said the community had been in shock.

She said: "We're absolutely distraught that somebody has come to harm when they've come to enjoy our wonderful coastline. It's most upsetting for all of us."

Marloes, she said, was remote and hard to access, adding that some beaches were safer than others.

She said: "It's a very dynamic environment. The sea can change at any minute, the weather can change at any minute, so people need to be aware of the risks."

On social media, Angle Lifeboat RNLI said its crew "worked tirelessly" for 22 hours at sea in a major, multi-agency search for the missing swimmer.

On Sunday, Broad Haven and Dale coastguard rescue teams were in attendance, alongside RNLI lifeboats from Angle, Tenby and St Davids and a pilot boat.

A coastguard helicopter and a HM Coastguard fixed wing aircraft were sent, along with the Welsh Ambulance Service.

The search was suspended at about 03:30 BST on Monday and started again later that morning, before being called off in the evening.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency said, despite an extensive search, "sadly, no sign of the missing person was found".

Angle Lifeboat RNLI added its crew had "shown immense dedication over the past two days".

It thanked the Milford Haven Coastguard for "their fantastic coordination and support" in what they said has been a "lengthy and tiring incident".

"Our thoughts are with the swimmer's family and friends at this difficult time," it added.

News.title: Noughties garage track named TikTok's UK song of the summer
News.content:
British singer Kyla's Do You Mind has been named as TikTok's song of the summer in the UK after the noughties garage track experienced a resurgence on the app.

The song gained popularity when it was first released in 2008, but it became known worldwide in 2016 when Canadian rapper Drake sampled it on his chart-topping single One Dance.

It has now found a new audience by trending on TikTok, generating more than 500 million views from about 650,000 videos posted in the UK over the summer, according to the platform.

Kyla, who created the song with her husband DJ Paleface, tells BBC Newsbeat it is "surreal" but "incredible" that Do You Mind is getting another moment nearly 20 years on.

News.title: Watch: Notting Hill Carnival celebrates 60th anniversary
News.content:
London's Notting Hill Carnival celebrated its 60th anniversary with hundreds of dancers, drummers and other performers celebrating Caribbean arts and culture.

"Notting Hill Carnival is about community, it's about having fun, celebrating history and culture", said a festival-goer.

"It's so fun, it's a good energy", said another participant on the last day of the event.

The three-day event in west London normally attracts about two million people each year.

Follow the BBC's coverage of this year's Notting Hill Carnival for all the best moments.

Donald Trump has threatened Tehran with “the biggest attack of them all” after the US launched fresh strikes in Iran on Tuesday.

Several explosions have been heard along the Strait of Hormuz, which come in retaliation for Iranian attacks on shipping and American service members in the Middle East, the US military said.

Iran has since responded by firing drones and missiles, telling the US that “severe punishment awaits the aggressors”.

It comes after President Trump warned Iran not to hit back at its “large and powerful” strikes, saying the US “will be hit again at a much harder and higher level.

“It will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he added.

The US fired rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday in the first clash in more than a month, causing Iran to retaliate by launching ballistic missiles at American bases in Jordan.

On Monday, President Trump said more strikes might be necessary, telling reporters: “We’ll see what happens.”

News.title: Transfer deadline day LIVE: Chelsea agree late Enzo Fernandez replacement, Man Utd in shock move for left back, Balogun to Everton in doubt
News.content:
Manchester City are poised to announce the record-equalling transfer of Enzo Fernandez from Chelsea for £125m. The long-running saga finally reached a conclusion in the final hours of deadline day as City reached an agreement with Chelsea to sign the midfielder, matching the British record transfer fee Liverpool paid Newcastle United for Alexander Isak last summer. Chelsea wanted to have a replacement lined up, with Monaco’s Lamine Camara top of Xabi Alonso’s list, and the Blues have now agreed a £47m deal for the 22-year-old.

Manchester City have meanwhile announced the £60m arrival of Iliman Ndiaye while Everton are set for a busy few hours as they look to finalise deals for Folarin Balogun, Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles. Reports emerging from France suggest the £40m move for Monaco striker Balogun is now in doubt, however. Tottenham have signed Mykhailo Mudryk on loan while the story of the night concerns Malick Fofana: Sunderland are set to beat Crystal Palace to Fofana after a dramatic tug-of-war for the £30m Lyon winger.

Manchester United will not be signing a left back, despite being offered the chance to sign Rayan Ait-Nouri from rivals Manchester City. United were offered a loan with obligation to but had no interest in a permanent move for the City defender, while Liverpool’s business appears done after signing Bradley Barcola and agreeing to sign 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans next summer. Harvey Elliot, meanwhile, has joined Valencia on loan.

Arsenal’s pursuit of Julian Alvarez is set to conclude with the forward remaining at Atletico Madrid, who also refused to allow the Argentina international to join Barcelona. The Gunners have sold Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus and allowed Ethan Nwaneri to depart on loan but are not expected to return to the market.

An anonymous federal official has warned members of Congress that Donald Trump’s “secretive, rushed” and “chaotic” plans for the U.S. Postal Service to implement new rules for mail-in ballots could disenfranchise millions of voters this fall.

Tuesday’s whistleblower report outlines “potentially catastrophic problems” with the administration’s brand-new system, including a “zero-percent failure policy” that could reject tens of thousands of ballots at a time if any single mistakes are made, including misread barcodes or inadvertent errors from postal workers.

Postal officials and IT specialists called it a “mess” and a “s*** show” that illegally defied court orders against putting the new ballot-tracking system in place ahead of crucial midterm elections, according to the report.

“We are crossing the Rubicon of American elections,” said Libby Liu, CEO of WhistleblowerAid.org, which is representing the anonymous official who submitted the complaints.

“This dangerously defective mail-in ballot process could disenfranchise millions of voters, ensnaring ballots in red tape under the guise of solving a non-existent problem,” she added. “People in states that rely heavily on vote-by-mail will have a more difficult time making their voices heard in our challenged democracy this November. The whistleblower’s service to our nation is warning the public that their ability to vote is in serious jeopardy.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump’s new mail-in ballot rules for the US Postal Service, which have been temporarily blocked in court, could pose enormous risks for millions of voters this fall, according to a new whistleblower report ( AFP/Getty )

Federal courts have repeatedly blocked the Postal Service from implementing Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots, which called for the creation of a national voter registration list that would be used to decide who is eligible to cast a ballot.

On August 21, the USPS published its new certification requirements, changes that could not go into effect until federal courts lifted an injunction against them. The Supreme Court allowed Trump’s executive order to stand, for now, leaving the door open for lawsuits to proceed against the new USPS rules themselves.

Three days after the Supreme Court’s decision, District Judge Indira Talwani issued a temporary restraining order that blocks the changes, but the administration is continuing to fight the case in court to overhaul mail-in voting rules just weeks before Election Day.

Dozens of election officials from across the country have repeatedly warned that a last-minute scramble to upload lists of voters into an online portal designed by USPS would amount to an unconstitutional attack on election administration that would only sow more confusion and introduce potentially catastrophic errors.

If the plans are allowed to go into effect, USPS workers would be required to scan barcodes on a sample of envelopes to ensure the voters appear on the state’s list, according to the whistleblower report. If there is even one mismatch, that whole batch of ballots — which could be in the thousands at a time — could be rejected, the whistleblower said.

“As designed, the process is entirely unforgiving,” according to the report. “It could delay ballots by the thousands in repeated verification cycles — and thus prevent states from mailing enormous numbers of ballots.”

States are constantly updating their voter rolls, the lists sent to USPS could be out of date shortly after voters re-register with new personal information or addresses, or if new voters sign up but aren’t reflected in the already-approved list designed by the administration.

open image in gallery Trump’s executive order compelled USPS to develop an online portal for a national voter registration list that would be used to decide who is eligible to cast a ballot, but officials have warned that potential errors could risk disenfranchising voters ( AFP/Getty )

USPS and the Department of Justice have repeatedly defended the program, though election officials fear the government’s list could be dangerously too slow to reflect changes from the states.

“Their system is set up to fail — and risk the right to vote for millions of Americans who cast their ballots by mail,” according to Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, whose office received the whistleblower report.

“Given this new information, such sloppiness and haste seems clearly part of a purposeful attempt to create chaos and prevent people from voting,” he said in a statement Tuesday. “I am demanding answers and accountability.”

Voting rights groups fear the president’s efforts to centralize control over election administration, which is left to the states under the Constitution, is an attempt to boost Republican candidates and suppress Democratic turnout during an election that is likely to determine the balance of power in Congress — and the fate of Trump’s remaining years in office.

open image in gallery Connecticut Democrat Senator Richard Blumenthal, whose office received the whistleblower report, says Trump’s mail-in ballot rules are ‘set up to fail’ in a ‘purposeful attempt’ to sow chaos in midterm elections ( Reuters )

Trump spent years baselessly insisting that voting by mail is ripe for fraud, and that manipulated ballots were “rigged” against him in elections he lost. He complained throughout 2020 elections that Republicans would “never” win without changing rules for voting by mail, which he has called “inherently corrupt” and “cheating” despite routinely casting his own ballots by mail.

The administration is pushing for mail-in ballot changes in court while the president simultaneously demands Senate passage his SAVE America Act, which would also severely restrict mail-in voting and impose nationwide voter ID rules, among other changes.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune has repeatedly expressed doubts about sacrificing the filibuster to pass Trump’s bill. Still, Trump has tried to argue for its passage in increasingly desperate terms, including not ruling out the possibility of a national emergency to put the rules in place.

“The crown jewel of American democracy, our historic record of free and fair elections, deserves so much better than this slipshod effort,” WhistleblowerAid.org senior vice president and special counsel David Kligerman, who is representing the whistleblower, said in a statement.

States are scrambling to prepare for midterm elections, with impending deadlines for voters to receive ballots that can be filled out and returned in time to count by November.

Officials in North Carolina have already started preparing ballots under a new state law requiring voters to start receiving them 60 days before an election. More states are set to start mailing out ballots in the coming days and weeks.

But the “slapdash rollout” of Trump’s new system “could prove a major threat to voting rights in upcoming midterm elections,” Kligerman said. “We hope that the courts across the country looking at this issue are able to take note of these fundamentally troubling revelations.”

Britain will pursue a "pragmatic relationship" with China over trade while addressing the "sensitive" issue of global imbalances, Chief Secretary to the UK Treasury Emma Reynolds said on Tuesday.

In a Reuters interview during the G20 finance leaders' meeting in North Carolina, Reynolds explained that the UK keeps open commercial ties with friendly allies while imposing strict sanctions and embargoes against Iran, Russia and other states starting wars or seeking to acquire nuclear weapons.

"We have a pragmatic relationship with China, one where we cooperate on things that we agree on, but also challenge in areas where we disagree," Reynolds said.

"The whole issue of global imbalances is quite a sensitive one and a tricky one, but it's one that we will we will navigate."

Asked if reducing global imbalances meant meeting U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's calls for G20 countries to consider more trade ‌barriers to Chinese goods like the ​U.S. has done, Reynolds said Britain would ‌generally seek to maintain open ⁠trade.

open image in gallery Emma Reynolds speaks as finance ministers and central bank governors from G20 countries meet in Asheville, North Carolina ( REUTERS/Sam Wolfe )

"As a general rule, we are a very open trading economy, and we believe, sort of as a general principle, that free trade is better than putting up barriers," she said.

Bessent says he's urging some of his G20 counterparts to take a page from the Trump administration's playbook of using tariffs and other measures to crack down on trade imbalances.

Bessent told reporters that he had warned other nations at the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term that the new U.S. “tariff wall” would mean that Chinese goods would flood their markets.

“And unfortunately, I was right,” Bessent told reporters on the sidelines of the G20 finance minister meetings. “The rest of the world probably needs to take a hard look at what they should be doing to protect their citizens’ jobs, their manufacturing base, so that everything they do doesn’t get offshored.”

The Trump administration's tariff policies have been criticized by economists and politicians for raising costs for U.S. consumers and, in many cases, for punishing allies. The Tax Foundation, an independent think tank, found that the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration throughout 2025 raised the overall retail price of imported consumer goods by roughly 7% relative to pre-tariff trends.

One American town is becoming a true retiree haven, and — no surprise — it's located in Florida.

According to a new report from MoneyLion, a fintech mobile banking company, 11 of the 30 fastest-growing retirement communities are located in the Sunshine State, and the city of Wildwood is top of the list.

Wildwood is approximately 52 miles from Orlando and 77 miles from Tampa. Over the last five years, the city has seen a 256 percent increase in its retiree community, including a 16 percent increase in the past year alone, according to the report.

The city's population is 19,436, per the U.S. Census Bureau, meaning that nearly half — 47 percent — of its population is aged 65 or older.

Wildwood is also located just south of the world's largest retirement community, The Villages.

open image in gallery A boat ramp at Lake Deaton Park in Wildwood, Florida. Wildwood has the nation's fastest-growing population of people aged 65 and older ( City of Wildwood )

Like its larger neighbor, Wildwood has a number of draws that might entice seniors to put down roots. It has a historic downtown — which is undergoing a 30-year redevelopment project — as well as golf courses, lakes for fishing and boating, parks, and horseback riding.

Jason McHugh, Wildwood's city manager, told WESH in 2023 that its proximity to The Villages helped kickstart the city's growth among retirees and that has allowed the city to undertake major renovation projects.

"We're seeing other private developers coming in here and providing other single-family homes and other apartments," McHugh said at the time. "If we didn't have this growth coming in, we wouldn't have the financial resources to improve the downtown and to make Wildwood a better place."

Home prices in the area aren't bad either. According to Zillow, the average home value is $296,915, which is approximately $100,000 less than the average property prices in The Villages.

open image in gallery Residents of The Villages, Florida dancing during a party. The Villages is the world's largest retirement community and is just south of Wildwood, Florida ( AFP/Getty )

The cost of living in Wildwood is seven percent higher than the national average, per Salary.com. It costs $2,637 per month for singles and $5,808 per month for a family-of-four living in the city. But Florida law has eliminated Social Security and individual home taxes, which helps mitigate some of the costs.

The second fastest-growing retirement community is in Bluffton, South Carolina, according to the report. In Bluffton, people aged 65 and older make up 24.6 percent of the town's overall population. Its retiree population has increased nearly 150 percent in the past five years and 28.3 percent in the past year.

Taking the third spot is Goodyear, Arizona, with retirees making up 20 percent of the city's population. That represents a 68 percent increase in the last five years and a 15.8 percent increase over the last year, per MoneyLion.

Everton have brought Jack Grealish back to Hill Dickinson Stadium after signing him on loan for a second consecutive season.

It in effect brings to an end to Grealish’s Manchester City career, with the England international in the last year of his contract at the Etihad Stadium, and probably meaning the £100m man will then leave on a free transfer.

Grealish was borrowed by Everton last season, getting four assists in his first two starts and winning the Premier League Player of the Month award for August, before injury ended his season in January.

open image in gallery Jack Grealish will have another loan spell with Everton ( PA Archive )

The 30-year-old became the second player to swap clubs between Everton and City on deadline day and in effect replaces Iliman Ndiaye, who moved to the FA Cup winners for an initial £60m.

Grealish, who became Everton’s sixth summer signing, said he felt loved by manager David Moyes.

He explained: “It feels so good. I'm so happy. I think I'm at my best at everything in life, not just football, when I feel loved. That's what the manager has given me, what my teammates have given me and especially what the fans have given me.

"Every time I see an Everton fan, it's just pure love and the way they've welcomed me since that first game against Leeds, I'll never forget that. It means a lot to me and hopefully I've made a few Everton fans happy.

"I had a perfect time here for the first six months, then I stayed around after I got injured. I’ve been watching all the Everton games in pre-season and since the season started. Now I feel ready to go.

“I love him, the manager. I think he’s such a great guy. He was a big reason why I wanted to come back here as well.

"I’ve had certain managers in the past where I feel I’ve played my best football under them – and he falls into that category, for sure.”
