World.title: Houston mayor says his city is a better location than Austin for an NHL expansion franchise
World.content:
After a strong round of expansion over the last decade, bringing in the Vegas Golden Knights, Seattle Kraken and Utah Mammoth (who are considered an expansion team; confusing, I know), the NHL is looking to grow again.

The league wants to add two more clubs, one of which will be based in Texas. The question is whether it will be Houston or Austin joining the league.

Now, Houston's mayor is making his case for why his city is the best option for the league.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Both cities offer upsides. For Austin, the league has a chance to be the first of the four major leagues to set up shop there, a strategy that worked well in Las Vegas.

However, Houston is currently the biggest media market in the nation without an NHL team, something NHL Deputy Commissioner Bill Daly recently confirmed is a big factor in the decision.

"We're ready. In fact, we're talking to multiple parties that are interested," Mayor John Whitmire said in an interview with The Sporting News. "So when we get a proposal, if the city can do something to a system, we'll be there. We'll definitely be a better location than Austin."

Houston has never had an NHL team, but was home to the World Hockey Association's Houston Aeros in the 1970s. Since then, it has been home to some minor league teams, as has Austin.

World.content:
Dan Le Batard is unhappy with the racial makeup of NFL analysts on television. He says there are too many white analysts and not enough black ones for his liking.

"Luke Kuechly is now the up-and-coming broadcasting star that people like. When they look at Tony Romo and they put him on the bench for a while, they replace him with J.J. Watt," Le Batard said on his podcast. "[Rob Gronkowski] has a job, even though Gronk is a notoriously bad talker. I just wonder if you guys notice that the sport is disproportionately black, and the broadcasters that get hired are disproportionately white, and it’s on purpose. I’m asking the question. It’s to make it palatable to the broadest section of people."

He continued, asking his co-hosts and listeners to, at least, notice the whiteness on air.

"I’m just asking if you guys notice that all of the up-and-coming people are always the white guys. There aren’t that many white stars in football. There are plenty of black stars. Why are the white ones the only ones who get the broadcasting jobs?… I’m just wondering whether people notice. It’s always J.J. Watt. It’s always Luke Kuechly. As if there aren’t a bunch of Jonathan Vilmas out there that are available."

JEMELE HILL POSTS MISLEADING STUDY TO SUGGEST THERE ARE TOO MANY 'WHITE MEN' IN SPORTS MEDIA

Imagine hosting a sports show and choosing that as your topic on Sept. 1, just days before the start of the college football season and a week before the NFL season.

For background, Le Batard has spent much of the past year complaining about the number of white people he sees on television. More on that later.

Not only is Le Batard pandering, but his gripe is also invalid. He cherry-picked a few media hires while ignoring many others.

Le Batard pointed to the promotions of Kuechly and Watt. Notice how he ignored ESPN adding Jason McCourty to Monday Night Countdown, the pregame show that will serve as bumper programming for the Super Bowl this season. CBS elevated Charles Davis to its lead college football game analyst role this offseason. Fox Sports recently added Robert Griffin III to its color-commentator lineup. Le Batard mentioned neither move.

ESPN’s featured NFL analysts include Orlovsky, Mina Kimes, an Asian woman, and several black former players, including McCourty, Marcus Spears, Chris Canty, Andrew Hawkins, Louis Riddick, Sam Acho and Booger McFarland.

DAN LE BATARD DEMANDS THE MEDIA MAKE JAXSON DART 'UNCOMFORTABLE' FOR INTRODUCING TRUMP

World.title: Glen Powell reveals wild night with country stars ended with beer pong at Jelly Roll’s Nashville bar

Glen Powell recalled having a wild night out in Nashville with country music royalty while preparing for his role in the upcoming movie, "The Comeback King."

In the Judd Apatow-directed comedy, the 37-year-old actor plays Aubrey King, a disgraced country star who attempts to rebuild his life and career after experiencing a dramatic downfall.

During a recent appearance on "Jimmy Kimmer Live," which was guest-hosted by Jelly Roll, Powell, who co-wrote the script with Apatow, explained how he collaborated with real-life country musicians and set out to fully immerse himself in Music City’s culture to make the project feel authentic.

JELLY ROLL ROLLS AWAY FROM APOLITICAL PAST AFTER TRUMP JOKES SPARK MAGA AND ‘SNOWFLAKE’ LABELS

"I've been a fan of country music my whole life, and I wanted to make sure that we did this right," Powell told Jelly Roll. "We made it not about country music. We wanted to make it with country music.

"And one of the things I did as we were, like, writing, I was like, 'Oh, I want to get the full experience of writing with Nashville,'" he remembered.

Powell recalled that he decided to team up with country singer-songwriter Hardy for a daytime writing session.

"Did y'all write, or did y'all go out drinking?" Jelly Roll joked.

"We first wrote, then we drank," Powell replied. "So, we wrote this great song. I was really excited about it. And then he's like, 'Hey man, we should go out and really hit the town.'"

Powell said he and Hardy joined his "buddies," country duo Dan + Shay, for an outing in Lower Broadway, Nashville's iconic entertainment district known for its packed honky-tonks and live country music.

GLEN POWELL SHOTGUNS A BEER ON STAGE WITH COUNTRY SUPERSTAR LUKE COMBS

"All of a sudden, like, one bar turned to 12," Powell recalled.

"Oh, you went honky-tonk," Jelly Roll quipped.

JELLY ROLL UNLEASHES CRUDE JOKES ABOUT TRUMP'S WEIGHT ON 'KIMMEL', 'FROM ONE FAT PIG TO ANOTHER'

Powell remembered that, 12 stops later, the group finally landed at Jelly Roll’s Broadway establishment Goodnight in the early morning hours.

"We ended up playing beer pong there, I think, at like 3 in the morning," Powell admitted.

"Let's go!" Jelly Roll exclaimed. "You strike me as a great beer pong player. How'd you fair?"

Powell said that while he considers himself a "pretty good" player, he proved no match for Hardy.

"Hardy smoked me," he said. "I'll be honest with you."

"Hardy's an absolute rager," Jelly Roll agreed.

JELLY ROLL HID PAINFUL 'SECRET' WHILE CELEBRATING AT AWARDS SHOW

"Do you recall the first time you ever played beer pong?" the "Save Me" hitmaker asked Powell.

"First time I ever played beer pong? Oh, wow. That's a good question. Do you remember yours?" Powell asked.

"Well, I went to prison instead of college, so I missed the entire beer pong era, you know," Jelly Roll, who has been open about his past incarcerations quipped.

"You know, I missed out on the whole prison beer pong experience, but that one's not on my bucket list," Powell joked as the audience laughed.

Jelly Roll was among the country stars, including Miranda Lambert, Brad Paisley and Riley Green, who made cameos in "The Comeback King."

During his appearance on the late-night show, Powell recalled how "The Comeback King" marks the first time he has ever sung on screen. The "Top Gun: Maverick" star credited his voice coach, Eric Vitro; his experience singing with his mother in nursing homes; and his sister Leslie for guiding him through the vocal preparation.

World.title: Ex-NFL star believes Odell Beckham Jr 'still better than most of the receivers' in NFL as he returns to Giants
World.content:
The full circle career moment for Odell Beckham Jr. truly hit its peak on Tuesday when the New York Giants announced that the 33-year-old receiver, who became a household name with the franchise over a decade ago, will be wearing the No. 13 after making the 53-man roster out of training camp.

Giants fans have been hoping Beckham would show new head coach John Harbaugh and the rest of the offensive staff enough to warrant a roster spot to open the season, and even at 33 years old and seven years removed from being a Giants superstar, Beckham did just that.

Beckham told reporters that Harbaugh put his arm around him and congratulated him on making the team following a solid final preseason game against the New York Jets. The former first-round pick out of LSU has been through quite the career rollercoaster since he was traded to the Cleveland Browns by former GM Dave Gettleman in 2019, but he’s excited for this second chance to do what he envisioned when he was drafted in 2014: win a championship in New York.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Beckham’s return to New York has fans and peers alike celebrating with him, including former Cincinnati Bengals star wide receiver Chad Ochocinco, who told OutKick that Beckham’s movement and performance with the Giants certainly earned him a spot on an NFL 53-man roster.

"I mean, there’s no scenario — I don’t care what camp he was in on any of the other 31 teams where he wouldn’t have made the team," Ochocinco said, while highlighting his partnership with DraftKings. "A healthy Odell that can create separation, that can beat any DB, that is still fast, that can take a slant route or hitch route and take it 80, 90, 70 [yards]. Whatever it may be. Odell Beckham Jr., even at 33 years old, that can still take the top off a defense? That Odell?

ODELL BECKHAM JR EYES HIS OLD NUMBER AMID DRAMATIC RETURN TO THE GIANTS

"I don’t need him to be the Odell of old that was with the Giants when he first got there. I don’t need him to be the Odell in his prime. I need him to be the Odell that, when your opportunities come, make the most of those opportunities. Those few opportunities he does get? He can take a slant to the house. He can make people miss. He still has flashes of greatness. I don’t need him to be the old Odell. But even at 33, Odell is still better than most of the receivers in the NFL. And not your elite receivers — let’s be realistic here."

The patented separation and speed that Beckham is known for was on full display throughout training camp and the Giants’ preseason games, where he had ample opportunity to prove himself in a crowded wide receivers room.

But to Ochocinco’s point, the Giants are not expecting Beckham to be their top dog once more, even if he is back in his old threads wearing his old number. Malik Nabers, whom the Giants hope will be ready for Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys, is another first-round pick out of LSU who has shown flashes of greatness. He heads into his third season coming off a severe knee injury suffered in Week 4 of last year, but should be the top dog in terms of targets and catches.

Ochocinco, then, is thinking about those other opportunities where Beckham is going to have to make the best of what he’s given.

"Now, making an impact, it all comes down to the opportunities that he’s given. That’s what it comes down to," he explained. "Preseason’s one thing. Now, game-planning and having plays for him, that’s a completely different animal.

"You have a group of receivers, all of them do something different. There’s some things they do well and there’s some things they don’t do well. Where are those opportunities and where will Odell go do what he does well? It’s not going to be like it was years ago, it’s just not. You have to understand that, especially at 33. They weed you out of the offense once you start to hit your 30s in general anyway."

Ochocinco admits he has "no idea" what the Giants and their new offensive coordinator Matt Nagy have in store for Beckham. Still, the fact he made the roster says everything you need to know: Harbaugh and the Giants believe in Beckham to make an impact — whatever that may be.

"They got to use him. He’s special even at 33," Ochocinco said.

Come Week 1, Giants fans will dust off their own No. 13 jerseys and wear them to MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, for the return of their former mercurial superstar. Beckham, meanwhile, will be waiting for an opportunity to help his team — no longer his old team — earn a win against an NFC East foe.

OCHO LOVES DRAFTKINGS GAMEDAY

We’ll see how the 17-game-plus season shakes out for Beckham, but Ochocinco is simply happy because football is back, and he’s excited to impact the fan experience with DraftKings.

"DraftKings Gameday," which will take place on Sept. 2, was announced on Monday with quite the activation as it celebrates the first football season with DraftKings Sports & Casino available in all 50 states. As a way to fuel fans with the return of football, DraftKings will be offering free gas, while supplies last, to passenger vehicles at select gas stations in Los Angeles, Miami, Dallas, Atlanta and Detroit. Specific locations and event times will be announced separately.

"For me, I think it’s fun because who else would do something like this outside of DraftKings? This is a great touch for NFL fans to start the season," Ochocinco said. "We’re giving you free gas, so when your respective team plays, you’re fueled up to go. And word of mouth will be, ‘You won’t believe this? You know what DraftKings did? I was able to save money and get tickets to go to a game because they paid for my gas.’ That makes sense."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There will also be exclusive DraftKings Gameday promotions for customers, a customized in-app experience, in-person activations, a charitable donation through the DraftKings SERVES program and a new campaign featuring Kevin Hart and Nick Jonas this season.

"It’s all about the fan experience, so some of the offers and luxuries throughout the season is what sets us apart from everybody else. I’m happy to be a part of them," Ochocinco said.

World.title: UN pushes nations to consider slavery reparations but legal group says idea 'not going to fly in the US'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The United Nations said on Monday that countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and other measures to address what it says is the enduring legacy of racial discrimination, but an attorney seeking to shut down the effort insists it won't work in the U.S.

The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) is calling on "states to implement comprehensive restorative justice, combining compensation, restitution, rehabilitation and structural reforms," the UN News reported.

"Irrespective of the legal characterization of the original historical acts, States Parties remain bound by their present obligations under the Convention to address structural inequalities," the U.N. document states.

Guidance published by CERD stated that the obligations stem from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed during the slave trade era.

1619 PROJECT CREATOR CLAIMS PAYING REPARATIONS WOULD BE ADMISSION THAT US EXISTENCE IS A 'CRIME'

"It's just outrageous that the United Nations comes in and tells countries that they have to give free money away to their citizens," Michael Bekesha, a senior attorney at Judicial Watch, told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, who are they to say what we can and can't do? The bigger issue for Judicial Watch and something we'll be watching is if the States were ever to do something like this, they would have to follow our Constitution and our laws, and the U.N. doesn't care about that… whatever the U.N. is thinking isn't going to be constitutional and is not going to fly in the United States."

Bekesha made the comments after the DOJ joined their class action lawsuit challenging the Local Reparations Restorative Housing Program in the City of Evanston, Illinois.

TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES'

The DOJ contends the Chicago suburb's initiative unlawfully distributes public benefits based strictly on race and ancestry. The DOJ’s proposed complaint alleges that the program violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment, as well as the Fair Housing Act, because the housing-related financial assistance is distributed on the basis of race.

The litigation began in May 2024 when Judicial Watch, a conservative legal group, filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of six non-Black descendants of Evanston residents, arguing they were unconstitutionally excluded from the program.

The announcement came after the U.N. General Assembly adopted a resolution earlier this year declaring the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity and for member states to pursue reparations to rectify "historical wrongs."

The implementation of reparations has been a growing trend in the United States, spanning from the East to West Coast.

Evanston, Illinois was the first U.S. municipality to establish a reparations program and later began providing $25,000 benefits to eligible Black residents and descendants to address the city's history of housing discrimination.

CHICAGO SUBURB LOCALS HOPE REPARATIONS ADDRESSES 'AFFORDABILITY PRESSURES' AS BLACK POPULATION DWINDLES

Despite efforts to issue reparations, some of these programs are facing obstacles due to budgetary or legal pressures. While some states and local governments push for reparations, "financial compensation alone is not sufficient," according to the CERD.

The committee additionally called for comprehensive measures beyond financial compensation.

"It also advocates for comprehensive and far-reaching remedial measures, both financial, non-financial and structural, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-recurrence," UN News reported.

Reparations can take many forms but broadly refer to payments or other compensation intended to address harms suffered by Black Americans and their descendants because of slavery or discriminatory government policies.

"To ensure the effectiveness of reparations, they advocate the implementation of national action plans with specific deadlines, developed in consultation with people of African descent and the committees in charge of reparations," UN News reported.

Bekesha added that reparations are by nature discriminatory.

"If the Evanston case of Judicial Watch and the United States were to win this case, it would show not only the United Nations but every other state and city in the United States that you cannot in the United States provide benefits to individuals solely based on the color of their skin," Bekesha said.

World.title: LOVB owner defends WNBA’s Caitlin Clark handling, sees women’s sports as investment opportunity
World.content:
Chantell Preston thinks the WNBA has done a good job handling Caitlin Clark and the popularity she brought to the league.

That is ... a generous interpretation.

Preston, a healthcare entrepreneur and author of The Success Lie, is a co-founder and owner of the incoming San Francisco Signal, a League One Volleyball franchise. She also owns a stake in LOVB, the women’s professional volleyball league.

"Caitlin Clark’s done some phenomenal things for women’s sports as a whole," Preston told OutKick. "What Caitlin Clark has been able to do and the visibility that she’s brought to the WNBA has been invaluable to not just the WNBA, but all sports."

LOVB FRANCHISE OWNER SAYS TRANSGENDER ATHLETES 'SHOULD BE ABLE TO PLAY' IN WOMEN'S VOLLEYBALL

Clark brought record ratings, sold-out arenas and a fan base the WNBA had spent nearly three decades trying to find. Preston said the league didn't do everything perfectly, but she believes it handled the moment well.

"Nothing’s ever perfect," she said. "And I think they’ve done a good job. I think there’s still some areas of opportunity."

In May, the WNBA promoted a Fever game on NBC and Peacock with a social media graphic featuring A’ja Wilson, Angel Reese, Zia Cooke and Fever guard Raven Johnson, who was averaging one point per game at the time. Clark wasn't included.

ESPN followed in July with a six-part documentary about the WNBA’s growth. It centered on Wilson, Napheesa Collier and DeWanna Bonner. Clark appeared in game and All-Star footage, but the documentary didn't interview Clark or feature her in any storylines, and barely acknowledged her role in the league’s popularity boom.

The filmmakers also didn't answer OutKick’s questions about whether they asked Clark to participate.

Preston would rather see attention on the league’s players than the drama surrounding them.

"How do we focus on the positive, not the negative?" she said. "Talk about the incredible players that are coming in, the ones coming from college. You’ve got Caitlin Clark, but then you’ve also got three or four other players that have come up in the last few years that are making huge, huge differences."

The WNBA doesn't need to pretend every player is Caitlin Clark

Preston said the league shouldn't sell only one player.

"It doesn’t have to be one individual," Preston said. "It can be multiple individuals, but really focusing on what they’ve done well for their teams and how they can help as a whole. It’s about visibility and storytelling."

The WNBA doesn’t need to put Clark on every graphic because she’ll get people to watch either way. But it also can’t act like she isn’t the main reason those people are tuning in.

CAITLIN CLARK HELPS WNBA SHATTER ANOTHER TV RATINGS RECORD AS FEVER-DREAM DRAWS MASSIVE AUDIENCE

Fever-Sky on Aug. 23 averaged 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock. It was the most-watched WNBA regular-season game since the league’s opening weekend in 1997 and peaked at 3.82 million viewers. Fever-Aces in July averaged 2.64 million viewers, the second-largest WNBA regular-season audience of the season.

ION Sports left Clark off an August graphic naming its five MVP candidates and fans were not thrilled. It's not just the league that has seemed eager to ignore Clark's impact. ION’s graphic was another example of the disconnect between how the sport is often marketed and what viewers are actually watching.

Some people who came to the WNBA for Clark will stick around for Wilson, Collier, Bueckers or another player, and some will only watch games that involve Clark. Let them. But the league is not helping itself by arguing with the audience it has.

Preston sees a business opportunity in volleyball

Preston said she spent three years looking at different leagues before putting money into LOVB.

"When I’m looking at businesses to invest in, I’m looking at where can I get the best return on my investment?" she said. "For a long time, people say, ‘Oh, well, invest in women. It’s charity.’ No, it’s not."

It's refreshing to hear Preston say that women's sports leagues should act like businesses. Some of the biggest complaints about the WNBA come from the idea that it's run like a charity instead of as a for-profit entity.

For a long time, that was simply the truth. The WNBA has long operated with NBA backing and has reported losses, but Clark’s arrival changed the economic conversation. The league hasn't adjusted to the audience and money that followed.

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

Preston is betting on volleyball following a similar trajectory. She said youth participation and the Olympic audience helped convince her that the sport presents a new opportunity.

"Volleyball is the No. 1 girls’ sport in the U.S.," Preston said. "You look at how many people watch it in the Olympics, there’s a lot of tailwinds and we see growth."

LOVB began play in 2025 and has announced expansion franchises in Los Angeles, Miami, Minnesota and the San Francisco Bay Area to start play in 2027. Preston said she also liked that team owners hold a stake in the league.

"We own part of the team, and we own part of the league," she said. "So everyone’s aligned. When the league is doing well, everyone’s doing well. When teams are doing well, everyone’s doing well."

That doesn't mean she assumes women’s sports will keep growing forever.

"We’re not quite sure," she said. "Is this sustainable for all sports, women’s sports, or is it just the WNBA?"

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Preston thinks the next few years will depend on brands and media companies.

"If the brands and the media come together and realize that there’s a great opportunity to support women’s sport, I think that to me shows sustainability across the board," she said.

LOVB has to give people a reason to care about its players, too.

"It’s our responsibility and job to make sure that we’re telling the stories of those players so they become household names," Preston said. "That’s the storytelling, that’s the branding."

World.title: Colin Kaepernick is done with the NFL. He isn’t done fighting.
World.content:
The same league that let Michael Vick play again after he went to prison for dogfighting, and allowed Deshaun Watson to sign a contract for $230 million following accusations of sexual misconduct by more than 20 women (Watson has maintained his innocence), was keeping Kaepernick out.

“There’s not a definitive moment that I would point to,” Kaepernick says about when he realized what was happening.

Instead, it was more of a culmination.

“Coming on the back of going to a Super Bowl, going to an NFC Championship, setting records, and not a single team would bring me in, even for a workout?” Kaepernick says.

In August 2017, the Miami Dolphins — whose owner Stephen Ross previously launched a nonprofit to fight systemic racism — signed quarterback Jay Cutler after an injury to starter Ryan Tannehill, even though Cutler had already retired. NFL team executives, meanwhile, used the media to try to throw water on the idea that Kaepernick was blackballed.

Some coaches and GMs did reach out, Kaepernick says, and explicitly told him, “Yeah, we want to bring you in, but it’s getting shut down above us.”

One of those coaches, Kaepernick writes in his book, was John Harbaugh, the then-head coach of the Baltimore Ravens. Kaepernick spoke extensively with Harbaugh during the summer of 2017. Harbaugh’s brother Jim was Kaepernick’s coach during the 49ers’ run to the Super Bowl.

Kaepernick writes that Harbaugh was “pushing” to sign him, but was “shut down from above.”

In October 2017, Kaepernick filed a grievance against the NFL under the terms of the league’s and players’ collective bargaining agreement, alleging that owners were colluding against signing him due to his protest.

“Everybody believes that he was blackballed,” says one former player who was in the league during 2016. “Players knew that this would happen. That was a firm belief around the league.”

Goodell pushed back on the notion of organized collusion to keep Kaepernick out of the NFL.

“Those are decisions that each individual owner has to make and their clubs, coaches, GMs,” Goodell told NBC in 2020. “And I’ve talked to a lot of our clubs about it and I’ve encouraged them. I’d love to see him play again.”

Jesse Dittmar for NBC News

In November 2019 — months after the NFL settled Kaepernick’s lawsuit — the league tried to arrange a midseason workout for him in front of all 32 teams. The details of this day are now infamous, as Kaepernick ultimately called off the NFL’s workout the morning of due to an extensive waiver he refused to sign — a waiver Kaepernick believed would sign away his employment rights and potential future claims — and instead managed to organize a workout of his own.

The dissolution of the workout drew another round of skepticism, with many claiming Kaepernick was pulling a media stunt or was not serious about wanting to play again.

While Kaepernick was out of the league, the NFL went about trying to turn the temperature down on his protest, battling the aftermath of an especially divisive election and a ratings slide some attributed to the player demonstrations.

The league partnered in 2017 with the Players Coalition, a group founded to address systemic racism, and has since committed more than half a billion dollars to various social justice causes. Kaepernick wasn’t part of the group. (Reid said in 2017 that Kaepernick was kicked out of communications with the group by co-founder Malcolm Jenkins, which Jenkins denied.)

The NFL did whatever it could to stop the kneeling, the former player says, believing the league wanted to weed out players who kneeled: “What happened was the league and the Players Coalition came to a deal, and then the league did what they were going to do … They wanted their games to go back to normal.”

Kaepernick’s protest likely cost him tens of millions of dollars, even accounting for whatever he got from the NFL in the settlement.

But as his career was sacked, as television pundits continued to make personal attacks, and as 986 people were killed by police in 2017, Kaepernick stayed largely quiet.

He says that was by design.

“No individual should be speaking for everyone across the country. I don’t think that’s a responsible way to approach things,” Kaepernick says. “It’s also being able to enable other people to step into leadership positions, because that’s what movements actually are. It’s not one person just driving things.”

Months after his workout snafu, events unrelated to Kaepernick raised the volume on his protest once more.

On May 25, 2020, 46-year-old George Floyd was killed by police officer Derek Chauvin in Minnesota.

Video revealed Chauvin kneeled on Floyd’s neck for over nine minutes, killing him. Chauvin was convicted on multiple murder charges in 2021.

Nearly four years after Kaepernick kneeled in response to police brutality, worldwide protests emerged in the wake of Floyd’s killing. Kaepernick says seeing the protests around the world made him hopeful in the moment, especially as people in some cases risked their own well-being to be heard in the middle of the pandemic.

Nike included Kaepernick in its 30th anniversary "Just Do It" campaign in 2018. Supporters gathered outside NFL headquarters in New York City after Kaepernick filed a grievance against the league alleging that owners were colluding against signing him because of his protest. Getty Images file

“There was a significant portion of the population that previously was disconnected from these realities,” Kaepernick says. “It was like, oh, actually I have to sit with this now and I have to grapple with this. And am I OK with this? And what is my role within this? Am I complicit?”

Corporations also scrambled to meet the moment, including the NFL. In June 2020, several NFL players coordinated social media posts asking for the league to condemn racism and “admit wrong in silencing our players from peacefully protesting.”

The next day, Goodell responded in a video message.

“We, the National Football League, condemn racism and the systematic oppression of Black people,” Goodell said in the video, echoing the words players demanded from him. “We, the National Football League, admit we were wrong for not listening to NFL players earlier and encourage all to speak out and peacefully protest. We, the National Football League, believe Black lives matter.”

Kaepernick wasn’t impressed.

“His response through that video was only because of pressure from players, not because it was altruistic,” Kaepernick says.

The idea that the league should have listened to protesting players “is so laughable in my mind, and so disingenuous,” Kaepernick says. “We had been trying to address the issue that the NFL created with blackballing me for years. To come out and say we should have listened on the back of that — while I’m still actively trying to play in the NFL — it’s so performative.”

World.title: House passes short-term funding bill to prevent a shutdown before the election
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The House voted Tuesday to pass a short-term funding bill and avert a government shutdown at the end of September, keeping money flowing at current levels until Dec. 11.

The legislation, which has already passed the Senate, sailed through the chamber by a vote of 370-48. It now goes to President Donald Trump, who is expected to sign it.

That would take the biggest legislative item off the to-do list for Congress ahead of the elections Nov. 3, punting stalled negotiations over a full-year funding deal until after the midterms.

The two parties have clashed over the scope of federal spending as Democrats reject Trump’s call for a massive $1.5 trillion military budget, a spike from the already record-breaking $1 trillion that Congress gave the military this year.

Funding the government requires 60 Senate votes to defeat a filibuster, meaning it must have bipartisan support even though Republicans control both chambers and the White House.

House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole, R-Okla., accused Democrats of blocking a deal to weaken politically vulnerable Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee.

“I do want to finish all the bills before the end of the year. Now, whether we can do that or not is another matter,” Cole said, referring to the 12 appropriations bills that fund the government. “We won’t know if we’ll be doing that till after the election.”

The winners of the midterm elections will feel empowered to press their demands in the lame-duck negotiations, knowing that they’ll have more power in the upcoming year.

The election “has a tremendous impact,” Cole said. “We will act like we can come back and things will be exactly the way they were when we left. They won’t be. Everybody’s calculations will change. Everybody’s point of view will change. It’ll have an enormous impact about what happens for the balance of the year.”

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., said she hopes to become chair of the Appropriations Committee again if Democrats win the House.

But she said her only priority now is to finalize a full government funding deal for the new fiscal year before 2027 begins.

“The midterm election will have an effect, but the goal is that we need to pass appropriations bills before the end of the year. That is a bipartisan view of where we need to go with the committee, and so that’s what we are going to press for,” DeLauro said. “Let’s get to the finish line.”

World.title: Whistleblower says USPS system Trump ordered for mail ballots is flawed and untested
World.content:
An anonymous federal official warned in a whistleblower complaint this week that the technical system the U.S. Postal Service built for mail voting is flawed, untested and likely to cause major disruptions in this fall’s midterm elections if it is implemented.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March that directed his administration to create federal lists of citizens and asked the Postal Service to transmit mail ballots to only those people. A federal judge has blocked the order from going into effect amid ongoing litigation over its constitutionality; the whistleblower complaint highlights potential issues that could arise if the courts ultimately declare it lawful.

The USPS typically is responsible only for transporting mail ballots between election officials and voters, and the federal government has never kept a central list of all American citizens. Trump ordered the agency to take on an unprecedented and complex role in the process this year amid a broader attempt to exert greater control over the country’s elections and his continued unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.

The technical system the USPS assembled to vet voters was developed in a “rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed process,” according to a whistleblower complaint sent to the office of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Blumenthal sent the complaint to Postmaster General David Steiner on Monday asking for more information.

“This administration seems hell-bent on changing the framework of casting ballots in this country, clearly for political reasons,” Blumenthal said on a call with reporters Monday. “It is unconstitutional, as is argued in the courts by the litigation that is ongoing, but this disclosure indicates that it is also blatantly incompetent and incapable of actually delivering ballots that are lawful in this midterm election.”

In a statement on Tuesday, the White House disputed the whistleblower’s allegations.

“The process of building software to carry out this new verification check is neither complex nor unique for USPS since the Postal Service regularly uses bulk mailing and intelligent mail barcodes for a wide variety of large customers,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson.

The USPS did not respond to a request for comment.

The whistleblower is identified as an anonymous federal official who is being represented by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit group that represents public- and private-sector employees making such complaints. They allege that the USPS didn’t begin building its portal for verifying ballots “in earnest” until June, giving itself less than three months to complete a system that would ordinarily take at least nine to 12 months to build.

The agency last month finalized the rule for how it would implement the changes, which would create a massive new workload for election officials and put up hurdles for millions of voters to cast ballots by mail.

Large batches of ballots would be rejected by the portal if even a single ballot couldn’t be verified, the whistleblower said.

“As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state — effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the complaint reads. “Even under ordinary circumstances this would be problematic because of predictable errors in any barcode scanning process.”

The whistleblower said workers involved in developing the USPS system feared it would crash and described the process just days before the project was originally scheduled to be released to the public Tuesday as a “s--- show,” according to the complaint.

The whistleblower also said the USPS had ordered workers to continue developing its system, despite court orders blocking implementation of the project.

A federal court order Monday stated that the government could continue building its portal as long as the states aren’t required to participate.

World.title: U.S. military doesn’t plan to deploy troops to the polls in November, general says
World.content:
The U.S. military is not planning to send troops or other personnel to polling places during the 2026 midterm elections, according to Gen. Dan Caine, the country’s highest-ranking military officer.

Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, made the pledge in a letter to Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who had asked him and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about the role of the armed forces during the November elections.

“Election administration and security remain the fundamental responsibility of state and local officials,” Caine wrote to Slotkin. “The Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections. Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”

The letter, obtained by NBC News, was first reported by The Associated Press.

Caine wrote that “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.”

Federal law forbids the presence of U.S. troops at the polls “unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

The potential presence of troops at polling places has been the subject of debate since President Donald Trump told The New York Times in January that he regretted not having sent in the U.S. military to seize voting machines after his defeat in 2020.

Trump told the Times he “should have” done that after he considered it, and he falsely claimed that the 2020 election, which he lost, had been stolen.

Democrats are also wary after Trump last year sent National Guard troops to cities run by Democratic mayors — including Chicago and Washington — over their objections.

Slotkin and other Senate Democrats introduced legislation in June that would ban the president from sending armed military or federal agents to polling sites during elections.

During Trump’s first term in 2020, Slotkin — then serving in the House — and then-Rep. Mikie Sherrill, D-N.J., asked similar questions of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff at the time, Gen. Mark Milley.

Milley replied that the Constitution establishes procedures for carrying out elections, which he said were overseen by qualified officials from state and federal governments.

“We are a nation of laws. We follow the rule of law and have done so with regard to past elections and will continue to do so in the future. I do not see the U.S. military as part of this process; this is the responsibility of Congress, the Supreme Court and components of the Executive Branch,” he said.

World.title: Customers are losing their appetites over disturbing AI-generated menus
World.content:
AI “slop” is now increasingly on offer at brick-and-mortar establishments.

As AI image-making technology has grown more advanced — and cheaper to use, in some cases being free — images with a distinct “slop” flavor, namely ones with surreal or even disturbing attributes, have begun appearing on bodega, café and restaurant menus.

There’s the shrimp scampi whose shrimp look more like miniature life preservers.

A breakfast burrito with filling that looks more like something out of a horror movie.

And “protein” options that look like they’re covered in bugs.

One X user said she attempted to order an item advertised on a café’s outdoor menu only to learn it didn’t exist and was instead the product of ChatGPT.

The trend comes as the use of AI has grown from a tech-employee specialty to a nearly ubiquitous pursuit among white-collar workers — and as overall inflation in the economy has remained stubborn. The confluence of lingering cost pressures and advancing technology appears to be translating into a boom in smaller businesses deploying AI-designed graphics and logos.

There have been real-world consequences to the trend of AI slop making the jump from online into the real world. A coffee shop in San Francisco paid hundreds of dollars to have graffiti removed that appeared to be in response to its use of AI-generated food images on its facade, SFGate reported.

“I want people to come to our restaurant, but, like, why is this such a big deal that it influences people on such intense level,” co-owner Lyndsey Lozano told the outlet. “Like, is it really that horrific that you have to act on such a feeling?”

Lozano could not be reached for additional comment.

Many of the establishments displaying the food images likely created by AI are smaller, likely family-owned establishments, said Paul Shovlin, an assistant professor of English at Ohio University who studies AI. He said that it may simply be the case that many of the places displaying the AI food are running on shoestring budgets.

For some longtime designers, the advent of AI-related image making has been maddening — not to mention bad for their bottom lines.

World.title: Tropical Storm Edouard makes landfall in Louisiana, brings heavy rain to Texas
World.content:
Tropical Storm Edouard made landfall on Louisiana's coast Tuesday afternoon, the National Hurricane Center said.

Edouard had maximum sustained winds of about 60 mph when it made landfall near Johnson Bayou, Louisiana, close to the border with Texas, at 2:20 p.m. Central Time, the hurricane center said. Those winds dropped to 50 mph by 5 p.m. ET. It was moving northwest with a predicted path over Texas.

Earlier, forecasters warned that the storm could bring near-hurricane conditions to some areas along the U.S. Gulf Coast.

Maps show storm's path and forecast

A tropical storm warning is in effect for Texas's Port Bolivar, while the same alert for Louisiana's Vermilion/Cameron Parish Line has been discontinued, the hurricane center said in its 5 p.m. ET update.

Strong thunderstorms were expected to bring powerful wind gusts and dump heavy rain, with 3 to 6 inches possible along the Texas coast and inland, and some areas could get up to 9 inches.

Map shows the path of Tropical Storm Edouard, which is forecast to hit the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana on Tuesday. CBS News

A hurricane watch that had been issued earlier was also discontinued Tuesday. A storm surge watch was also discontinued for parts of Texas and southwest Louisiana, but the hurricane center still warned that coastlines could see rising water levels and possible flooding.

Forecasters warned heavy rain in both states "could produce flash flooding, especially in low-lying and urban areas."

After making landfall, Edouard moved inland along the northwestern Gulf Coast, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall across southeastern Texas on Tuesday night. The storm is forecast to rapidly weaken and dissipate by Wednesday night.

Map shows the rain forecast for Tropical Storm Edouard along the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana. CBS News

The storm was moving at about 7 mph on a northwest path on Tuesday afternoon.

Edouard is the fifth tropical storm so far during the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

World.title: Trump says Venezuelan oil could replenish depleted U.S. stockpiles. Will it?
World.content:
President Trump has framed last week's deal for the U.S. government to take a stake in Venezuela's oil reserves as a boon not just for gas prices, but also for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has dropped to historically low levels.

"One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves," Mr. Trump wrote on social media Sunday, saying "the 'topping out' process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States."

The plan could face hurdles, energy experts say. The oil produced in Venezuela is far heavier than most of the crude in U.S. reserves and would need to be converted. And rebuilding Venezuela's ailing oil industry could take years, requiring oil producers to invest billions while navigating the country's still-uncertain political and legal landscape.

"This project is very unlikely to produce new investment and new production anytime soon," said David Goldwyn, a former federal energy official who serves as president of the consulting firm Goldwyn Global Strategies and chairs the Atlantic Council's energy advisory group. He predicted the U.S. is "at least two years, if not five to seven years at best, away from seeing that production reach the SPR, directly or indirectly."

What is the Strategic Petroleum Reserve?

Established in the 1970s, after an oil embargo by Arab states choked off shipments to the U.S., the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has room for more than 700 million barrels of oil across a series of massive underground salt caverns in Texas and Louisiana.

But currently, the reserve holds just under 290 million barrels, its lowest level since the 1980s.

Mr. Trump has blamed the shortfall on the Biden administration, which released more than 200 million barrels of oil from the reserve in an effort to tamp down energy prices, especially in the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. The Trump administration has taken similar action to deal with the effects of the Iran war, pumping out over 100 million barrels in recent months.

The Department of Energy said in March it was planning to put 200 million barrels of oil back into the reserve within a year in order to make up for the Iran war-related drawdowns.

Then, last week, Mr. Trump announced the federal government struck a deal with Venezuela to take majority control of 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. The plan marks the Trump administration's most significant step to lure new investment to the Venezuelan oil industry since the U.S. military removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from power in January.

The White House has said the Pentagon will take a 35% equity stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, a private oil company that was granted concessions by the Venezuelan government to develop the oil fields.

As part of the arrangement, according to the White House, the U.S. will have the right to buy 20% of the oil drilled by the venture at the cost of production, "ensuring a stable supply of low-cost oil that can facilitate refilling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve."

Venezuelan heavy crude is "physically and chemically incompatible" with Strategic Petroleum Reserve

The crude oil that is typically stored in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is very different from the stuff that is typically drilled out of Venezuela.

Most of the crude from Venezuela's oil-rich Orinoco Belt is very heavy, compared to the lighter oil that is drilled in places like Texas, which makes transporting it and refining it into products like gasoline a more difficult endeavor. Oil producers often need to mix Venezuela's crude with other petroleum products so it can flow through pipelines.

Most of the oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, by comparison, is lighter.

"The kind of crude that [is] produced in Venezuela, which is very heavy, doesn't meet the specifications of the crude that is stored in the caverns," said Daniel Sternoff, a senior fellow at Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy and analyst at Energy Aspects.

Siddharth Misra, an engineering professor at Texas A&M University and chief technology officer of AlterNature LLC, told CBS News dense oil could pose technical challenges for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and would be difficult to extract from the caverns. It could be stored in the reserve if it were processed into a lighter product or carefully blended down, he said.

"Venezuelan extra-heavy crude is physically and chemically incompatible with the operating design of the SPR," Misra said in an email.

In the past, the Department of Energy has considered storing heavier crude in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in order to serve refineries on the Gulf Coast, many of which are designed to take dense imported oil. The department did not take that step, with one Government Accountability Office report citing the need to upgrade the reserve's infrastructure and the fact that stocking the caverns with heavy oil would make it harder to respond to shortfalls of light oil.

"DOE has analyzed heavy oil storage and found that the costs outweigh the benefits and storing heavy oil would present considerable operational difficulties," the Department of Energy said in a 2016 report to Congress. "The current inventory mix provides DOE with fungible crudes that maximize the flexibility of the Reserve in a crisis."

The department did store heavier Mexican crude oil in the 1980s and 1990s, but found that the need to keep it separate "had the effect of reducing the site's operational flexibility, efficiency, and drawdown capability during an energy emergency." It was later swapped for lighter crude.

Instead of pumping dense Venezuelan oil directly into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the federal government could essentially trade it for lighter oil that can be more easily stored in the caverns, Goldwyn and Misra said.

"While physically conditioning Venezuelan crude for static storage is technically possible, the most economically powerful way to execute the administration's plan is through an energy value exchange," Misra said. The oil from Venezuela could be sent to Gulf Coast refineries and sold, with the proceeds used to buy lighter crude, in what Misra called a "molecular swap."

CBS News has reached out to the White House for more details on the plan.

Rebuilding Venezuela's oil industry could take years

Many energy analysts believe the plan to push up Venezuelan oil production will take several years to translate to higher supply or lower prices stateside.

While Venezuela has the world's largest proven reserves, its oil industry has languished from decades of underinvestment and tight sanctions, and many large oil companies left the country when former President Hugo Chávez nationalized their assets almost 20 years ago.

Chevron is the only major U.S. oil company that continues to do business in the country. Other companies that left under Chávez have been slow to return, with ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods saying in a January event at the White House: "We've had our assets seized there twice. … To reenter a third time would require some pretty significant changes from what we've historically seen here and what is currently the state."

Goldwyn told CBS News it could take five to seven years to develop many of the Orinoco Belt oil fields that were included in last week's deal. Other previously active fields could be rehabilitated in a year and a half.

Building out the Orinoco Belt fields would require extensive investments in long-degraded oil wells, electrical transmission, infrastructure to transport the oil, facilities that can upgrade Venezuela's heavy crude oil and terminals to export it from the country, experts say.

"It requires a lot of further investment [and] a great deal of remediation of … production-related infrastructure, from wells all the way to pipelines, that has lacked any maintenance and has suffered a great deal of corrosion," said Scott Montgomery, a lecturer at the University of Washington and former petroleum geologist. "It's not going to happen quickly."

The White House has said NABEP is planning to invest up to $100 billion in the new oil venture.

Goldwyn also pointed to legal risks. The U.S.-Venezuela deal is controversial in both countries, with opponents questioning whether it complies with American and Venezuelan law — raising the prospect that after Mr. Trump leaves office or interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez is replaced by an elected leader, their successors could choose to walk away from the deal.

"That's a very expensive way to fill the SPR," he said, "and it's a long shot because it's not yet clear that Venezuela is commercially appealing enough for someone to spend billions of dollars to improve upgrading infrastructure, when it's not clear whether the next Venezuelan government or the next U.S. government will be at all interested in pursuing this arrangement."

World.title: Pa. police officer charged​ after fatally shooting student at wrong home
World.content:
An Upper Pottsgrove, Pennsylvania, police officer has been charged with voluntary manslaughter after allegedly shooting and killing a college student who was at the wrong house.

Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell was charged with voluntary manslaughter in the fatal shooting of 22-year-old Glenwood Earl Pysher IV on Aug. 23, Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele announced Tuesday.

Officials said Pysher knocked on the door of the wrong home after being out at a bar with friends. What followed was a very quick interaction with Farrell and a shooting that Steele said was not justified.

"This is not a legal use of lethal force," Steele said.

Steele said Pysher was out at a bar early on Aug. 23 before deciding to walk to a friend's house. But he knocked on the wrong door, leading the homeowners to report a break-in. According to a criminal complaint, Pysher had sent his friends a picture of the house he was at, and they realized he was in the wrong place, so he then sent them his location so they could come get him.

Before Pysher's friends arrived, Farrell showed up and found Pysher on a back patio, the complaint said. Officials said Pysher was unarmed. Farrell was equipped with a taser and a baton, but went straight to his pistol, according to Steele and the criminal complaint.

Steele said body camera video shows Farrell gave Pysher commands to put his hands up and drop to the ground. Body camera video showed Pysher putting his hands up and walking toward Farrell, according to a criminal complaint.

Farrell told Pysher to get down two more times and then yelled, "stoр or I'll-" but shot Pysher twice before finishing his sentence, the criminal complaint said. Pysher was about 17-20 feet away from Farrell at the time, the complaint said.

According to the criminal complaint, body camera video shows Farrell later telling another officer, "The guy f***ing charged me, screaming and yelling and wouldn't get down on the ground."

But Steele said that's not what they saw when they reviewed the video.

"The young man has his hands up, he does not have a weapon, he did not charge or act aggressively, he was not a threat to the homeowners, he was inebriated but listening to commands about putting his hands up," Steele said. "He's not trying to escape or didn't commit a forcible felony."

The complaint also noted "Farrell was a safe distance from Pysher, behind cover, as Pysher approached him with his hands in the air," alleging that "Corporal Farrell unreasonably used deadly force without any consideration of using less lethal means against Pysher."

CBS News spoke with Pysher's parents last week. They described their son as a good kid loved by his community. He was set to start at Saint Elizabeth University in New Jersey this week.

"They are trying very hard to understand why this happened, and why their son was taken away from them," Steele said.

Farrell turned himself in to Montgomery County detectives Tuesday. He is slated to be arraigned later Tuesday evening.

World.title: Rising bond yields threaten to push up U.S. borrowing costs
World.content:
Treasury yields edged higher on Tuesday, extending a global bond sell-off and threatening to raise borrowing costs for millions of Americans.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, rose to 4.78%, up from 4.75% late Monday and the highest level since January 2025. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for the Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions, rose to 4.37%, up from 4.34% late Monday. The 30-year Treasury hovered around 5.25% on Tuesday.

The global rout pushed a key Bloomberg gauge of bond yields to 3.72%, its highest level since June 2008. The sell-off is being driven partly by persistently high inflation and concerns about government debt, prompting investors to demand higher yields to compensate for the added risk.

"Fiscal concerns, rising energy prices and AI-related investment have lifted long-term government bond yields across major economies to multi-decade highs," James Reilly, a senior markets economist at Capital Economics, said in a research note Tuesday.

Here's what to know about the sell-off and what it means for you.

Why are bond yields rising?

Yields are rising as investors, spooked by inflation and rising government debt, dump their government bonds. Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions, with rising yields signaling that investors are demanding higher returns as investments grow increasingly risky.

Investors are also worried about rising energy prices as the U.S. and Iran continue to clash. The U.S. launched its military action against Iran in a month this weekend, causing oil prices to spike. Renewed tensions raised concerns that the war, now in its seventh month, could fuel inflation and prompt the Fed to raise the federal funds rate.

"The spike in borrowing costs comes as the latest flare-up in the U.S.-Iran war has raised concerns that central banks will hike interest rates to combat inflation from higher energy costs," Morningstar, an investment research company, said in a post on Tuesday.

Stubborn price pressures have been a concern for the Federal Reserve, which has sought to bring inflation down to its 2% annual target. Speaking at the central bank's annual conference in Wyoming last week, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said monetary policymakers will have "work to do" if inflation doesn't subside, suggesting the Fed could be prepared to raise interest rates when it next meets on Sept. 15-16.

Interest rate traders now assign a 66% chance that the Fed will raise its benchmark rate in September, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

What does the bond sell-off mean for you?

Movements in the U.S. bond market influence what everyday Americans pay for loans and how much interest they earn on their savings accounts.

Higher Treasury yields can push up costs for everything from auto loans and credit cards to personal loans and mortgages. The average 30-year mortgage rate tends to track the 10-year Treasury, meaning rising yields can push up home borrowing costs.

Elevated borrowing costs also tend to weigh on stock prices and make it more difficult for businesses to expand.

While higher yields hurt borrowers, they can help increase earnings for savers with high-yield savings accounts and CDs.

Where could bond yields go from here?

Yields could ease, but that's not likely in the near term, according to economists.

"Unlike past bond sell-offs, which had an obvious and often fixable cause, this one is unlikely to suddenly shift into reverse anytime soon," Reilly said in Capital Economics' note on Tuesday.

Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, the chief investment officer of the Americas and global head of equities for UBS Global Wealth Management, said in an email Tuesday that she expects yield volatility to persist in the near term before subsiding toward the end of the year. She projects 30-year and 10-year Treasury yields to end the year at 5% and 4.5%, respectively.

World.title: IRS audit revenue plunged following workforce reductions, watchdog finds
World.content:
Revenue from IRS audits plunged 35% in fiscal 2025 as the agency shed thousands of enforcement workers, according to a new report from the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, an agency watchdog.

The IRS collected a total of $6.5 billion from audits in fiscal 2025, which ended Sept. 30, down from $10 billion a year earlier, TIGTA said in its Aug. 26 report.

The group said that the number of IRS employees working in auditing and collections had dropped to 17,517 as of January 2026, a decline of almost 10,000 workers from fiscal 2024. The report added that the impact of the staff reductions may "become more apparent over time."

"These losses present a challenge to improving taxpayer service and enforcing the nation's tax laws," the tax watchdog said. "We are concerned about how staffing losses are impacting the IRS's ability to ensure that it meets department priorities."

Tax auditor exodus

The findings come after TIGTA last year found that the IRS lost one-third of its tax auditors during the first three months of the Trump administration. The employment decline was due to cost-cutting efforts by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, which sought to slash the federal workforce through a combination of layoffs and so-called deferred resignations.

The Treasury watchdog noted that because audits can take years to complete, some of the declines could be reversed as more cases are closed.

The IRS initiated 17% more large corporate audits in fiscal 2025 than a year earlier. But audits of new business partnerships fell 30% as a major reorganization at the agency shifted employees and delayed training for some revenue agents, the report said.

The IRS also started fewer audits of wealthy taxpayers. Agency staffers opened about 43,000 examinations of individuals with income over $400,000 in fiscal 2025, down 26% from a year earlier. As of January 2026, the agency's Global High Wealth program had 27% fewer employees than before the fiscal 2025 workforce reductions.

The Treasury didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Rising tax receipts

The IRS pointed to comments made by its CEO, Frank Bisignano, during congressional testimony in April, in which he said the agency is increasingly relying on technology to improve enforcement.

"Our advanced data and analytic strategies allow us to catch instances of tax evasion that would have been undetectable just a few years ago," Bisignano said. "Along those lines, the IRS is using artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced analytics to identify high-risk areas of non-compliance and fraud with greater accuracy."

Despite the decline in audit revenue, the IRS collected more total tax revenue in fiscal 2025 than the prior year, with federal taxes paid by taxpayers rising to $5.3 trillion, up 4.2% from the prior fiscal year, according to the Treasury watchdog group.

But Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts who has championed a federal wealth tax, said the data show that IRS employment cuts are a "dream come true" for high-income earners and corporations that skirt tax laws.

"Gutting the IRS is a win for wealthy tax cheats and a loss for working people who play by the rules," she said in a statement to CBS News.

IRS funding cuts

The drop in audit revenue marks a reversal from 2024, when the IRS planned to boost tax revenue through audits of wealthy taxpayers and corporations. Under the Biden administration, the Inflation Reduction Act directed $80 billion in funding to the IRS, enabling it to hire more auditors and revenue collectors.

In early 2024, the IRS forecast that the additional funding would help it reap hundreds of billions of dollars in additional tax revenue by pursuing overdue and unpaid taxes. However, Republican lawmakers warned that IRS auditors would target everyday Americans and cut billions in IRS funding.

The Trump administration has proposed additional IRS funding cuts for 2027. Policy experts have warned that further shrinking the agency's budget could make it harder to collect overdue taxes and go after tax cheats.

"The agency has fewer revenue agents, who audit the most complicated tax returns, than it has had since the 1950s, when the economy was far smaller and the tax code was far less complex," tax analysts with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan think tank, wrote in a June blog post.

They added, "Research shows that every dollar spent on IRS tax enforcement raises multiple dollars in revenue, which means that every dollar cut from IRS enforcement loses more than a dollar of revenue and adds to the deficit."

World.title: Which CD terms offer the best rates and returns this September?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

CD account interest rates are high across terms right now, but they aren't identical. sakchai vongsasiripat/Getty Images

A certificate of deposit (CD) account offers multiple advantages for savers in today's economic environment. A fixed interest rate that's higher than many alternatives is one of them. But not all CD accounts will come with the same rate and savers should expect to see a noticeable difference in what they're offered at their local branch and what they can otherwise secure by using an online institution. Since the latter doesn't have the same maintenance costs the former does, it can use those savings to offer better rates to account holders. Which bank you use, however, is only one factor determining the rate you can lock in. The account term, or length, is another critical one to understand.

CD terms can be as short as three months or as long as 10 years. Historically, rates (and, thus, returns) were higher on long-term accounts (those that mature in 18 months or longer). That dynamic then shifted in the volatile interest rate climate of recent years, in which banks often offered higher rates on short-term CDs. Is that still the case, however? With the high likelihood of an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve later this month, borrowers who have yet to take advantage of a CD should start by understanding which specific CD terms are currently offering the best rates and returns.

See how much interest you can be earning with a CD account here.

Which CD terms offer the best rates and returns this September?

Most CD rates sit around 4% this September, but there's a noticeable difference between 3.90% and 4.35%, both on paper and in what your ultimate return will look like when the account matures. Here are the four terms offering the highest rates this September:

18-month CD at 4.35%

2-year CD at 4.35%

3-year CD at 4.50%

5-year CD at 4.40%

And here are four accounts with lower rates to consider currently:

3-month CD at 3.95%

6-month CD at 4.20%

9-month CD at 4.10%

1-year CD at 4.30%

While it will be tempting to pursue the highest rate on this list, the reality is that if you won't be able to see the account through to its maturity date, it won't be worth opening. With early withdrawal penalties worth most or all of the interest earned on the account up to the point of withdrawal, it's critical that you only deposit an amount that you can keep frozen in the account through the maturity date.

In other words, the 4.30% on the 1-year CD may be better for you than the 4.35% on the 2-year option, even if the latter technically has the higher rate and the slightly better return.

Compare the best CD rates available to you here now.

Other accounts to consider

What about those savers who don't want to lock their money away at all? There are two alternative savings accounts for these savers to consider. High-yield savings and money market accounts both have competitive rates now, albeit both are a bit lower than the top CD accounts outlined above. The rates tied to both are also variable, meaning that they will rise or fall based on market conditions.

That said, the access to your funds with either account won't be restricted the way it would be with a CD, so it could be a viable option for those who want to take advantage of today's higher interest rate climate without sacrificing access to their money.

The bottom line

The best CD rates and, thus, most lucrative returns, are all aligned with long-term CDs this September. And while a 4.40% or 4.50% CD interest rate should never be discounted, savers should also evaluate their short-term account options, too, to see which fits in their savings strategy best. They should also evaluate their high-yield savings and money market account alternatives, neither of which will restrict access, which can be critical for many in today's unique economic landscape.
