World.title: BEL says temporary generation capacity to begin operations by mid-September
World.content:
BEL says temporary generation capacity to begin operations by mid-September

By Zoila Palma: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) says temporary generation capacity currently being installed at the Westlake Facility is expected to begin operations by mid-September as the company moves to strengthen electricity supply and reduce the risk of further disruptions to the national grid.

In a press release, BEL said recent power outages have highlighted the importance of maintaining adequate generation reserves, particularly when electricity supply from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) is temporarily unavailable.

“Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) informs its Customers and the public that the Company continues to actively manage available generation and advance measures to strengthen electricity supply and the reliability of the National Grid.”

BEL said that on August 25, available in-country generation stood at approximately 103 megawatts (MW), while evening demand reached 122 MW. On August 31, available generation was approximately 109 MW against demand of 117 MW.

“On both occasions, the temporary loss of electricity supply from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), at a time when local generation was already below demand, resulted in temporary loss of power to the National Grid.”

The company said available in-country generation continues to be affected by seasonal conditions, scheduled maintenance and reduced output from some generating facilities. BEL said it is closely managing these conditions while working to ensure adequate supply is available to meet customer demand.

BEL also pointed to measures taken following an anticipated electricity supply shortfall identified in 2025.

“As part of these efforts, BEL advised in October 2025 of a potential electricity supply shortfall in 2026, following which Cabinet made a declaration of emergency under the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) (Request for Proposals) Regulations, 2024.”

The company said the emergency declaration allowed it to procure temporary generation capacity, which is now being installed at the Westlake Facility and is expected to begin operations by mid-September 2026 for an initial six-month period. “

This additional generation will provide important support to the National Grid, particularly during periods of high demand or when another source of power becomes temporarily unavailable.”

BEL further noted that its August 26, 2026 letter to the PUC forms part of its ongoing regulatory responsibility to assess electricity supply requirements for the upcoming 12 months and ensure appropriate measures are taken to support Belize’s growing energy needs.

While BEL continues to strengthen available generation, it warned that controlled power interruptions or load shedding may still be necessary to maintain grid stability, particularly if a significant source of supply becomes unexpectedly unavailable. “BEL will continue taking all available measures to minimize any impact on Customers.”

World.title: Tents? No Way!
World.content:
The tent at Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth where some classes were held

MIDDLE QUARTERS, St Elizabeth — Describing tents as heat traps, Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett is insisting that all of her 252 students must be housed in ventilated classrooms when the new academic year opens next Monday.

“The tent cannot be used; it is extremely hot. We tried to use the tent last academic year. We had grade one initially in the tent and after the [Primary Exit Profile] exam we had grade six going to the tent and giving grade one a feel of a classroom space,” she told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“However, due to the heat the children were not able to use the tent for the entire day. They had to be out of it by midday. Right now it is hotter than what we were experiencing last academic year, so I don’t see where I can use that tent to host the classroom,” she added.

Last week, the Caribbean Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology and The University of the West Indies Climate Studies Group Mona advised governments, businesses, farmers and households across the region to step up preparations for potentially severe climate extremes as El Niño conditions are and set to intensify the hot and dry conditions already affecting parts of the Caribbean.

Both entities warned that the region should remain particularly vigilant as August to October marks the peak of the Caribbean’s heat season.

This year’s El Niño is on track to be the strongest on record, threatening to unleash extreme weather across the globe and make 2027 the hottest recorded year by far.

Under such severe heat, tents would not be suitable to serve as classrooms for children.

On Monday, when asked how all her students would be accommodated, Principal Watson-Barrett said the National Education Trust (NET) had promised to deploy temporary wooden classrooms, but up to Monday afternoon there was no structure or even foundation to give assurance of the buildings.

“I am yet to see them. Between the Ministry of Education, NET, and the contractor, they promised that we would be getting two buildings each holding two classrooms, so that would be a total of four classrooms. Up to this morning (Monday) there was no updated information. The contractor said he is waiting on NET to give approval for the building of the [wooden] classrooms,” Watson-Barrett told the Observer.

She said the school is exploring two options to accommodate students if the temporary buildings are not erected in time.

“We will have to look at rotation and/or merging of classrooms into one room. For instance, last academic year I had a classroom with two grade two classes and they were placed in one room and then the teachers team-teach,” she said.

“Because of the heat, also, I am not considering a shift system. Imagine coming to school at 12 o’clock to start classes in this heat on a shift system,” added Watson-Barrett.

She said the school is expected to have seven accessible classrooms based on ongoing construction work.

“Currently, we have one block that is 85 per cent complete. That block can host two classrooms. The other two blocks that are available are currently being worked on and we are hopeful that by this Friday those two blocks will be completely cleaned and ready for the opening of school, September 7,” she said.

A deteriorating building had to be demolished last week at the school.

“That would leave me wanting five more classrooms to accommodate the other students, because as of last week I lost a building that had four classrooms, the guidance counselling room and the library on it,” said Watson-Barrett.

She said Middle Quarters Primary and Infant will be receiving students from the now shuttered Giddy Hall Primary School, three-and-a-half kilometres away.

“Even without the inclusion of the Giddy Hall Primary children I would be short of classrooms. I have 170 students expected to attend school in the primary department with an additional 29 from Giddy Hall Primary School, seeing that the school was consolidated and we are the receiving school,” she said while pointing out that five academic and two auxiliary staff were moved to her school from Giddy Hall.

“The ministry has made the decision to close down smaller schools based on the enrolment there… For the infant department we are expecting to have about 52 students,” she added.

When asked about the availability of potable water, Watson-Barrett said the school has been getting reliable water supply from the National Water Commission.

“Currently, I am seeing where improvement has been made on the water system; it is still being worked on, but whenever it is locked off we purchase water,” she said.

“During Hurricane Melissa [last October] the drums were blown off the building. However, we have a large metal tank that we store water in. Those drums that were blown down are yet to be replaced,” she added.

World.title: Tough guardrails
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen (second left) gestures while speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. Flanking him are CGC executives (from left) Caleigh Reid, legal officer; Damion McKenzie, senior director, investigations and enforcement; and Shainee Myles, director of human resource. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

WITH Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator set to commence operations by March next year, once all outstanding conditions are met, the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) is assuring that stringent guardrails are in place to keep criminal elements out, with operators required to verify players, monitor suspicious transactions, and protect vulnerable gamblers.

Speaking during this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange, both CGC Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen and Senior Director of Enforcement and Investigation Damion McKenzie outlined a multi-layered system of checks that will follow casino operations from the moment a player registers to the regulator’s ongoing monitoring of the business.

The safeguards include know-your-customer (KYC) checks, scrutiny of suspicious transactions and sources of wealth, anti-money laundering controls, surveillance systems, responsible-gaming interventions, and direct regulatory access to the casino’s operations.

The officials were speaking as Adamas Grand Casino Limited, Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator, moves towards opening at Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover. The CGC granted the operator its licence on July 29, but the licence is conditional and does not yet authorise the casino to begin operations.

CGC Legal Officer Caleigh Reid said the operator must first satisfy all remaining requirements, with March 31, 2027 set as the deadline to commence operations.

“They have a specific time frame in which to open. There are certain deliverables that they have to satisfy us with, certain things that they have to provide us with before they get the go-ahead. Right now they have the licence, but they are not authorised to begin operations until all of those other deliverables are satisfied, which is all outlined in their conditions of licence,” she said.

The safeguards are intended to address several risks associated with casino gaming, particularly money laundering, organised crime, problem gambling, and the potential exploitation of vulnerable players.

At the heart of the CGC’s financial crime controls will be requirements for casinos to know who their customers are and to scrutinise the money moving through their operations.

According to McKenzie, the regulator will not simply assess an operator’s anti-money laundering system once and walk away.

“A part of our legislation requires us to do ongoing monitoring as it relates to money laundering and proceeds from illicit means. We will continue to monitor, but the training that we provided to our officers… allow them to understand the different typologies that are related to money laundering in the gaming sector, to understand the myriad things that happen that can be classified as money laundering,” McKenzie said.

The commission will also examine whether an operator has properly carried out those checks and whether the financial profile of a player makes sense.

“Our audit plan also allows us to go in and check on persons who have signed up, if you did the proper KYC and anti-money laundering check against this person: What does this person do? How did they come about the cash? The source of wealth? So all those checks continue throughout the lifecycle of the licence,” McKenzie added.

Furthermore, Allen noted that the commission is designated as the competent authority for casino gaming under the Proceeds of Crime Act, with responsibility for anti-money laundering, counter-financing of terrorism and counter-proliferation financing compliance in the casino sector.

He explained that casino gaming in Jamaica is restricted to approved Integrated Resort Developments, meaning a casino cannot operate as a stand-alone gambling establishment.

Therefore, this creates a two-stage screening process.

“At the first stage of the development of it, the Government wants to be satisfied that the operators, the financiers, their funding is from good sources, they have good standing in other jurisdictions, not just for the development but for the operations of the casino… and when you come to stage two, when you come to us, we then conduct our own due diligence, specifically in respect to the conduct and operations of a casino,” Allen said.

He also noted operators will be required to maintain surveillance systems capable of supporting regulatory monitoring, as well as provide space for commission officers at the premises.

“In Las Vegas, on any one casino property, there are about 5,000 cameras. These cameras can zoom in and read the serial number on a note at a table four miles down the road. We have similar surveillance and monitoring requirements for the casino. More than that, the operator is required to have facilities on its premises for the commission and our officers to be able to have access to and at any time go on site and monitor,” Allen said.

The CGC’s guardrails are not limited to criminal activity. Allen explained that the regulator’s responsible-gaming framework is designed to identify people who may be developing harmful gambling habits and provide avenues for intervention.

That framework includes staff training, player information, behaviour monitoring, exclusion and self-exclusion mechanisms, as well as controls on advertising. The commission has worked with the Responsible Gaming Council of Ontario and signed an MOU with RISE Life Management, which has experience in counselling and self-exclusion relating to gambling.

“The mechanism behind responsible gaming is that the staff will be trained to spot persons who have a problem, persons who sit all day and gamble. There’s some form of intervention from the staff to allow some kind of cooling-out period for this individual. Also, because Jamaica will be a cashless system, they’ll also be able to track the pattern of a player to see his betting patterns and some form of intervention can be implemented because of that pattern of constant gambling, constant topping up, constant chasing, constant losses,” he added.

Allen also assured that responsible-gaming controls will extend to how casinos advertise and promote their services.

He said s should not target children or young people and should not rely on influential figures who children might look up to.

He also noted that the CGC intends to leverage existing responsible-gambling programmes, including initiatives involving schools, while keeping casino-related promotion within the resort environment.

World.title: 60 years of Tastee: A celebration of food, music and Jamaican legacy
World.content:
Patrons enjoy the free concert hosted by Tastee Jamaica as part of their 60th anniversary celebrations.(Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FOR 60 years, Tastee Jamaica has commanded the support of Jamaicans, becoming as synonymous with the island as the patty itself. But the company’s legacy stretches far beyond food. Having established itself as a key contributor to the discovery of some of Jamaica’s most talented entertainers, Tastee has firmly cemented its place in the hearts of Jamaicans globally. On Friday night, the company showed its appreciation to its local fanbase, treating scores of Jamaicans to a free concert of the highest entertainment quality.

With Emancipation Park transformed into a sprawling celebration of music and memories, the event was far more than an anniversary concert. Hosted by veteran broadcaster Jennifer “Jenny Jenny” Small, it was as much a celebration of Jamaican music as it was a birthday party for the company. Agent Sasco, Tarrus Riley, King Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland and a host of others created an atmosphere that reflected both legacy and loyalty.

For some of the night’s performers, however, appearing on the Tastee stage carried even greater significance, having gained their break in the industry decades ago through the talent search spearheaded by the company.

“We a eat patty over 60 years. Big up Tastee. Tastee is the one that make people know me international,” said King Yellowman as he paused his set to remind the audience of his third-place finish in the inaugural Tastee Talent Contest in 1979.

Giving a commanding performance, Yellowman treated the crowd to a short yet energetic set, which included songs such as I’m Getting Married in the Morning and Zungguzungguguzungguzeng.

Also turning in a vibrant performance was the 1979 competition winner, Nadine Sutherland. She performed hits such as Action, Starvation — which she released a year after her win — and Babyface. In what she described as a full-circle moment, Sutherland recalled how Tastee changed her life when she was just 11 years old.

“I’m still in disbelief that it’s been 46 years since the 11-year-old me was brave enough to get on that stage. I was known as ‘the little girl from Above Rocks’ who was brimming with confidence. I had to draw back for that little girl tonight and just soak it all in. I’m grateful that I’m still here, and I still love this,” she said.

Tastee’s own story began in 1966 when Vincent and Valerie Chang opened the company’s first operation at Union Square in downtown Kingston. As demand grew, the business expanded, eventually establishing its headquarters in Cross Roads and developing a footprint across the island. Somewhere along that journey, Tastee’s relationship with Jamaica began extending beyond what it served across the counter.

Over its decades-long run, the Tastee Talent Contest — later known as the Tastee Talent Trail — became an important proving ground for emerging Jamaican performers, including Beenie Man, Papa San, Cobra, Mr Vegas, T.O.K., Glacia Robinson, Brian and Tony Gold, and several others.

It was therefore little surprise that the company received an abundance of praise from the night’s performers.

That spirit of giving was not confined to Tastee’s entertainment history. After the company awarded 13 students $60,000 each towards tuition through its back-to-school initiative, Agent Sasco extended the gesture from the stage, committing to cover the tuition of another high-school student.

Sasco’s giveback didn’t stop there, as he treated patrons to a delightful set, which included spirited performances of crowd favourites such as Winning Right Now, Hand To Mouth, Hand Inna Di Air, Idiot Thing Dat, Banks of the Hope, and others.

Alaine also turned in a quality set, performing songs such as Dreaming, Rise In Love, Bye Bye and Ordinary Love.

Abijah, Carey Sayles, Tony Rebel, Sista Pat, Tarrus Riley, Richie Stephens and saxophonist Dean Fraser were among the evening’s other performers, rounding out a musical package that traversed generations and genres.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the concert, patrons sought to explain Tastee’s longevity. Noting that not many companies would think to give back to their supporters in such a tangible way, concertgoers said Tastee’s knack for recognising the support of its consumers has helped establish its 60-year legacy.

“Tastee is not just about the patties. They’ve always been about giving back in some way, shape or form. If it weren’t for Tastee, Jamaica and the world would not have discovered talent such as Beenie Man, Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland, and so many others,” said Suzette Morgan.

“Their dedication to the Jamaican people has always been evident and it was proven again tonight when they hosted this free concert. The fact that we didn’t have to pay anything didn’t take away from the quality of the show. We got solid performances while we nibbled away on patties. It was a perfect way to celebrate their anniversary.”

Marcia Stewart agreed.

“Tastee is big in Jamaica because it’s big on supporting Jamaicans. We love our patty and the company has proven over the years that they value the support of their consumers. Hosting a free concert showed exactly how much they appreciate Jamaicans, and I hope they last another 60 years,” she said.

Friday night proved that while patties built the Tastee name, the company’s legacy has also been shaped by the love of the Jamaican people.

For decades, Tastee fed Jamaicans more than simply food. Through its talent competition, it also helped feed an entertainment industry that would eventually send some of the artistes it discovered onto stages around the world.

Behind the songs, the memories and generations of performers sharing one stage was the story of a Jamaican institution that has managed to remain part of the country’s everyday rhythm for six decades.

At 60, that relationship remains as much a part of Tastee’s legacy as the patties themselves.

World.title: Jamaica secures Tottori training base
World.content:
(From left, front) Tottori Athletics Association President Shinichi Hamasaki, Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association President Garth Gayle and Tottori Prefecture Governor Shinji Hirai; (back) Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie, Sports Minister Olivia Grange and Japan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Jamaica Kohei Maruyama during yesterday’s ceremonial signing of a partnership agreement between Jamaica and Tottori Prefecture in Kingston.Garfield Robinson

JAMAICA’S preparations for the 2027 World Athletics Championships received a boost yesterday with the signing of a 2027 World Athletics Championships Training Camp Agreement between Jamaica and Tottori Prefecture in Japan.

The agreement represents the latest chapter in a sporting partnership that began in 2007 following the World Athletics Championships in Osaka and has since developed into a nearly two-decade relationship built around athletics, cultural exchange and friendship.

Garth Gayle, president of the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA), was pleased with the agreement, which he believes sets the tone for a successful campaign at the championships.

“We want to ensure the best facilities and all that is needed for a successful campaign in Beijing 2027,” Gayle said.

Gayle says the Japanese will provide additional technical support, while the camp will also allow Jamaica to stage trial meets for its athletes. He said the trial meets proved pivotal for Oblique Seville, who went on to strike gold at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo.

“The camp also allows the athletes to acclimatise as there is not much difference between Japan and China, so this is a good opportunity for coaches, managers and athletes to get ready for a successful championship,” Gayle said.

Sports Minister Olivia Grange described the renewed agreement as an important step in strengthening Jamaica’s sporting diplomacy and international partnerships.

“Today’s signing represents another decisive step in strengthening Jamaica’s sporting diplomacy, international partnerships and preparations for continued success globally,” Grange said.

She said the relationship with Tottori had evolved beyond simply providing Jamaican athletes with a venue to train, becoming a lasting friendship between Jamaica and Japan.

“What began in 2007, in the wake of the World Athletics Championships in Osaka, has evolved into more than a training arrangement. It has become a lasting friendship between Jamaica and Tottori,” Grange said.

The partnership has already produced tangible benefits for Jamaica’s athletes, particularly through the 2025 training camp ahead of the World Championships in Tokyo.

Grange says Team Jamaica was provided with world-class facilities and comprehensive support services, allowing athletes and staff to concentrate fully on competition preparation.

She also highlighted the contribution of hundreds of volunteers, interpreters, medical personnel, officials, sponsors and community members who helped make the Jamaican delegation feel at home during its stay.

Grange also pointed to exchanges between Jamaican athletes and Japanese communities, including a visit by Assinie Wilson, Kelly-Ann Beckford and teammates to students at Hakuto Special Needs School. That interaction subsequently inspired the Buddy Art Project, through which artwork created by students with disabilities was incorporated into flags displayed to welcome the Jamaican delegation.

Other exchanges included Jamaican athletes interacting with kindergarten children in Sendai, where they played games and received handmade medals.

“These moments remind us that this relationship extends far beyond training and competition; it is a bond of friendship, community, and shared humanity,” Grange said.

The sporting ties between the two countries have also been strengthened through the Japan Exchange and Teaching Programme, which saw Jamaican Olympian Christine Day appointed Jamaica’s first sports exchange advisor.

Day is based in Tottori, where she shares her sprinting knowledge and mentors athletes, providing another avenue for the development of athletics and cultural links between Jamaica and Japan.

Tottori Governor Shinji Hirai and Chairman Shinichi Hamazaki attended the signing and greeted guests in Jamaican dialect with “What a gwaan” before reverting to Japanese, with their remarks translated by an interpreter.

Minister of Local Government and Community Development Desmond McKenzie was also on hand for the signing and highlighted the broader relationship between Jamaica and Japan, including the friendship and cooperation between Tottori Prefecture and Westmoreland.

McKenzie says Jamaica and Japan are celebrating 62 years of bilateral relations, with cooperation extending beyond sport into community development, emergency communications and economic revitalisation.

He also highlighted the impact of Japan’s Grant Assistance for Grassroots Human Projects programme on micro and small businesses and municipal corporations, while noting the Social Development Commission’s continued collaboration with Japan on community initiatives, including sport.

World.title: MESSI’S IMPACT
World.content:
Argentina Captain Lionel Messi poses with the FIFA World Cup Trophy after Argentina won the 2022 World Cup final football match against France at Lusail Stadium in Lusail, Qatar, on Sunday, December 18, 2022. (Photo: AFP)

FOLLOWING Lionel Messi’s decision to retire from international football, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts believes the Argentine legend has made a significant impact on Jamaican football through his exploits on the international stage.

Messi made the announcement in a statement on social media on Monday, bringing an end to his 21-year stint with the national team.

“This is one that hurts me a lot. I love, I loved, and I will always love being part of the national team. I gave everything I had, and I don’t have anything more to give,” he said.

“I leave with peace and pride, knowing that together with my teammates we gave you moments we once dreamed of. It was crazy to experience all of this with you. I love you! Thank you God for making me Argentine.”

The 39-year-old cemented his legacy in 2022 after guiding Argentina to the FIFA World Cup, ending a 36-year drought. He almost made it two World Cup title lifts in a row in this summer’s World Cup in the USA, Mexico and Canada but went down 1-0 to Spain in the final.

Eight-time Ballon d’Or winner Messi leaves as the country’s all-time leading goal scorer and most capped player with 125 goals in 207 appearances. He also led Argentina to the 2021 and 2024 Copa America titles and the gold medal at the 2008 Olympics in Beijing.

Ricketts says Messi’s contribution on football, particularly in Jamaica, cannot be ignored.

“Messi in contemporary football would be arguably the most talked about player and probably the most highly rated player right now. He would have impacted the lives of so many young boys and girls,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer. “If you walk around any township, you will always see somebody, some youngster wearing a shirt marked Messi and that just goes to show what sport generally, and what football in particular, can do to the psyche of a nation.”

“Every good thing must come to an end and it has been an era for Messi and even his impact on the just-concluded World Cup speaks volumes for his footballing skills and of course the impact that he would have made in global football. Truly, Messi has impacted not just Jamaica but the world.”

One of Messi’s milestone international games came against the Reggae Boyz, when he made his 100th appearance for Argentina in a 1-0 win at the 2015 Copa America in Chile.

Former national midfielder Jobi McAnuff played the full 90 minutes and swapped shirts with Messi at full time, which he says is one of the greatest moments of his career.

McAnuff, though, says he developed an even greater respect for the Argentine maestro after his kind gesture towards the entire Jamaican team following the game.

“There was a queue of Jamaican players, staff, everything, waiting for him outside the changing room,” he said. “He just took his time, signed every autograph, shaking hands, pictures, like [he was] class. He did not have to do that. They’re the little things for me that just set him apart for me, yes he’s a great footballer, but we come back to people as people and just respect that you can show to people.”

The Reggae Boyz would face off with Messi again seven years later in an international friendly in New Jersey, just months before lifting his first-ever World Cup title. Messi came off the bench and scored twice to lead Argentina to a 3-0 win.

“Everybody wanted to get to the touching distance of Messi — not even so much to touch him, but to get close to him — and a number of our players tried to embrace him, tried to take pictures with him. Our coaching staff really wanted to be identified with arguably one of the best footballers of all time,” Ricketts recalled.

“I don’t know if it’s fair to say we have lost an icon but he has now gone into retirement, but the name Messi will probably live forever in the minds of those who have an interest in the sport of football.”

Many players over the years have been dubbed the “next Messi”, including former Reggae Boy Chevone Marsh, who earned the nickname during his days at Cavalier FC and Calabar High.

Ricketts says the chances of the world producing another Messi are slim but hasn’t ruled it out, especially with the possibility that talent could come from Jamaica.

“What has happened in recent times is that coaching education now has improved leaps and bounds, not just locally, but throughout the Caribbean, throughout Concacaf and throughout the world,” he said.

“We would have established probably the best coaching education programme, so it’s not far-fetched. It’s not impossible but certainly, based on the newness of our coaching skills and our coaching workshops, it’s not far-fetched. It’s certainly not impossible.”

World.title: Fashion Radar: House of Clay
World.content:
​An intimate behind-the-scenes moment dressing the bride on her wedding day in an off-white stretch-satin slip gown. (Photo courtesy of House of Clay)

Tuesday Style Fashion (TSF) spotlights Keisha Allen, creative director of luxury for bridal fashion brand House of Clay.

TSF: Please share your House of Clay story — how you started, and the reason behind the name.

House of Clay: My journey to House of Clay officially began when I studied garment production and fashion design for two years at Garmex HEART Academy between 2005 and 2007. Following my training, my first job was at a prominent bridal boutique here in Jamaica. That experience proved to be pivotal. I fell in love with the transformational power of a wedding gown — that exact moment when a woman saw herself in the right dress and her entire demeanour changed. I could physically see her confidence bloom and watch her realise just how beautiful she was. I knew then that I wanted to dedicate my life to creating that feeling for women of all shapes and sizes.

Working directly with gowns from international designers and doing minor alterations also exposed me to global standards. I had already resolved in my heart before that any brand I built would be of such high quality that it could stand beside any international designer brand and not feel out of place. Seeing those gowns up close simply confirmed that this was standard work I could definitely do and surpass.

The reason behind the name ties back to my faith. I remember reading a story in Jeremiah 18 about a potter working at his wheel, taking a vessel of clay that didn’t turn out as he wanted, squashing it, and starting over to reshape it. I thought about the significance of how a potter takes a lump of clay — which, to most people, and as we say in Jamaica, is really just “dirt” — and turns it into something meaningful. Clay seems insignificant to the untrained eye, yet in the hands of a skilled artisan, it becomes a masterpiece. That mirrors my process with textiles. Taking a flat, two-dimensional piece of fabric and sculpting it to perfectly contour or fit a three-dimensional woman’s body is an art form.

Initially, the brand was simply supposed to just be called Clay. However, when we went to register the business in 2011, we were told we couldn’t register the single word “Clay” on its own because it’s a common substance, so we had to add something to it and registered as “Clay Fashioned.” But that felt a bit too on-the-nose so I could not settle with it. Having always been a fan of global couture houses, I realised that many of them use “House of” before their brand name — like House of Chanel. I knew this was the kind of house and legacy I was building, so we decided on House of Clay in 2015. While our inner garment labels simply read “Clay,” the company name reflects our commitment to couture, uncompromising quality, and the legacy we are building in how we make women feel… like “The Most Beautiful Woman in the Room”.

TSF:When did you thread that first needle and know this was your destiny?

House of Clay: I don’t think I knew it was my destiny the exact moment I threaded my first needle. As a child, I was always making clothes for my dolls. My father was very perceptive and good at recognising those subtle traits and creative gifts, so he bought me my first sewing kit when I was about nine years old. Even then, I wasn’t dreaming of fashion yet — I actually wanted to be a paediatrician!

It wasn’t until high school, around third form, that I realised I had a bit of a love-hate relationship with the sciences. I started evaluating what I genuinely loved doing and what I was naturally good at. I loved working with my hands, creating, and engaging in meticulous tasks like hand-sewing and embroidery — even the most tedious parts. That was when the thought clearly hit me: I want to be a fashion designer. From that moment on, I set my mind to pursuing it.

I grew up with a very meticulous mother, so a detailed and deliberate approach to my work came naturally. Because of that, I was never drawn to “fast” fashion or quick, ready-to-wear pieces you could whip up in a few hours. In my early days, of course, I made those kinds of garments because I had to master every aspect of garment construction. But I found that I was always most at peace, happy, and in my element when doing intricate, labour-intensive work — like hand-beading an entire gown over several days. Where others might feel anxious or restless during such tedious processes, I enter a state of complete calm and focus. Looking back, I realise that inclination is rare; even among talented creators, not everyone gravitates toward the technical, painstaking side of couture. That affinity was the quiet signal that this was where I belonged.

TSF:Why wedding dresses?

House of Clay: There are two primary reasons why I chose bridal wear. First, from a purely technical standpoint, bridal is the pinnacle of couture. Virtually every major couture runway show concludes with a showstopping bridal gown because it represents the highest, most complex form of garment construction — and naturally, that level of craftsmanship is where I gravitated.

Second, and most importantly, a wedding dress is arguably the most significant garment a woman will ever wear in her lifetime. From my earliest days working with brides, I fell in love with being part of that sacred moment. It is a true privilege to create something that doesn’t just fit a woman, but honours her and helps her feel breathtakingly beautiful and confident on one of the most important days of her life.

TSF: Take us back to the completion of that first gown.

House of Clay: When that very first bride trusts you with her wedding gown, the feeling is almost overwhelming. It comes with an incredible sense of reverence, paired with a genuine fear of messing up — because you know this is not just an ordinary dress; it is monumentally important to her. Looking back, I felt the fear and did it anyway, pouring absolutely everything I had into it. As a naturally creative person, the design aspect is often the easy part. Designing simply takes deep compassion — listening intently to what the bride desires, understanding her fears, and being mindful of her insecurities. Once you have that connection, and hopefully taste, creativity naturally flows to create a beautiful design. What truly makes it a masterpiece — what sets the process apart, is the technical execution — the desire and discipline to operate at the absolute highest standard.

After weeks upon weeks of meticulous, painstaking labour, stepping back to look at that finished gown on the hanger and thinking, “Wow, I made that,” was incredible. But the most significant moment — the moment that still defines my work to this day — is when she puts it on. Seeing her posture shift, her expression change, and watching that same transformational confidence and joy wash over her is my ultimate reward. Experiencing that same feeling that first made me fall in love with bridal wear as a young consultant confirmed everything for me.

TSF: Who in the field of wedding gowns do you most admire and why?

House of Clay: When I was first starting out, the designer I admired most was Vera Wang. Back then, her name was completely synonymous with luxury bridal, but what fascinated me was that she wasn’t creating typical, traditional wedding dresses. She essentially turned the bridal industry on its head.

She stepped into the space without trying to conform to it, which I thought was brilliant, brave, and deeply admirable. Her approach proved that there are always brides who want to wear something that authentically represents who they are, rather than simply following traditional expectations. That willingness to innovate and stay true to a distinct artistic vision is something I have always respected.

The Core Ethos of House of Clay



At the heart of House of Clay are three fundamental brand pillars that define every single gown we create:

Transformation: We believe that every woman’s body is inherently beautiful, regardless of shape or size. Our philosophy is that a woman should never have to force herself to fit into a gown; rather, the gown must be engineered to honour and fit her unique structure and architecture. It is about accentuating who she is so she feels completely radiant and confident.

Craftsmanship: This is at the very soul of what we do — from technical pattern drafting to intricate hand-finishing. In today’s fashion climate, true pattern drafting has become somewhat of a lost art, with many relying on shortcuts like “freehand cutting”. We hold fast to the mastery of pattern drafting because it unlocks endless structural possibilities and ensures precision fit right from the initial foundation. Coupled with traditional couture finishing techniques and meticulous attention to internal details (down to the millimeter on every seam allowance), our garments are built to world-class standards.

Made in Jamaica: We take immense pride in our roots. Jamaica is world-renowned for its global impact in music and athletics — we have given the world reggae and the fastest athletes alive. We believe Jamaican fashion deserves that exact same global stage. Growing up, there was often a stigma attached to local dressmaking, where “Made in Jamaica” was associated with ill-fitting, homemade, or poor-quality garments. House of Clay is actively dismantling that narrative. Everything we produce is designed and crafted in-house right here in Jamaica, serving as a standard for couture, luxury, and excellence.

Photos: Terry-Ann Miller | Merrick Cousley Photography | Courtesy of Keisha Allen

World.title: Sheree Martin named first female CEO of NCBJ, effective Sept 1
World.content:
Sheree Martin appointed CEO of National Commercial Bank Jamaica

KINGSTON, Jamaica — After months of acting in the post, Sheree Martin has been appointed chief executive officer by the Board of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), effective September 1, 2026.

She will be the first woman to hold the post.

Martin served as interim CEO since January 19, 2026, leading the bank’s strategic and operational priorities with a focus on efficiency, governance and the customer experience.

In a statement, the bank said her appointment provides continuity as it continues to work on the same priorities.

Group Chief Executive Officer of NCB Financial Group Limited and Chairman of NCBJ Robert Almeida said Martin’s leadership during the interim period reinforced the board’s confidence in her ability to lead the bank.

“Sheree brings deep institutional knowledge, a strong understanding of our customers and a clear appreciation of how the different parts of the Bank must work together to deliver,” Almeida said.

“She combines strategic judgement with practical, hands-on leadership and a strong focus on execution. These qualities will serve NCBJ well as it builds on the progress already underway.”

Martin said she was honoured by the appointment and energised by the opportunities ahead.

“NCBJ has an extraordinary legacy, talented people and a vital role in the lives of our customers and in Jamaica’s development,” she said. “I look forward to working with our board and teams to build on that foundation – accelerating our progress, strengthening the customer experience and bringing the full capabilities of the bank together more effectively.”

She added, “Our priorities are clear: empower our people within the right culture, improve the way we deliver and earn our customers’ confidence through the quality and consistency of the service, financial solutions and platforms they experience every day.”

Martin brings more than 20 years of executive leadership experience across the financial services and energy sectors. Before assuming the role of interim CEO at NCB, she had leadership responsibility for several functions including retail banking, operations, credit underwriting, marketing and enterprise information management.

World.title: Former gang member found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Rapper Tupac Shakur attends a voter registration event in South Central Los Angeles, August15, 1996. (AP Photo/Frank Wiese, File)

LAS VEGAS, United States (AFP) — Duane Davis, a former Los Angeles gang member, was found guilty on Monday by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur.

Thirty years after the rap legend’s death at a Las Vegas casino, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.

World.title: Security-Update: Wie hart treffen Deutschlands Konsequenzen Russland? – mit Peter Neumann
World.content:
Vier Wochen nach dem Anschlag auf eine ukrainische Frachtmaschine am Flughafen Leipzig/Halle hat die Bundesregierung heute offiziell Russland verantwortlich gemacht: Nach Erkenntnissen von Polizei, Nachrichtendiensten und internationalen Partnern soll ein russischer Geheimdienst hinter der Sprengstoffdrohne stecken.

Innenminister Alexander Dobrindt und Außenminister Johann Wadephul kündigten als Reaktion die Schließung des russischen Generalkonsulats in Bonn, die Kündigung des Russischen Hauses in Berlin sowie neue EU-Sanktionen an. Am selben Tag wurde ein Umspannwerk in Brandenburg angegriffen – mutmaßlich mit selbstgebauten Raketen.

Im Gespräch mit Rixa Fürsen ordnet Peter Neumann (King’s College London) ein, ob die Reaktion aus Berlin wirklich die „konsequente Antwort” ist, die Wadephul versprochen hatte und wie verwundbar Deutschland tatsächlich ist, wenn Flughäfen und Kraftwerke gleichermaßen zur Zielscheibe werden.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.
