World.title: Aboriginal community still damaged, without key services months after floods
World.content:
At the end of a dust-laden road on the banks of the Daly River, the remote Indigenous community of Nauiyu bears the scars of disaster.

The entrance road is marred by large potholes eating into speed bumps, while mounds of silt line the outskirts of town.

Potholes can still be seen around Nauiyu / Daly River after the remote NT community flooded earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

It has been three months since residents of Nauiyu, also known as Daly River, returned home after back-to-back record floods in February and March forced them to evacuate.

Outside his house at the end of town, life-long Nauiyu resident James Parry can point to the exact step the floodwaters rose to.

"It covered 15 stairs — the whole bottom half of the house," he said.

James Parry says his family were lucky because they could move some of their belongings to the second-floor of their home. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"The tables were flipped over, the couches were flipped, my bed, my freezer."

He said he was one of the luckier members of the community, as he and his family were able to move some of their belongings upstairs.

"Everybody else lost everything — cars, homes, the lot," he said.

James Parry says so many Nauiyu residents lost everything in the floods. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mr Parry said the 2026 floods were the worst he has ever seen and there is mounting frustration that key services in the community were not yet fully online.

"The aged care centre is full of asbestos, and we only have a few old people left," he said.

"Kids are not turning up to school since they got back; the teachers have to go around door-to-door to get these kids to come to school."

James Parry showed the ABC areas still damaged by flooding in Nauiyu / Daly River earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He also said various repair works have not been done well, noting large gaps beneath doors leading to dust travelling inside and glass windows replaced with plastic.

"Some of those council homes had wooden benches, wooden drawers, wooden floors, they were all ripped out," he said.

Of particular concern is the boil water alert still in place for the community.

Ever since their return, residents' drinking water supply has come from pallets of bottled water packages routinely unloaded outside the Nauiyu general store.

"No one's told us anything," Mr Parry said.

The only access to clean drinking water is from deliveries of pallets of bottled water to the town. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

'It doesn't feel like home'

Nauiyu resident Kieren Karritpul said the damage had fundamentally changed the town.

"This place is not really 100 per cent," he said.

"It doesn't feel like home."

As of the end of August, several residential buildings in the community were still without power, impacting living arrangements and preventing key workers from returning to the community.

Kieren Karritpul is reviewing the damage to the Merrepen Arts Centre and its equipment in Nauiyu / Daly River. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"My brother and my niece have been staying over at my house because their house still doesn't have power," Mr Karritpul said.

On a shady street in the centre of the community, Merrepen Arts Centre, where Mr Karritpul works, stands dormant among mounds of dirt and damaged art materials.

The centre, which employs more than 40 artists, is one of the buildings that has gone without power since the flood, depriving residents of a source of income and community.

Kieren Karritpul says the art centre's closure has meant tourists have to travel to Darwin to purchase local artists' work. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"Every now and then I get pulled up at the shop or clinic by people asking when it will open, or when they will get their canvases," he said.

" We have to tell [tourists] to go on the three-hour drive to Darwin if they want to buy things. "

Though empty and without power, Merrepen Arts Centre managers have still been issued a power and water bill covering "fixed daily charges" for the first half of 2026.

Questions raised around flood response

The sorry state of Nauiyu several months on from the floods has prompted questions about plans for remediation.

After the last wet season, the Northern Territory government announced a $100 million flood recovery fund to repair damaged infrastructure and aid with flood mitigation.

Daly River faces massive clean-up bill after record flood Residents of the Northern Territory town of Nauiyu / Daly River have started returning home after spending three months in evacuation centres following extensive flooding.

So far, only $12.5 million of the fund has been spent, with just $500,000 put toward Nauiyu in the form of a plan to relocate the town to higher ground.

Labor MLA Dheran Young, who represents the Daly electorate in the Territory parliament, said it was disappointing the community had been left behind

"The CLP government need to apply for the Commonwealth Disaster Relief Fund to ensure services can get back up and running," he said.

" To date, my understanding is that they haven't applied after the disaster relief fund under these extraordinary circumstances. "

In August, the Commonwealth made a million-dollar investment in Nauiyu through the National Indigenous Australians Agency.

"The scale of damage experienced by the community has been immense," Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy said.

Malarndirri McCarthy says the damage done to Nauiyu from flooding earlier this year has been significant. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

"These investments will support community-led recovery efforts, helping to restore critical community facilities [and] strengthen local services."

The funding package, primarily aimed at local Indigenous corporations, sought to restore essential services, assets and accommodation for key workers.

The Northern Territory government did not respond to questions on Nauiyu or the recovery.

Mr Parry said the community has been visited by engineers and other personnel planning the town's relocation, in accordance with the NT government's investment.

He was frustrated, however, that there has not been more action ahead of the coming wet season.

James Parry says he is frustrated that the NT government has not done more to prepare for the next wet season. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"You got mango flowering now, you got tamarind, you got the cashew; those three things tell you that the rain's on the way here," he said.

With the near future uncertain, he wants a solid commitment from governments that funding will flow through to key services, and a plan will be in place should flooding re-occur.

"They've got everything, they've got homes to go to," he said.

World.title: The fight to save Cavendish bananas as farms fall to Panama disease
World.content:
Leon Collins's banana farm south of Cairns is the newest front in the war against a soil-borne fungus threatening global production of Cavendish bananas.

"Some days you think you're fighting a losing battle. It is really hard," the Tully farmer said.

"It's heartbreaking, but it's just what we've got to live through."

For more than a decade, growers along the Tully River have been living with Panama disease tropical race 4 (TR4), which, despite their best efforts, has been slowly spreading down the waterway.

The fungus cannot be eradicated.

Its spores live in the soil for decades, waiting to attack banana plants through their roots and eventually kill them.

It poses a particular risk to the Cavendish variety of banana, which accounts for more than 97 per cent of fruit produced in Australia, and much of the world.

The latest incursion of TR4 was detected on one of Leon Collins's farms. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

As the chair of the Australian Banana Growers' Council, Mr Collins had been leading the fight against TR4, but the latest, and 11th, local detection means he is now also in the trenches.

"It's a fact of life and sometimes you get dealt the wrong cards," he said.

But he hoped the rest of the industry would be spared the same battle.

"I believe our saviour is going to be plant breeding," Mr Collins said.

Researchers, scientists and plant breeders have been edging ever closer to a new weapon, one growers can deploy ahead of an incursion: a Cavendish banana variety that can withstand the disease.

New frontline, new frontiers

In 2024, researchers at the Queensland University of Technology received federal government approval to commercialise the world's first genetically modified banana, developed specifically to resist TR4.

Genetically modified bananas could be on shelves by 2027 Australia's first genetically modified banana has been tweaked to protect it from a disease that's on the verge of wiping out crops around the world. Researchers hope it may be on our shelves by 2027.

Named QCAV-4, it looks and tastes the same as a Cavendish, the only difference being the added resistant gene.

The fruit was trialled in the Northern Territory, where Panama disease has been established since the 1990s, but currently no-one is growing it commercially.

But Anthony James from QUT's Centre for Agriculture and the Bioeconomy said growers were showing interest.

"Growers in the Tully Valley would love to see our bananas trialled more extensively so they can understand whether they're comparable to current varieties," he said.

"We have a commercialisation department that will work with the industry, growers and retailers in the future to progress the commercialisation."

While the bananas are not currently available to Australian consumers, historically shoppers have been sceptical about genetically modified foods.

The Office of Gene Technology Regulator's most recent report on community attitudes (2024) found only 32 per cent of respondents were willing to eat GM fruit and vegetables.

But Dr James said QCAV-4 had undergone rigorous scientific and regulatory assessment, and that when the banana became available to consumers, they could be confident it was safe to eat.

Queensland University of Technology developed a GM banana resistant to TR4. (Supplied: Queensland University of Technology)

Other projects, like the one led by Naomi Abbott from North Queensland Banana Research, are using more established methods, like crossbreeding.

"We've commenced plant breeders' rights on a few of our key lines … so we're expecting to have our first Cavendish line available by 2028," she said.

"But there's still many other varieties in the pipeline and hopefully some of those will also make it the whole way through our testing process and reach commercialisation."

She said the TR4-resistant breeds were developed in collaboration with FIA, a Honduran banana breeding program.

"In our pipeline now, we've probably got 30 to 40 hybrids that we're working with … we've four that we're dealing with a bit more seriously," she said.

" In terms of Cavendish, there's two we're working with and one clear frontrunner. "

Outward symptoms of panama disease start with the banana plant's leaves beginning to wilt and go yellow. (ABC Rural: Charlie McKillop)

Queensland's Department of Primary Industries was also working towards introducing TR4-resistant Cavendish varieties, with help from overseas.

Principal Horticulturalist Jeff Daniels said seven Cavendish lines had shown sufficient resistance, but they did not also produce enough fruit to be suitable for the Australian industry.

"They all have a yield penalty ranging from 60 to 90 per cent of the industry standard," he said.

" We're not there yet and … additional investment is required to develop a better TR4-resistant Cavendish than we currently have available. "

Living with Panama disease

So far, the strict biosecurity measures implemented by Tully region growers appear to have contained TR4 to that district.

"It's a whole approach that we're using all together and it's very hard to slow this thing down," Mr Collins said.

"Innisfail [50km south] is our largest growing area now so we have to protect that and make sure we keep it free of disease."

Banana farmers in the Tully region have employed strict biosecurity measures to slow the spread of TR4. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Nearby Tully banana farmer Adrian Crema did not have TR4 on his farm, but said the threat was never far from his mind.

He was encouraged by the progress towards resistant varieties.

"I was really, really happy to hear that the research is getting done and there's possibly some varieties coming on the horizon," he said.

World.title: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams's body double in movie, makes US Open debut
World.content:
Making a US Open debut as a teenager is a daunting task, but American Thea Frodin is no stranger to the bright lights.

The 17-year-old played at her home slam for the first time, going down in straight sets to world number two Elena Rybakina 6-3, 6-2.

There were plenty of fans at Grandstand who were there to see Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, but Frodin was a mini-celebrity in her own right.

Frodin, from California, was a body double at the age of 12 in the 2021 film King Richard, a movie starring Will Smith about the rise of Serena and Venus Williams with the help of their father, Richard Williams.

Fordin was the body double for actor Demi Singleton, who played Serena in the film, and is now forging her own path at Flushing Meadows.

There was no Hollywood screenwriting for Fordin's debut, with Rybakina never troubled in the win that came after a near three-hour rain delay.

Fordin was not disgraced in the straight-sets defeat. Down 1-5 in the second set, the teenager fired four aces, saving three match points, to extend the match just one extra game.

"She played really well today, and she has great shots," Rybakina said of her teenage opponent.

Fifth seed comes from behind to avoid another US Open boilover

Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli has rallied from two sets down to win his first-round match at the US Open, avoiding another early upset on the men's side.

Flavio Cobolli needed more than four hours, and five sets, to make it to the US Open second round. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The French Open runner-up beat Francisco Comesana 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, finishing his match that lasted 4 hours, 12 minutes, not long after some sun had broken through the clouds and allowed play to start on all the outside courts after a morning of rain.

Cobolli made his first career two-set comeback to avoid joining Novak Djokovic (fourth seed) and Arthur Fils (10th seed) among early losers in a men's draw that was already missing top-ranked Jannik Sinner due to injury.

Cobolli said he took a bathroom break after the second set and decided to change everything.

"So I changed all the dress that I started with today and it works," Cobolli said.

"In grand slams it's never done. You have to fight until the last point."

Ninth seed Taylor Fritz, the 2024 runner-up, rolled to a 6-3, 6-2, 6-4 victory over 18-year-old fellow American Darwin Blanch.

Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Madison Keys was the only other player to move into the second round early in a tournament where rain threatened to hamper the schedule for a couple of days.

Showers that began Monday night, local time, and could be on and off through the middle of the week delayed play on all the outer courts, allowing action only in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, which have retractable roofs.

Keys, the 22nd seed, beat 19-year-old Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 in the leadoff match in Ashe. The 2017 US Open runner-up was knocked off in the first round last year in Flushing Meadows.

"It's always tough playing someone young and up-and-coming, and they're going after their shots," Keys said.

"And it's so hard to play a first round of a Grand Slam, so nervous and just wanting to do so well. So, really happy I was able to kind of fight through that and win today."

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, 17th seed Alex Eala, and men's first seed Alexander Zverev are scheduled to play later on the final night of round one matches.

ABC/AP

World.title: Suaalii to return as Wallabies embrace painful lessons of Santa Fe drubbing
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii to return as Wallabies embrace painful lessons of Santa Fe drubbing Iain Payten September 2, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star winger Max Jorgensen said the painful lessons of a record drubbing in Santa Fe in 2024 are driving the Wallabies to another win in Argentina on Sunday – and they’ll have Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back on deck to help the cause, too. Ikitau and Suaalii are set to re-unite in the Wallabies’ midfield for the first time in over a month, after the duo’s last started together in Australia’s 57-10 win over Italy in Perth. Loading Ikitau subsequently underwent an ankle operation and missed the first three Tests under Les Kiss, and after sitting out the second Test win over Japan with a hamstring injury, Suaalii was named on the bench for last week’s win over the Pumas. Hunter Paisami and Isaac Henry performed well in the midfield for the last two Tests, but Kiss is set to re-install Ikitau and Suaalii for the Mendoza clash, in which the Wallabies will be chasing rare back-to-back wins over the Pumas in the same year.



Ikitau and Suaalii were first paired together in the latter’s debut at Twickenham in late 2024, and were a mainstay under Joe Schmidt. In 25 Tests since Suaalii’s debut, the duo have been the starting centres on 16 occasions, including against the Lions and the win in Johannesburg. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate after Max Jorgensen’s winning try in 2024. AP Related Article Wallabies The Wallabies have never won consecutive Tests in Argentina. This is why that could change Ikitau won the John Eales medallist last year and Suaalii was nominated for World Rugby’s breakthrough player of the year in 2025. Debate has continued to rage about where Suaalii is best deployed, however, and that was heightened when Paisami and Henry both took their opportunities well in Kiss’ early games. But Suaalii also responded by providing strong impact from the bench last week.



Kiss has kept several fresh players up his sleeve for the Mendoza clash, knowing the grim recent history of the Wallabies in their second games in Argentina. Since the Rugby Championship changed to biennial mini-tours in 2022, where teams tour and play consecutive games in one country, the Wallabies have won the first game and been thumped in the second. In 2022, they were beaten 48-17 by the Michael Cheika-coached Pumas, and in 2024, a win in La Plata was followed by 67-27 drubbing, the highest ever score conceded by the Wallabies. Len Ikitau passing against Ireland in July. Getty Images The Wallabies were leading 20-3 after 30 minutes but then fell apart in the Santa Fe heat, conceding 64-7 in the next 50 minutes. “A big motivation is looking back at two ... years ago when we were over here last time. We had a close win in the first game. It was good to get that and then sort of went to Santa Fe the week after and put in a pretty poor game, and lost by a fair bit, as everyone knows,” Jorgensen said.



“It’s looking back at that and seeing how we cannot let that happen again.” Jorgensen made his run-on debut that day, and was one of several players battling illness. The rookie was so crook he even hospitalised after the game and missed Tests in subsequent weeks. Jorgensen said the lesson was you can never rest on your laurels when playing the Pumas. Harry Wilson leaves the field after the Wallabies were thumped by Argentina in Santa Fe in 2024. Getty Images “Never count them out. We were obviously, I think we were up 19-0 (sic) in that game in Santa Fe. And so it feels like you’re on the front foot and then everything just flips. So it’s sort of not letting them back into the game, knowing they have the ability to do that and then not allowing it to happen.”



Jorgensen said while he was enjoying the continuity of selection in the back three, with Tom Wright and Harry Potter also getting an extended run, there were no concerns about the chopping-and-changing happening in most other positions. Related Article Australian rugby Tahs send SOS to club rugby playmaker amid ugly contract stoush Following on from Schmidt, Kiss has also been shuffling his cards every week, but Jorgensen said the team’s bonds were strong enough to prevent any lack of cohesion. “With all the changes happening, I don’t think it matters too much,” he said. “We’re such a tight group, so well-connected. No matter who comes in, in what jersey, we know they’re going to do a job for the team. And yeah, as I said, it actually really doesn’t matter.



“Everyone knows what each player brings and their skill set, knows how to work with them. That connection is there for whoever comes on the field.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Number of Australians missing in Nepal, Tibet revised to 38; US launches major strikes against Iran
World.content:
Housing Minister Clare O’Neil says a temporary downturn in house prices should not alarm Australians after a report by CBA said a price recovery would not occur until 2027.

“It’s clear that house prices are softening around the country, and I really recognise that, you know, for many Australians, their house is their most important asset,” O’Neil told Seven’s Sunrise.

Minister for Housing Clare O’Neil. Dominic Lorrimer

“What that report also shows us is that house prices will start to grow again, and CBA says that will happen at some stage next year. The housing market in Australia is inherently cyclical. We see periods of really strong house price growths that are followed by a period of housing downturn. That’s happened now about four times in the last decade.”

O’Neil said downturns in property prices were always expected, and were an inevitable outcome of the government’s attempt to stabilise intergenerational inequality in the housing market after it made major changes to property taxes in its May budget.

“We’ve seen house prices in our country grow by 300 per cent since the year 2000. If that happens for another generation in our country, our nation is going to be unrecognisable to us in terms of equality and aspiration.”

World.title: ASX set to slump as Wall Street falls on higher oil prices, yields
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump as Wall Street falls on higher oil prices, yields Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated September 2, 2026 — 6:33am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks closed broadly lower as another round of US military strikes on Iran sent oil prices higher, stoking worries about stubbornly high inflation. A bond market sell-off deepened, putting more pressure on stocks. The S&P 500 index fell 0.7 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.8 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slid 1 per cent. The major indexes have lost ground three days in a row. Wall Street went backwards on Tuesday, with technology stocks weighing down indexes. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to slump, with futures at 6.11am AEST pointing to a fall of 78 points, or 0.9 per cent at the open. The ASX lost 0.1 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is weaker at US71.47¢. The weak start to September follows a shaky but mostly positive month for Wall Street. Every major index notched monthly gains in August. Rising yields signal that investors are demanding a higher return from Treasurys because they are becoming riskier. Growing government debt is highlighting that risk.



The US debt surpassed $US40 trillion ($US56 trillion) two weeks ago, a shocking milestone as defence costs and interest on the burgeoning deficit make up an enormous share of federal spending. World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCrime Bank of America vice president killed in Times Square stabbing Myles Miller September 2, 2026 — 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: A knife-wielding suspect killed a Bank of America vice president in Times Square on Monday (US time), in an attack that injured another victim and left the suspect dead. Erin Piacenti died at the hospital from the stabbing injuries, according to the New York City Police Department. Piacenti was a vice president of business selection and conflicts at the bank, according to a LinkedIn profile. Times Square stabbing victim Erin Piacenti was a vice president at Bank of America. LinkedIn Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Pamela Cisneros, 49, first approached a 68-year-old Rhode Island tourist near West 41st Street and Seventh Avenue around 4.30pm (local time) with two knives, stabbing the man in the abdomen as he stood with his wife waiting to cross the street. He was hospitalised in stable condition. Cisneros then continued north on Seventh Avenue and stabbed Piacenti in the abdomen near 42nd Street, about 20 seconds after the first attack, Tisch said.



“We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague,” a Bank of America spokesperson said in a statement. “She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones.” Witnesses flagged down nearby officers, who confronted Cisneros between West 42nd and 43rd streets while she was still holding both knives. Officers spent about four minutes trying to persuade her to drop them. Loading “I’m not dropping anything. I would rather kill both of you,” Cisneros told the officers, according to Tisch. Officers used Tasers as Cisneros advanced toward them, but they were ineffective, Tisch said. Two officers then opened fire, striking her. Cisneros was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she died.



Related Article Updated

Crime Luigi Mangione admits killing insurance CEO, asks to void state murder trial Cisneros had no arrest history with the NYPD, though department records showed two previous encounters involving mental illness, in 2018 and 2019, Tisch said. Investigators have no reason to believe the attack was an act of terrorism, she said. Bank of America’s main Manhattan office is located right near the heart of Times Square at One Bryant Park. It’s also built out its presence in the city with a financial centre at nearby Two Bryant Park and space at the Grace Building. Major crime has declined in New York City for four straight years. Murders fell to a record low in the first half of this year, and major crime overall dropped 5.6 per cent. Still, felony assaults have risen for six consecutive years. World.title: The quality you should most wish for your children if you want to build family wealth
World.content:
MoneySavingParenting The quality you should most wish for your children if you want to build family wealth The Economist September 2, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you could bestow any quality on your children, which one would you pick? Great intelligence? Empathy for humanity? Much greater respect for their parents? The ability to pass a fridge without opening it? Deborah Cobb-Clark, an economist at the University of Sydney, has a different answer: an internal locus of control. Closely linked to the idea of agency, an internal locus is linked to self-control. One paper concluded that households with a greater sense of agency save more of their wealth. iStock The concept of a locus of control was developed in the 1960s by a psychologist with the tremendous name of Julian Rotter. It is closely linked to the idea of agency. People with an internal locus of control believe that they are able to shape the world around them; those with an external locus of control tend to think that luck, destiny or other people determine their fate. It turns out that being an internal is pretty useful. It motivates effort: one study by Ms Cobb-Clark and her co-authors looked at a cohort of newly unemployed people in Germany, and found that people with a more external locus of control searched less intensively for work than internals.



Why spend time hunting for jobs, after all, if outcomes are disconnected from actions? Externals also had lower reservation wages, the minimum pay they were prepared to accept for a job. Related Article Analysis

IVF Superbabies for the white and wealthy? The societal debate we need to have An internal locus is linked to self-control: another paper concluded that households with a greater sense of agency save more of their wealth. It helps turn intention into action, too, seeming to prompt people with entrepreneurial aspirations to actually take the leap and become a founder. Being an internal also seems to help your descendants. A paper by Warn Lekfuangfu of Universidad Carlos III de Madrid and her co-authors found that, other things being equal, the locus of control of expectant mothers is correlated with the effort they put into active parenting. Internals are more likely to think that time spent developing the skills of their sprogs will pay off. Externals are more likely to think: “Little Rodney is just a helpless plaything of the gods.”



The locus of control exists on a spectrum. Ms Cobb-Clark worries most about the small minority of people who never really develop a sense of their own agency at all. But many more routinely underestimate their power to exert control over their circumstances. In her pointedly titled book, You Can Just Do Things, Cate Hall cites research by Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake, then of Columbia University, showing that people misjudge how likely others are to respond to requests for help. In a series of experiments, the researchers asked participants how many strangers they would have to approach to complete a range of tasks, from filling out questionnaires to borrowing a mobile phone to make a call. The actual numbers were much lower than the estimates, not because people are unbelievably nice, but because it is awkward to reject a direct request for help.



In another experiment, Steven Levitt of the University of Chicago got people who were dithering over a big decision to toss a virtual coin to help them make their choice. A toss in favour of change made it much more likely that someone would go ahead and break with the status quo. Those who did reported being much happier than those who did not. That suggests many people who would benefit from change lack the sense of agency to seize control of their own destiny without a nudge. Related Article Opinion

Inheritance ‘I didn’t earn this’: The silent shame of inheriting family wealth Paridhi Jain Money contributor If an external locus of control is holding back individuals, it could be hindering organisations, too. A new paper, co-written by Feng Xu of the Harbin Institute of Technology, looks at adoption of artificial intelligence by manufacturing firms in Shenzhen. The researchers find that internals, who are more likely to see AI as a skill to master, are happier to share knowledge about their experiences of it. Externals, who are more likely to see the technology as a threat to their job security, are more prone to hiding information. What should managers do about this? They could test for locus of control in hiring processes: Andrej Karpathy, a quotable AI researcher, has said that as a trait, agency is both more powerful and scarcer than intelligence.



Compensation and promotion systems should reward achievement as a matter of course, but that link can be made more explicit. Cultural norms can also be set to prompt people towards taking action. “Ask forgiveness, not permission” is a mantra that can have some pretty ugly consequences if you have lots of high-agency people and no guardrails. But the idea behind it is sound. For the story behind the headlines, listen to The Morning Edition, with a new episode live every weekday from 5am. World.title: This Met Gala controversy may be the most tone-deaf move she’s made. What now for Anna Wintour?
World.content:
Listen LifestyleFashionStyle This Met Gala controversy may be the most tone-deaf move she’s made. What now for Anna Wintour? Samantha Selinger-Morris September 2, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Galliano – the fashion world’s theatrical ringmaster par excellence – has always enjoyed his contradictions, and champions. The one-time head designer of one of France’s most storied fashion houses, Christian Dior, Galliano once quipped: “Fashion is above all an art of change.” Yet for all his headline-grabbing and famously fantastical runway shows, he was perennially looking one way: backwards. Historicism was a hallmark of his craft. His 1997 haute couture debut for Dior, after all, celebrated the opulence of 1930s opium dens in Shanghai. Then came this week, when he announced on social media that he would be stepping back from the highly anticipated – and controversial – planned retrospective of his work, which was to be the centrepiece of next year’s Met Gala. John Galliano has taken the unprecedented step of withdrawing from a planned exhibition in his honour at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. What does this mean for Met Gala tsar Anna Wintour? The duo is pictured here in January 2025 in Paris. WWD via Getty Images



The one year Galliano has tried, for decades, to leave behind, has finally caught up with him, in a way it arguably hasn’t before. This was 2011, when a French court handed Galliano a total of €6000 ($13,565 now) in suspended fines, after he was found guilty of “public insults” based on origin, religion, race or ethnicity. This, after he was caught on film, hurling antisemitic rants at people in a Parisian bar. Among other moments of racism. Many of fashion’s most illustrious figures have tried to rehabilitate Galliano’s image over the years. Supermodel Kate Moss famously chose Galliano to design her wedding dress for her 2011 nuptials, telling Vogue she wanted “a classic Galliano, those chiffon Thirties kind. I’ve lived in his dresses for years, and they just make me feel so comfortable.” But it’s arguably Vogue’s global editorial director Anna Wintour who has acted as his rehabilitator-in-chief, reportedly smoothing the way for him to nab lucrative fashion roles, after Dior fired him.



Related Article Met Gala John Galliano withdraws from Met Museum exhibition following backlash And then, the Met Gala. “She’s wanted this for years, and she seemed to have gotten her way,” says Amy Odell, host of the Back Row with Amy Odell podcast, and author of Anna: The Biography, about Wintour. Speaking with host Samantha Selinger-Morris on The Morning Edition podcast, Amy Odell says the cancellation of Galliano’s retrospective is about far more than Galliano’s own troubled history, revealing that the wider fashion industry is now being reigned in after years of tolerating egregious behaviour. Click the player below to listen to the full episode, or read on for an edited extract of the conversation.



Selinger-Morris: Can you just remind listeners of what John Galliano actually did? It’s about 15 years ago now … you have called Galliano previously, “the industry’s most famous antisemite”, not without good reason. What did he say and do? And what does it say about the fashion industry that he was chosen then for this in the first place? Odell: There were two incidents, one of which was filmed and released by The Sun newspaper. In that video, Galliano was saying, “I love Hitler.” I believe that’s a direct quote. And, “Your forefathers would be gassed and dead,” something like that. And there was another incident at a café in Paris where he was drinking, and he was saying racist and antisemitic things to another couple. One of the people involved in that incident is named Philippe Virgitti, and he appears in the John Galliano documentary, John Galliano: High and Low, which Anna Wintour had a hand in pulling together. Condé Nast is a producer on that, and she sat for an interview for that. But that also seemed like a way for her to rehabilitate John Galliano’s career following these horrific incidents. Anyway, Virgitti spoke to Kevin Macdonald, who did that documentary, and he said he didn’t think John Galliano was sorry. He never apologised to him. And he testified at the hate crime trial in Paris. And he said at that trial that he didn’t think Galliano was racist. And he said in the documentary that he regretted saying that, basically, and that he does believe that Galliano is racist because he never apologised to him.



Galliano and Wintour at a party at Bergdorf Goodman (1998). Wintour nurtured a young Galliano’s career, helping him secure positions and Givenchy and Dior. Getty Images Selinger-Morris: So is this cancellation of John Galliano a rebuke of Anna Wintour? She’s always been his champion. And it has to be said that it was a very unusual choice to have him celebrated with a Metropolitan Museum retrospective because it’s only twice before in the history of the Met Gala that a living designer has been chosen to be the focus of a retrospective: that was Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017. So is this something of a public recognition that her taste doesn’t matter, or it’s off? Related Article Opinion

Met Gala The Amazon takeover of the Met Gala signals an apocalypse for fashion Damien Woolnough Fashion editor Odell: I think she’s made some extremely tone-deaf moves, particularly around the Met Gala, and this may be the biggest. And the Met could not risk the donors pulling funding and pulling donations. And it also – I don’t think it could risk the … how should I say this? – I mean, I don’t think it could risk that round of backlash. And I don’t know at this time, the story just broke really hours ago. But what was Vogue hearing aside from the stuff that we’ve been reading in the press? Were they hearing from celebrity publicists who were saying, “We can’t have our clients go”? How do you attend the event if it becomes the “Antisemitic Pro-Hitler Met Gala”? How do you attend as a celebrity? What good does that do you?



Listen to the full podcast episode in the player above. Hear the story behind the headlines on The Morning Edition podcast, every weekday from 5am on Apple, Spotify or your favourite podcast platform.

World.title: Suaalii to return as Wallabies embrace painful lessons of Santa Fe drubbing
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii to return as Wallabies embrace painful lessons of Santa Fe drubbing Iain Payten September 2, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star winger Max Jorgensen said the painful lessons of a record drubbing in Santa Fe in 2024 are driving the Wallabies to another win in Argentina on Sunday – and they’ll have Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back on deck to help the cause, too. Ikitau and Suaalii are set to re-unite in the Wallabies’ midfield for the first time in over a month, after the duo’s last started together in Australia’s 57-10 win over Italy in Perth. Loading Ikitau subsequently underwent an ankle operation and missed the first three Tests under Les Kiss, and after sitting out the second Test win over Japan with a hamstring injury, Suaalii was named on the bench for last week’s win over the Pumas. Hunter Paisami and Isaac Henry performed well in the midfield for the last two Tests, but Kiss is set to re-install Ikitau and Suaalii for the Mendoza clash, in which the Wallabies will be chasing rare back-to-back wins over the Pumas in the same year.



Ikitau and Suaalii were first paired together in the latter’s debut at Twickenham in late 2024, and were a mainstay under Joe Schmidt. In 25 Tests since Suaalii’s debut, the duo have been the starting centres on 16 occasions, including against the Lions and the win in Johannesburg. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate after Max Jorgensen’s winning try in 2024. AP Related Article Wallabies The Wallabies have never won consecutive Tests in Argentina. This is why that could change Ikitau won the John Eales medallist last year and Suaalii was nominated for World Rugby’s breakthrough player of the year in 2025. Debate has continued to rage about where Suaalii is best deployed, however, and that was heightened when Paisami and Henry both took their opportunities well in Kiss’ early games. But Suaalii also responded by providing strong impact from the bench last week.



Kiss has kept several fresh players up his sleeve for the Mendoza clash, knowing the grim recent history of the Wallabies in their second games in Argentina. Since the Rugby Championship changed to biennial mini-tours in 2022, where teams tour and play consecutive games in one country, the Wallabies have won the first game and been thumped in the second. In 2022, they were beaten 48-17 by the Michael Cheika-coached Pumas, and in 2024, a win in La Plata was followed by 67-27 drubbing, the highest ever score conceded by the Wallabies. Len Ikitau passing against Ireland in July. Getty Images The Wallabies were leading 20-3 after 30 minutes but then fell apart in the Santa Fe heat, conceding 64-7 in the next 50 minutes. “A big motivation is looking back at two ... years ago when we were over here last time. We had a close win in the first game. It was good to get that and then sort of went to Santa Fe the week after and put in a pretty poor game, and lost by a fair bit, as everyone knows,” Jorgensen said.



“It’s looking back at that and seeing how we cannot let that happen again.” Jorgensen made his run-on debut that day, and was one of several players battling illness. The rookie was so crook he even hospitalised after the game and missed Tests in subsequent weeks. Jorgensen said the lesson was you can never rest on your laurels when playing the Pumas. Harry Wilson leaves the field after the Wallabies were thumped by Argentina in Santa Fe in 2024. Getty Images “Never count them out. We were obviously, I think we were up 19-0 (sic) in that game in Santa Fe. And so it feels like you’re on the front foot and then everything just flips. So it’s sort of not letting them back into the game, knowing they have the ability to do that and then not allowing it to happen.”



Jorgensen said while he was enjoying the continuity of selection in the back three, with Tom Wright and Harry Potter also getting an extended run, there were no concerns about the chopping-and-changing happening in most other positions. Related Article Australian rugby Tahs send SOS to club rugby playmaker amid ugly contract stoush Following on from Schmidt, Kiss has also been shuffling his cards every week, but Jorgensen said the team’s bonds were strong enough to prevent any lack of cohesion. “With all the changes happening, I don’t think it matters too much,” he said. “We’re such a tight group, so well-connected. No matter who comes in, in what jersey, we know they’re going to do a job for the team. And yeah, as I said, it actually really doesn’t matter.



“Everyone knows what each player brings and their skill set, knows how to work with them. That connection is there for whoever comes on the field.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Housing Minister Clare O’Neil says a temporary downturn in house prices should not alarm Australians after a report by CBA said a price recovery would not occur until 2027.

“It’s clear that house prices are softening around the country, and I really recognise that, you know, for many Australians, their house is their most important asset,” O’Neil told Seven’s Sunrise.

Minister for Housing Clare O’Neil. Dominic Lorrimer

“What that report also shows us is that house prices will start to grow again, and CBA says that will happen at some stage next year. The housing market in Australia is inherently cyclical. We see periods of really strong house price growths that are followed by a period of housing downturn. That’s happened now about four times in the last decade.”

O’Neil said downturns in property prices were always expected, and were an inevitable outcome of the government’s attempt to stabilise intergenerational inequality in the housing market after it made major changes to property taxes in its May budget.

“We’ve seen house prices in our country grow by 300 per cent since the year 2000. If that happens for another generation in our country, our nation is going to be unrecognisable to us in terms of equality and aspiration.”

Erin Piacenti died at the hospital from the stabbing injuries, according to the New York City Police Department. Piacenti was a vice president of business selection and conflicts at the bank, according to a LinkedIn profile. Times Square stabbing victim Erin Piacenti was a vice president at Bank of America. LinkedIn Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Pamela Cisneros, 49, first approached a 68-year-old Rhode Island tourist near West 41st Street and Seventh Avenue around 4.30pm (local time) with two knives, stabbing the man in the abdomen as he stood with his wife waiting to cross the street. He was hospitalised in stable condition. Cisneros then continued north on Seventh Avenue and stabbed Piacenti in the abdomen near 42nd Street, about 20 seconds after the first attack, Tisch said.



“We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague,” a Bank of America spokesperson said in a statement. “She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones.” Witnesses flagged down nearby officers, who confronted Cisneros between West 42nd and 43rd streets while she was still holding both knives. Officers spent about four minutes trying to persuade her to drop them. Loading “I’m not dropping anything. I would rather kill both of you,” Cisneros told the officers, according to Tisch. Officers used Tasers as Cisneros advanced toward them, but they were ineffective, Tisch said. Two officers then opened fire, striking her. Cisneros was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she died.



Related Article Updated

Crime Luigi Mangione admits killing insurance CEO, asks to void state murder trial Cisneros had no arrest history with the NYPD, though department records showed two previous encounters involving mental illness, in 2018 and 2019, Tisch said. Investigators have no reason to believe the attack was an act of terrorism, she said. Bank of America’s main Manhattan office is located right near the heart of Times Square at One Bryant Park. It’s also built out its presence in the city with a financial centre at nearby Two Bryant Park and space at the Grace Building. Major crime has declined in New York City for four straight years. Murders fell to a record low in the first half of this year, and major crime overall dropped 5.6 per cent. Still, felony assaults have risen for six consecutive years. World.title: The quality you should most wish for your children if you want to build family wealth
World.content:
MoneySavingParenting The quality you should most wish for your children if you want to build family wealth The Economist September 2, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you could bestow any quality on your children, which one would you pick? Great intelligence? Empathy for humanity? Much greater respect for their parents? The ability to pass a fridge without opening it? Deborah Cobb-Clark, an economist at the University of Sydney, has a different answer: an internal locus of control. Closely linked to the idea of agency, an internal locus is linked to self-control. One paper concluded that households with a greater sense of agency save more of their wealth. iStock The concept of a locus of control was developed in the 1960s by a psychologist with the tremendous name of Julian Rotter. It is closely linked to the idea of agency. People with an internal locus of control believe that they are able to shape the world around them; those with an external locus of control tend to think that luck, destiny or other people determine their fate. It turns out that being an internal is pretty useful. It motivates effort: one study by Ms Cobb-Clark and her co-authors looked at a cohort of newly unemployed people in Germany, and found that people with a more external locus of control searched less intensively for work than internals.



Why spend time hunting for jobs, after all, if outcomes are disconnected from actions? Externals also had lower reservation wages, the minimum pay they were prepared to accept for a job. Related Article Analysis

IVF Superbabies for the white and wealthy? The societal debate we need to have An internal locus is linked to self-control: another paper concluded that households with a greater sense of agency save more of their wealth. It helps turn intention into action, too, seeming to prompt people with entrepreneurial aspirations to actually take the leap and become a founder. Being an internal also seems to help your descendants. A paper by Warn Lekfuangfu of Universidad Carlos III de Madrid and her co-authors found that, other things being equal, the locus of control of expectant mothers is correlated with the effort they put into active parenting. Internals are more likely to think that time spent developing the skills of their sprogs will pay off. Externals are more likely to think: “Little Rodney is just a helpless plaything of the gods.”



The locus of control exists on a spectrum. Ms Cobb-Clark worries most about the small minority of people who never really develop a sense of their own agency at all. But many more routinely underestimate their power to exert control over their circumstances. In her pointedly titled book, You Can Just Do Things, Cate Hall cites research by Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake, then of Columbia University, showing that people misjudge how likely others are to respond to requests for help. In a series of experiments, the researchers asked participants how many strangers they would have to approach to complete a range of tasks, from filling out questionnaires to borrowing a mobile phone to make a call. The actual numbers were much lower than the estimates, not because people are unbelievably nice, but because it is awkward to reject a direct request for help.



In another experiment, Steven Levitt of the University of Chicago got people who were dithering over a big decision to toss a virtual coin to help them make their choice. A toss in favour of change made it much more likely that someone would go ahead and break with the status quo. Those who did reported being much happier than those who did not. That suggests many people who would benefit from change lack the sense of agency to seize control of their own destiny without a nudge. Related Article Opinion

Inheritance ‘I didn’t earn this’: The silent shame of inheriting family wealth Paridhi Jain Money contributor If an external locus of control is holding back individuals, it could be hindering organisations, too. A new paper, co-written by Feng Xu of the Harbin Institute of Technology, looks at adoption of artificial intelligence by manufacturing firms in Shenzhen. The researchers find that internals, who are more likely to see AI as a skill to master, are happier to share knowledge about their experiences of it. Externals, who are more likely to see the technology as a threat to their job security, are more prone to hiding information. What should managers do about this? They could test for locus of control in hiring processes: Andrej Karpathy, a quotable AI researcher, has said that as a trait, agency is both more powerful and scarcer than intelligence.



Compensation and promotion systems should reward achievement as a matter of course, but that link can be made more explicit. Cultural norms can also be set to prompt people towards taking action. “Ask forgiveness, not permission” is a mantra that can have some pretty ugly consequences if you have lots of high-agency people and no guardrails. But the idea behind it is sound. For the story behind the headlines, listen to The Morning Edition, with a new episode live every weekday from 5am.
