World.title: This Met Gala controversy may be the most tone-deaf move she’s made. What now for Anna Wintour?
World.content:
Listen LifestyleFashionStyle This Met Gala controversy may be the most tone-deaf move she’s made. What now for Anna Wintour? Samantha Selinger-Morris September 2, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Galliano – the fashion world’s theatrical ringmaster par excellence – has always enjoyed his contradictions, and champions. The one-time head designer of one of France’s most storied fashion houses, Christian Dior, Galliano once quipped: “Fashion is above all an art of change.” Yet for all his headline-grabbing and famously fantastical runway shows, he was perennially looking one way: backwards. Historicism was a hallmark of his craft. His 1997 haute couture debut for Dior, after all, celebrated the opulence of 1930s opium dens in Shanghai. Then came this week, when he announced on social media that he would be stepping back from the highly anticipated – and controversial – planned retrospective of his work, which was to be the centrepiece of next year’s Met Gala. John Galliano has taken the unprecedented step of withdrawing from a planned exhibition in his honour at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. What does this mean for Met Gala tsar Anna Wintour? The duo is pictured here in January 2025 in Paris. WWD via Getty Images



The one year Galliano has tried, for decades, to leave behind, has finally caught up with him, in a way it arguably hasn’t before. This was 2011, when a French court handed Galliano a total of €6000 ($13,565 now) in suspended fines, after he was found guilty of “public insults” based on origin, religion, race or ethnicity. This, after he was caught on film, hurling antisemitic rants at people in a Parisian bar. Among other moments of racism. Many of fashion’s most illustrious figures have tried to rehabilitate Galliano’s image over the years. Supermodel Kate Moss famously chose Galliano to design her wedding dress for her 2011 nuptials, telling Vogue she wanted “a classic Galliano, those chiffon Thirties kind. I’ve lived in his dresses for years, and they just make me feel so comfortable.” But it’s arguably Vogue’s global editorial director Anna Wintour who has acted as his rehabilitator-in-chief, reportedly smoothing the way for him to nab lucrative fashion roles, after Dior fired him.



Related Article Met Gala John Galliano withdraws from Met Museum exhibition following backlash And then, the Met Gala. “She’s wanted this for years, and she seemed to have gotten her way,” says Amy Odell, host of the Back Row with Amy Odell podcast, and author of Anna: The Biography, about Wintour. Speaking with host Samantha Selinger-Morris on The Morning Edition podcast, Amy Odell says the cancellation of Galliano’s retrospective is about far more than Galliano’s own troubled history, revealing that the wider fashion industry is now being reigned in after years of tolerating egregious behaviour. Click the player below to listen to the full episode, or read on for an edited extract of the conversation.



Selinger-Morris: Can you just remind listeners of what John Galliano actually did? It’s about 15 years ago now … you have called Galliano previously, “the industry’s most famous antisemite”, not without good reason. What did he say and do? And what does it say about the fashion industry that he was chosen then for this in the first place? Odell: There were two incidents, one of which was filmed and released by The Sun newspaper. In that video, Galliano was saying, “I love Hitler.” I believe that’s a direct quote. And, “Your forefathers would be gassed and dead,” something like that. And there was another incident at a café in Paris where he was drinking, and he was saying racist and antisemitic things to another couple. One of the people involved in that incident is named Philippe Virgitti, and he appears in the John Galliano documentary, John Galliano: High and Low, which Anna Wintour had a hand in pulling together. Condé Nast is a producer on that, and she sat for an interview for that. But that also seemed like a way for her to rehabilitate John Galliano’s career following these horrific incidents. Anyway, Virgitti spoke to Kevin Macdonald, who did that documentary, and he said he didn’t think John Galliano was sorry. He never apologised to him. And he testified at the hate crime trial in Paris. And he said at that trial that he didn’t think Galliano was racist. And he said in the documentary that he regretted saying that, basically, and that he does believe that Galliano is racist because he never apologised to him.



Galliano and Wintour at a party at Bergdorf Goodman (1998). Wintour nurtured a young Galliano’s career, helping him secure positions and Givenchy and Dior. Getty Images Selinger-Morris: So is this cancellation of John Galliano a rebuke of Anna Wintour? She’s always been his champion. And it has to be said that it was a very unusual choice to have him celebrated with a Metropolitan Museum retrospective because it’s only twice before in the history of the Met Gala that a living designer has been chosen to be the focus of a retrospective: that was Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017. So is this something of a public recognition that her taste doesn’t matter, or it’s off? Related Article Opinion

Met Gala The Amazon takeover of the Met Gala signals an apocalypse for fashion Damien Woolnough Fashion editor Odell: I think she’s made some extremely tone-deaf moves, particularly around the Met Gala, and this may be the biggest. And the Met could not risk the donors pulling funding and pulling donations. And it also – I don’t think it could risk the … how should I say this? – I mean, I don’t think it could risk that round of backlash. And I don’t know at this time, the story just broke really hours ago. But what was Vogue hearing aside from the stuff that we’ve been reading in the press? Were they hearing from celebrity publicists who were saying, “We can’t have our clients go”? How do you attend the event if it becomes the “Antisemitic Pro-Hitler Met Gala”? How do you attend as a celebrity? What good does that do you?



Listen to the full podcast episode in the player above. Hear the story behind the headlines on The Morning Edition podcast, every weekday from 5am on Apple, Spotify or your favourite podcast platform.

World.title: Police staffer facing nearly 40 charges including rape and kidnapping
World.content:
A police staffer is facing nearly 40 charges including rape, indecent assault, kidnapping and unlawful sexual connection, RNZ can reveal.

The person is one of 10 facing criminal charges following investigations by the National Integrity Unit (NIU).

The NIU was established in 2020, with then-Police Commissioner Mike Bush saying it had been created to "bolster police's capability in protecting against the risk of corruption and, where appropriate, investigating corruption within New Zealand Police".

This week, NZ Police confirmed under the Official Information Act that as of May, there were 10 active NIU prosecutions.

This includes one case involving a police staffer who is before the courts on 39 charges including three of rape, five of indecent assault, one of unlawful sexual connection and two charges of making an intimate visual recording.

* Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

The person is also accused of kidnapping, assault and threatening to kill/do grievous bodily harm. RNZ asked Police for comment on the charges including whether the staffer was a police officer, when the alleged offending occurred and where.

A police spokesperson said there were some suppression orders in place for the case.

"Providing any further information would likely identify the subject."

Another staffer faces seven charges of assaulting a woman as well as charges of blackmail and indecent assault.

The charges faced by the other staff include providing false particulars when they joined the police, accessing a computer for a dishonest purpose, firearms trafficking offences and obstructing/perverting the course of justice.

One person is also charged with drug-related offending.

Police Minister Mark Mitchell said in a statement to RNZ that on becoming minister, he made it clear that there was to be a "focus on standards and the application of standards which matter in a service like the police".

"It is inappropriate as minister to get involved with employment cases. These are operational matters for police, and I do not expect briefings on cases.

He said he expected Police to "take action" when employees did not meet the standards or values of police.

RNZ earlier obtained figures under the OIA which revealed that as of May, there were about 40 staff under investigation by the unit.

In the response, director of integrity and conduct Detective Superintendent Kylie Schaare said the NIU received information from a wide variety of sources, much of it often incomplete or unverified.

"Each piece of information is recorded as a "matter" and undergoes preliminary assessment. A matter may be progressed to a criminal investigation where it can be corroborated or expanded or, it may be closed as having no substance or insufficient merit."

From January 2020 to May 2026, 117 "matters" had progressed to investigations, with no further action taken by the NIU.

"This generally reflects cases where there is no evidence of criminal offending or there is insufficient evidence for a prosecution.

"However, this does not preclude action being taken by other police work groups, such as employment investigations or preventative interventions at a district level."

World.title: Christopher Luxon denies Pacific Islands Forum's clout weakened by five leaders' absence
World.content:
Winston Peters speaks at the Pacific Islands Forum Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The prime minister is brushing off threats to the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF)'s authority, talking up his confidence in turning the grouping into a centralising force for the region.

Christopher Luxon denies the forum's clout is weakened by five leaders' absence; by its inability to reach consensus on condemning China's recent ballistic missile test; or by a series of recent bilateral deals between Australia and Pacific neighbours.

He said a deal with the United States to build a port in the Cook Islands is not sending a message to Beijing, and is optimistic the forum could emulate and pair up with the ASEAN grouping in Southeast Asia.

It also comes ahead of an expected regional security announcement.

Departing Wednesday morning, Luxon is set to spend just under 36 hours on the ground in Palau for the Forum's leaders' meeting, where Foreign Minister Winston Peters has been since Sunday.

With New Zealand set to host the forum next year, he told reporters the trip was about elevating the forum.

"We get Pacific solutions to Pacific challenges ... the model in my head is very strongly around ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations], where I see ASEAN centrality speaking for Southeast Asia.

"PIF really is the body that should be the central way in which development partners come in and out through the PIF door and gate".

The official PIF Foreign Leaders' Meeting group photo in Fiji on 7 August 2026. Supplied / Alvaro Hoyos Ramos

New Zealand, Australia, and two Pacific Island nations - Marshall Islands and Palau, which both recognise Taiwan - last month were among dozens of countries that signed a joint statement by the US condemning China's ballistic missile test in early July.

But that came just days after a PIF Foreign Ministers meeting in Suva was unable to reach agreement on a similar statement despite the majority of members pushing for one.

Luxon denied that showed PIF being weakened as a mechanism for resolving region-wide difficulties.

"No, I think it's about strengthening it, though," Luxon said.

"We just want to see it go from strength to strength each and every year ... we just want perpetual, continual improvement and strengthening and deepening of PIF being the central organisation by which we deal with Pacific issues and challenges."

His comments echoed a position laid out on Sunday by Peters, who said it would be "defying gravity and logic if you said it wasn't a big problem", but that the "centrality of the Pacific Islands Forum is not going to be compromised because of this".

Foreign Minister Winston Peters in Palau for the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting. Pacific Islands Forum

He acknowledged the window for such a statement to have an impact had passed.

"The impact really is in the moment, and that's why you saw New Zealand make a very strong statement ... it'll be something we'll discuss in the leaders' retreat I'm sure, but again really what we're trying to do is make sure that we build more experience of working together, more unity," he said.

"At the time ... there was a number of leaders came out with strong statements. Yes, it would be ideal if PIF had a statement that could come together but frankly individual leaders have made those statements at that time, which I thought was important."

He said he would be open to a broader statement against testing in the Pacific but "I just wouldn't conflate those two issues ... we'll see what emerges".

Luxon also disagreed bilateral deals like the recent defence pact agreed between Australia and Fiji could undermine his centrality goals, saying "the reality is you can have strong bilateral relationships and also be part of multilateral forum as well".

His arrival in Koror - Palau's largest city and home to about 12,600 people, half the country's population - follows an announcement on Tuesday by Peters, Cook Islands PM Mark Brown and US Deputy State Secretary Christopher Landau of co-funding for a new "lifeline" port for the Cooks' Penrhyn atoll.

The US would provide US$50 million (NZ$84.8m) and New Zealand US$10m (NZ$17m) for the port, building on the Critical Minerals Framework the Cooks signed with the US in February.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters and Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown together in Palau announce a new upgrade of the port on Penrhyn atoll in the Cooks. RNZ / Teuila Fuatai

On Wednesday, Peters said the Penrhyn Port project was a strategic investment in the Cook Islands' future.

Speaking to Morning Report, the foreign minister defended the move.

"We're deciding to put a port in there because of fishing illegality, transnational crime and a host of other reasons why it is a very strategic place to have a port. And the Americans are putting some serious money into it."

"Talk's one thing, but we need action, and these people need our assistance and our help in terms of our collective interest.

"The blue continent is 1/3 of the world's surface, and there's not enough contributors to its long-term economic and social survival."

Peters said he was delighted that the US had "stepped up big time".

"This is seriously what we were hoping for because what we were saying to them [the US] was, look, it's not only our front yard, it's your front yard as well."

China on Monday sent a travel warning urging Chinese citizens to "exercise caution" in travelling to Palau that was quickly denounced by the US and Taiwan as an attempt to undermine.

Luxon denied the port deal was about sending a message to Beijing.

"No, no, I think it's just genuinely about the fact that you know we want to upgrade ... to advance that country as it moves from ... low income to mid income to ultimately to high income countries."

Peters, speaking to Morning Report, also dismissed the notion it could be a message to China, instead saying he was "delighted" the US had stepped up "big time" in the last few days.

Peters has long been an advocate for greater US presence in the Pacific, having made a speech on the issue in 2018, and referring to his meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington DC last year, the signed agreement announced on Tuesday was "seriously what we were hoping for" in that meeting.

In terms of managing China's reaction to the deal, Peters said the forum was18 countries, and "we are having a discussion amongst ourselves, and we do not prefer or like outsiders to tell us what to do".

Luxon suggested the deal could be a model for how countries might continue to use New Zealand as a conduit or mediator for foreign investment in the Pacific, including from the likes of Japan, South Korea and India.

"They all want to be engaged in the Pacific in some form or another, and often the easiest way to actually make sure any investment has an impact is actually to focus the management of that project and all those funds as well.

"We can be good custodians and good stewards of that money, and work with our partner - in this case, the Cook Islands - where the two of us know what needs to be achieved."

The Ocean Partnership Roundtable in Koror, Palau, on 30 August 2026. Ohanna Rabo Galo/TMC Palau

He brushed off, too, suggestions the absence of five - possibly six - member nations' leaders from the forum could pose a threat to the centrality he wanted for the forum, though the impact on showing regional unity is undeniable.

"The reality is ... [those absences are a] sideshow ... when you're in the bilaterals, when you're around the table, a lot of the conversation is about the 18 countries and the Pacific Island Forum, not about the dialogue partners that may be sitting outside it or partnering with it," Luxon said.

While the meeting itself was important, the "relationships that happen in any given part through any year is also important", Luxon said.

Peters, speaking to Morning Report, also brushed off the absences, saying the meeting had been the "highest level Pacific Islands Forum conference ever".

Luxon also told reporters a suggestion from the Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr the date for the main annual PIF leaders' meeting could be fixed on a specific date in future to help with scheduling and support attendance.

"Yeah it's not a bad idea, I hadn't thought about that ... I think there's some value in that," he said.

He also talked up the possibility of a future connection with the ASEAN forum.

World.title: Vanuatu tries to take island dispute with France to UN's top court
World.content:
Vanuatu is trying to bring a decades-old dispute with France over two uninhabited islands before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations' top court said on Tuesday.

The ICJ, also known as the World Court, will not immediately accept the case because France has not agreed to so-called compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ over its disputes with other states. Vanuatu's claim has been sent to Paris to see whether France agrees to let the court take it on, the ICJ said.

"No action will be taken in the proceedings unless and until France consents to the Court's jurisdiction in the case," the ICJ said in a press statement.

The French government did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment on the matter.

Vanuatu's case focuses on Matthew Island and Hunter Island, two volcanic islands in the South Pacific some 300 kilometres (190 miles) east of the French territory of New Caledonia and south-east of Vanuatu.

While the islands are small and no one lives there, sovereignty over them also determines who controls the territorial waters surrounding them, which impacts fishing rights and exploitation of seabed resources.

In 2025, France and Vanuatu agreed to new rounds of bilateral negotiations about the islands and the demarcation of the maritime boundaries between the territories after two earlier rounds of talks in 2018 and 2019. Earlier this year, Vanuatu said the new talks had reached an impasse and it would take its case to an international court.

In July this year, a Vanuatu government official called France's refusal to let go of the two islands as an attempt by a coloniser to assert power.

"Colonisers will always be colonisers, that's not something that's not something that comes as a surprise," Toney Tevi, who was the acting director of Vanuatu's Department of Ocean and Maritime Boundaries, said at the time.

The ICJ, the United Nations' highest court, deals with disputes between states and violations of international treaties. It often rules on disputes between countries about land and maritime boundaries.

World.title: One job ad, 1000 applicants: How do you stand out in a world of AI job hunters?
World.content:
Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

Jobhunters using AI to help with their applications are flooding listings, leaving some recruiters sifting through thousands of potential hires for each position advertised.

Squirrel chief executive David Cunningham said he had noticed a "tsunami" of job applications in response to advertised positions, most clearly generated using AI.

Squirrel chief executive David Cunningham. Supplied / Squirrel

"We've had numerous roles where we have received hundreds of applications, and in one case, over 1000. AI is good at 'match my current CV to this job, update accordingly, and write a cover letter'."

He said Squirrel had to use an AI tool to filter them and look for people who were a fit.

"We tend to look more at their work experience, the cover letters are a waste of time now really, because you can write a cover letter to make it sound like you're a perfect fit for any job.

"We tend to use AI tools to analyse the job versus the work experience."

Money correspondent Susan Edmunds Morning Report Download MP3 2m

He said Squirrel would also usually give preference to people who were based in New Zealand, and run screening interviews to come up with a short list.

University of Otago associate professor and human resources expert Paula O'Kane said she had had a similar experience reviewing applications. "This is the problem, how do you actually get through all of those cover letters that are written relatively similarly and what can you do to stand out from the crowd from a candidate's point of view … I really think that's what candidates have to think about."

She said people should try to keep their cover letters "short and sweet".

University of Otago associate professor and human resources expert Paula O'Kane. Supplied / University of Otago

"So what are the really key things that are important to the job, how do you bring your skills, your attributes and your personality into your cover letter?

"That's the thing that's going to make you stand out. For candidates there's still a role to use AI in that initial thinking about it and thinking how they write but they need to bring it back to themselves in the final iteration of their cover letter. I think that's what employers are going to look at more and more … bring your own voice into it and think about who you are and how you want to come across."

She said employers would be most worried about false negatives - people not making it through the screening process who would have been a good fit.

"Whereas when you have false positives you will probably catch them later. Yes, they're a waste of your time but you're going to move on to the next level of selection tools which are probably going to be more face-to-face and personal. So it's the people who miss that are the biggest risk rather than the people you put through that you shouldn't have put through."

Hayley Pickard, managing director of recruiter Fortitude Group, said she saw the problem particularly when advertising for technical and engineering positions.

"AI has made it incredibly easy for someone to produce a polished CV and cover letter and apply for a large number of vacancies very quickly. The problem is that it hasn't necessarily improved the relevance or quality of those applications. It has simply removed much of the effort that previously went into submitting one," she said.

"I regularly receive applications that use the exact terminology from the job  but provide no real evidence behind it. Skills and responsibilities mentioned in the advert suddenly appear in the application, but the person provides no specific examples of when, where or how they gained that experience.

"When I ask the applicant for further details, it can become clear that the polished wording has overstated their actual level of experience - or, at the very least, made it extremely difficult to distinguish what the candidate genuinely knows from what AI has added.

"I don't think the answer is for applicants to avoid AI completely. It can be very useful for improving spelling, structure and presentation, particularly for people who don't naturally find writing easy or whose first language isn't English. However, it should be used as an editing tool, not as a substitute for the applicant's own experience, judgment or voice."

Recruiter Hayley Pickard says AI should be used as an editing tool when applying for jobs. 123rf

She said high application volumes created screening fatigue for recruiters. "When an employer is working through dozens or hundreds of similar-looking applications, they are not necessarily looking for the most beautifully written one. They are trying to quickly establish: Can this person do the job? Are they genuinely interested? Can I trust what they have told me?

"Ironically, a straightforward, specific and recognisably human application can now stand out more than an extremely polished one. Applicants shouldn't try to compete with AI-generated applications by producing even more generic AI content. They should compete through relevance, evidence and authenticity."

She said employers also had to be careful not to confuse polished writing with a strong application. "A capable person may not have the strongest writing skills, while someone with little relevant experience can now produce an impressive-looking application in seconds. Screening therefore needs to focus increasingly on verifiable examples and well-targeted follow-up questions."

Pickard's tips for jobhunters in an AI world

Apply selectively. Ten carefully chosen and genuinely relevant applications are likely to be more effective than 100 generic ones.

Replace broad claims with specific evidence. Rather than simply claiming to have a skill, explain where it was used, what the person was personally responsible for and what they achieved.

Include context. Employers need to understand what the person personally did, how independently they worked and what the outcome was - not just read a list of industry terms.

Write a short, genuine introduction explaining why that particular opportunity interests them. It doesn't need to be a long or overly formal cover letter.

Follow the application instructions. If an advert asks for particular information or a recruiter sends screening questions, answer them fully rather than sending a generic response.

Check every AI-generated statement for accuracy. If the candidate couldn't comfortably explain or defend it in an interview, it shouldn't be in the application.

Keep the language natural. Excessively formal phrases, repeated buzzwords and generic statements about being "passionate", "dynamic" or "results-driven" don't help without evidence.

Make sure the CV and cover letter agree with each other. AI-generated applications sometimes introduce skills, dates or responsibilities that aren't supported by the person's actual employment history.

Respond when contacted. A relevant, prompt and thoughtful reply to a recruiter's questions can make someone stand out immediately.
