Tech.title: No ‘DMV for AI’: US Pushes Against AI Regulations at Global Forum
Tech.content:
The US government’s message at the G20 Innovation Ministerial is clear: Nothing should slow down AI innovation – not regulation, not power shortages, not even serious safety concerns.

The forum, hosted this week in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, brings together government leaders from the G20 countries, including India, China, Russia and many European nations, to discuss technological advancements and subsequent policy challenges. The theme this year is, unsurprisingly, generative AI.

Michael Kratsios, director of the Trump administration’s Office of Science and Technology Policy, said in his opening remarks that “slow policy adaptation makes it harder to capture the full benefits of innovation.”

“Often, in the US and elsewhere, regulations built for a different technological era prove poor fits for rapidly evolving, generally applicable inventions, creating uncertainty for developers and policymakers alike,” Kratsios said. “That leaves development efforts abandoned, growth unrealized and nations falling behind, as innovation continues elsewhere.”

The US is pushing for a framework it’s calling the Carolina Principles, a “pro-innovation framework” that aims to bolster AI research, form pathways to commercialization and create industry-led standards for emerging technologies. Global leaders will hear from the biggest names in AI throughout their discussions.

At the end of the week, any policy agreements reached will feed into the broader agreement that the global community signs at the G20 Leaders Summit in Miami this December.

AI regulation is an increasingly important issue as AI models become more capable and autonomous. This week’s summit offers insight into how the global community is approaching the issue – and where it is drawing lines in the sand for Big Tech.

Trump AI adviser: No ‘DMV for AI’

It would be a “disaster” if the US adopted a version of the “FDA for AI,” said David Sacks, the Trump administration’s former AI czar and co-chair of the president’s council on science and technology, on Tuesday. “Any regulatory agency that has to approve AI product releases will become like a DMV for AI, where new models get stuck in a long queue waiting for approval.”

AI is “just too dynamic and fast-moving for that type of approach,” Sacks said in a virtual appearance. “And I don’t think we want to hamstring our innovation that way.”

Sacks argued against the idea of a regulatory agency for AI, one that would be similar to how the Food and Drug Administration authorizes new medicines or how the Federal Aviation Administration oversees airlines.

Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

It’s not the first time the idea of an AI-specific regulatory agency has been floated in the tech policy community, but Sacks’s remarks seem to take a direct swing at the only major AI company not in attendance at the event: Anthropic. Its CEO, Dario Amodei, advocated for such a government review process in a recent essay.

“Frontier AI models, like airplanes, should be required to go through technical testing and auditing, and their release should be blocked or reversed as a threat to public safety if they do not meet high standards of safety,” Amodei wrote. He added that because AI is being used in research, existing agencies like the FDA will have more proposals to evaluate, further taxing the regulators.

Sacks argued that there is already sufficient regulation around AI from existing laws, and existing regulatory agencies could deal with any AI threats.

This is far from the first time Anthropic and the US government have been at odds. After a deal between the Pentagon and Anthropic blew up, the AI company was declared a supply chain risk, though a judge blocked that order. Later, when Anthropic released its Fable 5 model, the US government ordered the company to prevent any foreign nationals from using it. To comply, Anthropic pulled the model, rereleasing it only after receiving an unofficial green light from the Trump administration.

Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg speak on AI

Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, which operates xAI, supported a hands-off regulatory approach in a virtual speech at the G20 Innovation Ministerial.

“What most countries tend to do is they tend to provide too much support to the large existing trees in the forest and not enough to the smallest saplings,” Musk said on Tuesday, comparing big corporations and startups to a forest. Musk said this should be flipped, and governments should adopt a philosophy where new inventions are “default legal as opposed to default illegal.”

Notably, Musk is CEO of one of the biggest tech companies in the world and the world’s richest person, aided by SpaceX’s recent IPO, which briefly made him the world’s first trillionaire. His businesses received $38 billion in government funding last year, according to a February report from The Washington Post.

But we’ve already seen how the US government is either unable or unwilling to address the worst, most abusive consequences of AI technology. When millions of AI-generated images of child sex abuse material flooded X months ago, US regulatory agencies did nothing to stop it.

By contrast, the European Union opened an investigation into X, countries like Malaysia and Indonesia banned the app, and many global leaders spoke out against the Musk-owned AI tool and platform.

Mark Zuckerberg, also speaking virtually, talked about how publicly available AI models help people create things, like learning to use new software or run small businesses.

“The ability to start new things is going to be immense, and that’s going to lead to this very dynamic period,” Zuckerberg said on Tuesday. “So I think it leads to wanting to have policies that make it easy to create things [and] easy to evolve and change the systems that we have today.”

The idea is that if AI is publicly available, like through an open-weights AI model, more people can use it. Tech policies that support open source AI fuel that creation. Zuckerberg’s open source approach to AI is unique in the industry, with Meta recently promising to publicly release its newest models. This came after it was rumored that the Trump administration was considering a ban on open-source models; many tech leaders said that would be harmful to global AI innovation and cybersecurity.

“Having the technology diffused … you can set up a system of checks and balances, rather than restricting it to only being available to a small number of people or companies or governments,” Zuckerberg said. (Zuckerberg, notably, would be one of the people with complete access.)

Over the past year, the Trump administration has flipped its previous hands-off approach to regulating AI. It seems to want to be involved, particularly as its tech and government leaders see generative AI technology as simultaneously a threat and a benefit to national security and cybersecurity.

Policy frameworks that emerge from forums like the G20 Innovation Ministerial could dramatically shape the limits on the power that Big Tech and AI companies have globally.

Tech.title: Apple TV and Peacock Bundle Prices Have Changed, Too
Tech.content:
Sorry to interrupt your Ted Lasso streak, but you’ll need to check your subscriptions to see if you have one of the Apple TV-Peacock bundles, because the streamer’s price hike affected those, too.

On Aug. 28, Apple announced it changed the pricing for its TV streaming service in the US, increasing rates on its monthly and annual plans, as well as on Apple One. Those changes have also affected the Apple TV bundles that package the platform with Peacock, which are available to purchase through both services. If you have Peacock Premium (with ads) and Apple TV, the bundle price is now $18 a month, while the Peacock Premium Plus (without ads) with Apple TV bundle has increased to $23 per month.

The bump reflects a $3 hike, as these packages were initially priced at $15 and $20 per month when they launched in October 2025. The bright side? If you have one of Xfinity’s StreamSaver bundles that includes Apple TV, there’s no price increase. Of the eight StreamSaver packages, five include Apple TV, with monthly costs ranging from $18 to $35.

Tech.title: Android’s New Features Have Me Excited, Especially This One for Motion Sickness
Tech.content:
Google on Tuesday rolled out its latest batch of Android updates, with a focus on practical improvements rather than blatantly AI-heavy features.

The new Android phone capabilities will help you keep tabs on your belongings, let you contribute to shared notes within a chat, identify objects around you with your camera and allow you to customize chat themes in Google Messages. A motion sickness feature can also help mitigate the challenges of staring at your screen in a moving vehicle — something I welcome with open arms.

The updates come weeks after Google launched its latest Pixel lineup, including the Pixel 11, 11 Pro and 11 Pro Fold. The phones run Android 17 and come with Gemini Intelligence, a suite of AI features designed to handle mundane tasks such as adding events to your calendar and sharing flight details with loved ones.

Many of those features felt helpful while I tested the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Rambler, for example, removes filler words and corrects errors as you speak, while Live Translate for media dubs YouTube videos in real time.

This month’s Android update incorporates Gemini into several refreshed capabilities, but emphasizes practical uses, such as remembering where you put your passport or quickly compiling a list with friends. A new accessibility feature also builds on other tools designed to make Android more useful for more people.

Here’s what’s landing on Android devices this month.

Track your important items

Find Hub can be used to keep tabs on your important items that don’t have a tracker tag on them. Google

Do you have a tendency to forget where you put items such as your passport or a spare key? You can now ask Gemini to remember where you placed those objects, and it’ll save their locations in Find Hub, Google’s tracking app for people, phones and accessories.

Just say something like, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer.” You can add a photo, too. When it’s time to track down that item, ask Gemini where it is or check your remembered items tab in Find Hub. This can be handy for smaller or everyday items you don’t put a tracker tag on.

This feature is available on devices running Android 16 and up, where Gemini and Find Hub are supported.

Motion Assist

Motion Assist on Android displays moving dots on a phone’s screen to counter the motion of a vehicle. Google

As someone who struggles with car sickness, one of my favorite features that launched on the iPhone with iOS 18 was Vehicle Motion Cues. It’s a layer of moving dots that appears across your screen and changes with the motion of a vehicle. Apple says the feature helps reduce the sensory conflict between what you see and what you feel, making it easier to look at your screen while in a car. I’ve definitely noticed the difference when Vehicle Motion Cues is on; I can scroll or read on my iPhone for longer without feeling nauseous.

At last, a similar feature is coming to Android. Called Motion Assist, this adds a bubble overlay to your phone’s screen that moves as the vehicle does. As Google put it in a blog post, “It’s designed to help bridge the gap between what your eyes see and the movement of your ride.”

You can adjust the shape, color and opacity of the bubbles. You can also set Motion Assist to turn on automatically when you’re in a moving vehicle, and add it to Quick Settings for easy access. Motion Assist is available on phones running Android 17.

Create and edit shared notes in a chat

You can now share and edit Google Keep notes within a chat. Google

Now, you can share and update a Google Keep note or list with friends within a chat — no need to switch apps to make an edit. That way, if you’re planning a trip or making a grocery list, it’s easier for everyone to contribute right within Google Messages.

Tap the plus (+) icon in Google Messages to add Google Keep to the conversation.

Chat themes in Google Messages

You can choose a custom background photo for your group chats. Google

Speaking of Google Messages updates, you can now customize each chat with different backgrounds and colors. You can choose a wallpaper or your own photo for the background, and the text bubbles will automatically match that theme — or you can choose a different hue altogether.

Guided Vision

Guided Vision can help someone pinpoint where an object is using their phone’s camera and Gemini Live. Google

By sharing your camera in Gemini Live, you can get descriptions of your surroundings. Gemini Live is part of the Gemini app, and lets you have a more in-depth, back-and-forth conversation with Google’s AI.

The new capability, called Guided Vision, can assist with reading fine print on a food label or ordering from a menu in a dimly lit restaurant. It can also help you identify something on your shelf or locate objects around the house. If an object isn’t aligned with the camera, voice feedback will help you reframe to better identify it. This feature can be especially helpful for people who are blind or have low vision. But, as is true with all accessibility features, anyone can benefit.

This is Google’s latest visual intelligence feature catered toward accessibility, following apps such as Lookout, which similarly helps people who are blind or low-vision identify objects and read documents, and which uses AI to generate detailed image descriptions. Guided Frame, which launched on the Pixel 7, is also designed to make it easier for people who are blind or low-vision to frame shots by using audio and haptic cues.

On the iPhone, features such as Live Recognition and Magnifier also use the camera to respectively describe someone’s surroundings and show information using large, high-contrast text.

On Android, you can launch Guided Vision from the TalkBack menu, or add it to your Accessibility shortcuts. The capability is coming soon to phones running Android 9 and up, in countries where Gemini is available.

Tech.title: Roku Pro TV Now One of Cheapest OLEDs Starting at $999
Tech.content:
Roku has launched a significant upgrade to its Pro television lineup, the first Roku Pro OLEDs. The best bit? They’re some of the most affordable OLED TVs on the market with prices starting at $999.

Also read: Best Roku TV for 2026

The Roku Pro Series OLED TV and step-up Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV replace the existing Pro TV and are available exclusively on Amazon. Unlike the existing Pro, which uses LCD, the new OLED should boost picture quality with infinite contrast and better off-angle viewing.

The standard 4K Roku Pro Series TV features a 120Hz panel with support for Dolby Vision and Roku’s Smart Picture Max. The TV also includes an Automatic Game Mode with FreeSync Premium and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) .

Meanwhile, the Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV upgrades include a brighter picture, a wider range of colors, a 144Hz variable refresh rate and an anti-reflective filter.

Both TVs include a ultra-thin metal bezel but, as a result, can no longer include the great Soundstage audio port from the old Pro. Roku’s Chris Larson told CNET the feature would make the TV too thick, which is a blow to people who want better sound quality built in.

Like the existing Roku TVs, the Pro includes usability features like an adjustable tool-free stand and velcro cable straps. The TVs come with a push-to-talk voice remote with backlit buttons and you can pair your Bluetooth headphones directly with the TV.

The Roku Pro (2025) was the company’s best TV yet, and the promise of OLED should make the new TVs better than ever. The price is also ultra-competitive, and these could be the late 2026 TVs to beat for their combination of price and picture performance. Given the upgrades of the LX — brighter panel and anti-reflective coating — it appears to be the one to choose of the two.

The Roku Pro Series OLED is now available in 55-inch and 65-inch sizes starting at $999. The Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV will be available starting in October 2026 for $1,299.

Tech.title: Sony’s New ULT Tower Max Wireless Party Speaker Delivered Massive Sound I Felt in My Chest
Tech.content:
Last year, Sony introduced new wireless Bluetooth speakers and an ULT Wear headphone as part of its new ULT Power Sound series of audio products. The floor-standing ULT Tower 9 speaker was part of the launch, but now Sony has expanded its party speaker offerings with three new ULT Tower models: the ULT Tower Max ($1,500), ULT Tower 7 ($650) and ULT Tower 5 ($650), with the two larger models featuring integrated wheels.

Ahead of the speakers’ launch, I had a chance to listen to all three speakers and came away impressed. They play loud and really pound out the bass while still offering good clarity and detail. Needless to say, the Tower Max, which weighs in at a massive 121 pounds, offers the most visceral listening experience, with bass that will shake you. That new flagship model has three woofers (two front-facing and one rear-facing) and four tweeters, along with midrange drivers. The drivers across the new speakers have been redesigned to take advantage of the new, larger speaker cabinets to push more air and sound, so the speakers live up to their ULT Power Sound billing.



All three new speakers have built-in handles (ULT Tower 5 shown here), though only the larger Tower ULT Max and Tower ULT 7 have wheels. David Carnoy/CNET

Amateur or professional DJs can mix and match the speakers, linking them together using a Party Chain mode to augment the sound, or create a stereo pair with two of the same model. They can also be used for karaoke or as a PA system (Sony’s ULT MIC two-pack is available for $118), and have XLR, RCA and USB-C connectivity. Sadly, the new models aren’t backward compatible with the ULT Tower 9 and ULT Tower 10 via Party Connect, which seems a little weird.

Sony has gone with a more industrial design that’s somewhat reminiscent of professional DJ speakers (but with rounded corners). The company says the lighting element has been improved with new lighting modes that make it “easier to switch the mood for different settings.” I also liked how when you raise or lower the volume, the lighting trail around the edge of the speaker retracts or extends to reflect the volume level as you adjust it.

The speakers have four sound modes that can be toggled on using the ULT button on the front of the speaker or the Sony Sound Connect app for iOS or Android. The modes include ULT1 (enhances deep bass), ULT2 (greater power boost), Flat (a neutral “true-to-source” setting) and Live (“spacious feel” of a live performance while preserving vocal clarity). Additionally, there are EQ settings to fiddle around with.

The speakers can be stood up vertically or laid down horizontally and have a sound calibration mode that automatically adjusts the sound to the room or environment the speaker is in. And in a first for Sony party speakers, the smaller ULT Tower 7 (50 pounds) and ULT Tower 5 (29 pounds) are IPX4 splash-proof (when stood up vertically). All three speakers have built-in handles.

The speakers have strong connectivity options. David Carnoy/CNET

While the ULT Tower Max is portable, it has to be plugged in and doesn’t have a built-in rechargeable battery. However, the ULT Tower 7 and ULT Tower 5 can be used untethered, with up to 30 hours of battery life for the Tower 7 and 20 hours for the Tower 5 at moderate volume levels. If you really crank the sound, the battery life ratings drop considerably.

After hearing all three speakers in action, I’d say the ULT Tower 7 will hit the sweet spot for a lot of folks looking for a party speaker that can deliver big, powerful sound while not breaking the bank with its $650 list price. That said, if you can afford two ULT Tower 7 speakers, they produce impressive sound as a stereo pair.

The ULT Tower Max is certainly more powerful and is a beast of a speaker, but it may be overkill unless you’re trying to power a pretty big party. Meanwhile, the more compact Tower ULT 5 would be a good speaker for a high school sports team looking to belt out music during its pregame warmups. It plays pretty loud but is more manageable to carry around at just under 30 pounds.

Tech.title: Google Is Showing Your Home to Anyone Who Looks. Here’s the Free Way to Remove It
Tech.content:
Google Street View photography is detailed enough to show house numbers, parked vehicles and the layout of a front yard, all publicly accessible to anyone who knows the address. Google Maps

Typing your home address into Google Maps and switching to Street View surfaces a level of visual detail most people have never paused to think about: the exact placement of windows and doors, the vehicles in the driveway, the security camera on the porch, the gap in the hedge that leads to the backyard. All of it is publicly accessible to anyone with an internet connection and 30 seconds to spare. Google has offered a way to remove that imagery through a blur request since Street View launched, but the option is buried far enough in the interface that most homeowners have never found it. Here’s where it is and how to use it.

Here’s exactly where it is and how the process works. It’s a simple way to take back control of your home’s online footprint and ensure that your driveway and windows aren’t part of a global database.

Here’s how to reduce how much of your home is visible online.

For more, check out essential Google Maps tips for travel.

Don’t miss any of our unbiased tech content and lab-based reviews. Add CNET as a preferred Google source.

How to blur your home on Google Maps

You’ll need to do this on your computer since the blurring feature isn’t available in the Google Maps application on iOS or Android. It is accessible through the web browser on your mobile device, but it’s rather difficult to use, so your best option is a trusted web browser on your Mac or PC.

At maps.google.com, enter your home address in the search bar at the top-right, hit return, then click the photo of your home that appears.

Click on the photo of your home, right above your address, on the top-left part of the page. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Next, you’ll see the Street View of your location. Click Report a Problem at the bottom-right. The text is super tiny, but it’s there.

This is the Street View of your location. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Now, it’s up to you to choose what you want Google to blur. Using your mouse, adjust the view of the image so that your home and anything else you want to blur are all contained within the red and black box. Use your cursor to move around and the plus and minus buttons to zoom in and out, respectively.

If you want to blur more than what’s in the red and black box, use the plus button to zoom in. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Once you’re finished adjusting the image, choose what you’re requesting to blur underneath:

A face

Your home

Car/license plate

A different object

You’ll be asked to provide a bit more detail about what you want blurred in case the image is busy with cars, people and other objects.

Also, be completely sure that what you select is exactly what you want blurred. Google cautions that once you blur something on Street View, it’s blurred permanently.

Finally, enter your email (this is required), verify the captcha (if needed), and click Submit.

You are required to provide additional information about what you want to blur, so be thorough. Screenshot by Nelson Aguilar/CNET

You should then receive an email from Google that says it’ll review your report and get back to you once the request is either denied or approved. You may receive more emails from Google asking for more information regarding your request. Google doesn’t offer any information on how long your request will take to process, so just keep an eye out for any further emails.

For more, take an inside look at how Google built Immersive View for Maps.
